abstract: We use constrained optimization to select operating parameters for two circuits: a simple 3-transistor square root circuit, and an analog VLSI artificial cochlea. This automated method uses computer controlled mea(cid:173) surement and test equipment to choose chip parameters which minimize the difference between the actual circuit's behavior and a specified goal behavior. Choosing the proper circuit parameters is important to com(cid:173) pensate for manufacturing deviations or adjust circuit performance within a certain range. As biologically-motivated analog VLSI circuits become increasingly complex, implying more parameters, setting these parameters by hand will become more cumbersome. Thus an automated parameter setting method can be of great value [Fleischer 90]. Automated parameter setting is an integral part of a goal-based engineering design methodology in which circuits are constructed with parameters enabling a wide range of behaviors, and are then "tuned" to the desired behaviors automatically.

paragraphs: This paper uses constrained optimization to tune the operating parameters of analog circuits automatically. The authors apply the method to a three-transistor square-root circuit and an analog VLSI artificial cochlea. The task is to make the behavior of a physical chip match a specified goal as closely as possible.

Computer-controlled measurement and test equipment measures the circuit’s behavior while the optimization method chooses its parameters. The objective is to reduce the difference between actual and desired behavior. This addresses two practical needs identified in the paper: compensating for manufacturing deviations and adjusting performance within the circuit’s available operating range.

The broader motivation is that increasingly complex biologically inspired circuits expose more parameters, making manual adjustment cumbersome. The work treats tuning as an integral part of engineering design: construct a circuit with enough adjustable behavior, then automatically select settings for a particular goal. Its significance lies in connecting physical measurements to parameter selection, so that desired behavior guides the tuning of the actual device.
summary.tldr: Constrained optimization and computer-controlled measurements automatically tune analog circuits toward specified behavior.

title: Constrained Optimization Applied to the Parameter Setting Problem for Analog Circuits

abstract: Large VC-dimension classifiers can learn difficult tasks, but are usually impractical because they generalize well only if they are trained with huge quantities of data. In this paper we show that even high-order polynomial classifiers in high dimensional spaces can be trained with a small amount of training data and yet generalize better than classifiers with a smaller VC-dimension. This is achieved with a maximum margin algorithm (the Generalized Portrait). The technique is applicable to a wide variety of classifiers, including Perceptrons, polynomial classifiers (sigma-pi unit net(cid:173) works) and Radial Basis Functions. The effective number of parameters is adjusted automatically by the training algorithm to match the complexity of the problem. It is shown to equal the number of those training patterns which are closest patterns to the decision boundary (supporting patterns). Bounds on the generalization error and the speed of convergence of the al(cid:173) gorithm are given. Experimental results on handwritten digit recognition demonstrate good generalization compared to other algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension between expressive classifiers and limited training data. A classifier with high VC dimension can represent difficult distinctions, but its flexibility can make generalization demanding. The authors show how high-order polynomial classifiers in high-dimensional spaces can generalize well from small training sets through a particular choice of training algorithm.

Their method uses the maximum margin Generalized Portrait algorithm. It automatically adjusts the effective number of parameters to the problem's complexity. The abstract identifies this effective count with the number of supporting training patterns closest to the decision boundary. This ties the learned classifier's effective complexity to particular examples that constrain its boundary.

The approach applies to perceptrons, polynomial classifiers, and radial basis functions. The paper supplies bounds on generalization error and convergence speed, alongside handwritten digit recognition experiments reporting good generalization compared with other algorithms. The central implication is that a large available function class need not determine the effective complexity of the classifier produced by training.
summary.tldr: Maximum margin training automatically controls effective classifier complexity, allowing highly expressive models to generalize from limited data.

title: Automatic Capacity Tuning of Very Large VC-Dimension Classifiers

abstract: We describe the reinforcement learning problem, motivate algo(cid:173) rithms which seek an approximation to the Q function, and present new convergence results for two such algorithms. 1 INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND Imagine an agent acting in some environment. At time t, the environment is in some state Xt chosen from a finite set of states. The agent perceives Xt, and is allowed to choose an action at from some finite set of actions. The environment then changes state, so that at time (t + 1) it is in a new state Xt+1 chosen from a probability distribution which depends only on Xt and at. Meanwhile, the agent experiences a real-valued cost Ct, chosen from a distribution which also depends only on Xt and at and which has finite mean and variance. Such an environment is called a Markov decision process, or MDP. The reinforce(cid:173) ment learning problem is to control an MDP to minimize the expected discounted cost Lt ,tCt for some discount factor, E [0,1]. Define the function Q so that Q(x, a) is the cost for being in state x at time 0, choosing action a, and behaving optimally from then on. If we can discover Q, we have solved the problem: at each step, we may simply choose at to minimize Q(xt, at). For more information about MDPs, see (Watkins, 1989, Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis, 1989). We may distinguish two classes of problems, online and offline. In the offline prob(cid:173) lem, we have a full model of the MDP: given a state and an action, we can describe the distributions of the cost and the next state. We will be concerned with the online problem, in which our knowledge of the MDP is limited to what we can dis(cid:173) cover by interacting with it. To solve an online problem, we may approximate the transition and cost functions, then proceed as for an offline problem (the indirect approach); or we may try to learn the Q function without the intermediate step (the direct approach). Either approach may work better for any given problem: the Stable Fitted Reinforcement Learning

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning through approximations to the Q function. In its cost-based formulation, Q describes the expected discounted cost of choosing an action in a state and behaving optimally afterward. Knowing this function makes action selection straightforward: choose the action with the smallest Q value.

The setting is a Markov decision process with finite state and action sets. The next state and immediate cost depend on the current state and chosen action, and costs have finite mean and variance. The paper focuses on online learning, where the agent obtains knowledge by interacting with the environment instead of starting with its complete model.

The authors motivate Q-approximation algorithms and present new convergence results for two of them. These results address the mathematical behavior of learning procedures that use fitted approximations. The supplied discussion also distinguishes learning an environment model first from learning Q directly, placing the convergence contribution within the broader problem of deriving effective decisions from interaction.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes convergence results for two reinforcement-learning algorithms that approximate the Q function.

title: Stable Fitted Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A classifier is called consistent with respect to a given set of class(cid:173) labeled points if it correctly classifies the set. We consider classi(cid:173) fiers defined by unions of local separators and propose algorithms for consistent classifier reduction. The expected complexities of the proposed algorithms are derived along with the expected classifier sizes. In particular, the proposed approach yields a consistent re(cid:173) duction of the nearest neighbor classifier, which performs "firm" classification, assigning each new object to a class, regardless of the data structure. The proposed reduction method suggests a notion of "soft" classification, allowing for indecision with respect to objects which are insufficiently or ambiguously supported by the data. The performances of the proposed classifiers in predict(cid:173) ing stock behavior are compared to that achieved by the nearest neighbor method.

We consider classi(cid:173) fiers defined by unions of local separators and propose algorithms for consistent classifier reduction. The expected complexities of the proposed algorithms are derived along with the expected classifier sizes. In particular, the proposed approach yields a consistent re(cid:173) duction of the nearest neighbor classifier, which performs "firm" classification, assigning each new object to a class, regardless of the data structure. The proposed reduction method suggests a notion of "soft" classification, allowing for indecision with respect to objects which are insufficiently or ambiguously supported by the data. The performances of the proposed classifiers in predict(cid:173) ing stock behavior are compared to that achieved by the nearest neighbor method.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to simplify a classifier while preserving correct classification of a supplied labeled dataset. It calls this property consistency. The classifiers are formed from unions of local separators, and the proposed algorithms reduce their representation without giving up agreement with the labeled points used to define the requirement.

The authors derive expected computational complexities and expected classifier sizes. Their approach includes a consistent reduction of nearest-neighbor classification. This provides a way to examine both the cost of constructing a reduced classifier and the size of the resulting representation, alongside the requirement that the original labeled examples remain correctly classified.

The reduction also motivates a distinction between firm and soft decisions. Firm classification always assigns a class, whereas soft classification permits indecision when the data provide insufficient or ambiguous support. The authors compare these classifiers with nearest neighbors on stock-behavior prediction. The conceptual contribution is to connect classifier reduction with an explicit option to withhold a decision when the surrounding evidence does not support a clear assignment.
summary.tldr: Classifier reduction preserves training-set consistency and motivates a soft classification rule that can abstain when evidence is weak or ambiguous.

title: Consistent Classification, Firm and Soft

abstract: We describe an iterative algorithm for building vector machines used in classification tasks. The algorithm builds on ideas from support vector machines, boosting, and generalized additive models. The algorithm can be used with various continuously differential functions that bound the discrete (0-1) classification loss and is very simple to implement. We test the proposed algorithm with two different loss functions on synthetic and natural data. We also describe a norm-penalized version of the algorithm for the exponential loss function used in AdaBoost. The performance of the algorithm on natural data is comparable to support vector machines while typically its running time is shorter than of SVM.

paragraphs: This paper introduces an iterative algorithm for building classifiers called vector machines. It draws together ideas from support vector machines, boosting, and generalized additive models. The goal is a practical classification procedure, and the authors describe the resulting algorithm as simple to implement.

The method can work with several continuously differentiable functions that bound the discrete classification loss, which counts incorrect predictions. These smooth functions provide alternatives to directly optimizing a loss that changes abruptly when a prediction crosses the decision boundary. The paper also presents a norm-penalized version for the exponential loss used in AdaBoost, adding a penalty tied to the size of the learned model.

The authors test two loss functions on synthetic and natural data. On the natural datasets, classification performance is comparable to support vector machines, while runtime is typically shorter. The finding is therefore a reported practical tradeoff: the iterative approach can retain comparable predictive performance in those experiments while often reducing the time needed to obtain it.
summary.tldr: An iterative vector-machine algorithm achieves performance comparable to SVMs on natural data while typically running faster.

title: Leveraged Vector Machines

abstract: We present a general framework for discriminative estimation based on the maximum entropy principle and its extensions. All calcula(cid:173) tions involve distributions over structures and/or parameters rather than specific settings and reduce to relative entropy projections. This holds even when the data is not separable within the chosen parametric class, in the context of anomaly detection rather than classification, or when the labels in the training set are uncertain or incomplete. Support vector machines are naturally subsumed un(cid:173) der this class and we provide several extensions. We are also able to estimate exactly and efficiently discriminative distributions over tree structures of class-conditional models within this framework. Preliminary experimental results are indicative of the potential in these techniques.

paragraphs: This paper presents a general framework for learning to discriminate using the maximum entropy principle and related extensions. Its calculations work with distributions over model parameters or structures, rather than selecting only one setting. The estimation problems are expressed as relative entropy projections, giving the framework a common mathematical basis.

The same formulation covers several complications: examples that cannot be separated within the selected model class, anomaly detection, and training labels that are uncertain or incomplete. Support vector machines arise naturally within the framework, and the authors develop extensions. This connects an established classification approach to a broader treatment of distributions and uncertainty.

The authors also show that discriminative distributions over tree structures for class-conditional models can be estimated exactly and efficiently. That is a specific computational result within the broader framework. Experimental findings are described as preliminary and suggestive of potential. The paper therefore combines a unifying formulation and exact structural estimation results with early empirical evidence, rather than presenting the experiments as a definitive demonstration of general superiority.
summary.tldr: Maximum entropy discrimination unifies distribution-based discriminative learning, includes SVMs, and supports uncertain labels and efficient estimation over tree structures.

title: Maximum Entropy Discrimination

abstract: Ascribing computational principles to neural feedback circuits is an important problem in theoretical neuroscience. We study symmetric threshold-linear networks and derive stability results that go beyond the insights that can be gained from Lyapunov theory or energy functions. By applying linear analysis to subnetworks composed of coactive neurons, we determine the stability of potential steady states. We find that stability depends on two types of eigenmodes. One type determines global stability and the other type determines whether or not multistability is possible. We can prove the equivalence of our stability criteria with criteria taken from quadratic programming. Also, we show that there are permitted sets of neurons that can be coactive at a steady state and forbidden sets that cannot. Permitted sets are clustered in the sense that subsets of permitted sets are permitted and supersets of forbidden sets are forbidden. By viewing permitted sets as memories stored in the synaptic connections, we can provide a formulation of longterm memory that is more general than the traditional perspective of fixed point attractor networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies which stable activity patterns can occur in symmetric threshold-linear neural networks. The authors analyze subnetworks made up of neurons that are active together. This local linear analysis determines the stability of candidate steady states and provides information beyond what the energy-function and Lyapunov approaches discussed in the abstract reveal.

The stability analysis identifies two kinds of eigenmodes. One governs global stability; the other determines whether multiple stable states are possible. The authors also prove equivalence between their stability criteria and criteria from quadratic programming. This connects the behavior of a recurrent neural circuit to a mathematical optimization framework.

The analysis separates neuron groups into permitted sets, which can be active together at a steady state, and forbidden sets, which cannot. Every subset of a permitted set is permitted, while every superset of a forbidden set remains forbidden. Interpreting permitted sets as stored memories yields a broader formulation of long-term memory than the traditional account based on individual fixed-point attractors.
summary.tldr: Stability analysis identifies which neuron groups can coexist at steady states and supports a broader account of stored memories.

title: Permitted and Forbidden Sets in Symmetric Threshold-Linear Networks

abstract: We report on the use of reinforcement learning with Cobot, a software agent residing in the well-known online community LambdaMOO. Our initial work on Cobot (Isbell et al.2000) provided him with the ability to collect social statistics and report them to users. Here we describe an application of RL allowing Cobot to take proactive actions in this complex social environment, and adapt behavior from multiple sources of human reward. After 5 months of training, and 3171 reward and punishment events from 254 different LambdaMOO users, Cobot learned nontrivial preferences for a number of users, modiﬁng his behavior based on his current state. Here we describe LambdaMOO and the state and action spaces of Cobot, and report the statistical results of the learning experiment.

paragraphs: Cobot is a software agent operating inside the online community LambdaMOO. Its earlier role was to collect social statistics and report them to users. This paper extends that role through reinforcement learning, allowing the agent to take proactive actions and adapt its behavior using rewards and punishments supplied by community members.

The learning setting involves multiple human sources of feedback rather than a single fixed evaluator. The paper describes the environment together with Cobot’s state and action spaces, which specify what situations it distinguishes and what actions it can take. Its behavior can therefore change according to its current state as learning proceeds.

After five months, Cobot had received 3,171 reward and punishment events from 254 users. The authors report that it learned nontrivial preferences for a number of users and modified its behavior according to its state. This is evidence of adaptation within a working social environment. The result shows how reinforcement learning can extend an informational community agent into one whose actions respond to accumulated human feedback.
summary.tldr: Cobot learned state-dependent social behavior from rewards and punishments supplied by users of an online community.

title: Cobot: A Social Reinforcement Learning Agent

abstract: (LLE) Locally Linear Embedding is an elegant nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique recently introduced by Roweis and Saul [2]. It fails when the data is divided into separate groups. We study a variant of LLE that can simultaneously group the data and calculate local embedding of each group. An estimate for the upper bound on the intrinsic dimension of the data set is obtained automatically.
originalAbstract: (LLE) Locally Linear Embedding is an elegant nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique recently introduced by Roweis and Saul [2]. It fails when the data is divided into separate groups. We study a variant of LLE that can simultaneously group the data and calculate local embedding of each group. An estimate for the upper bound on the intrinsic dimension of the data set is obtained automatically.

paragraphs: The paper studies a problem with Locally Linear Embedding, a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique: it fails when the data separates into distinct groups. Dimensionality reduction seeks a representation using fewer coordinates, but separate groups create an additional organizational question. The method must account for which observations belong together while constructing their representations.

The authors examine a variant of LLE that performs these two tasks simultaneously. It groups the data and computes a local embedding for each group. This makes the grouping part of the representation process, allowing separate portions of the dataset to receive their own local lower-dimensional descriptions.

The method also automatically obtains an estimate of an upper bound on the dataset’s intrinsic dimension. Intrinsic dimension concerns how many dimensions are needed to describe the data’s underlying structure. An estimated upper bound provides information about that requirement without claiming to identify the exact dimension. The contribution combines grouping, local embedding, and dimension estimation within a variant designed for separated data.
summary.tldr: A variant of LLE jointly groups separated data, embeds each group, and estimates an upper bound on intrinsic dimension.

title: Grouping and dimensionality reduction by locally linear embedding

abstract: Compressed sensing is an emerging ﬁeld based on the revelation that a small group of linear projections of a sparse signal contains enough information for reconstruc- tion. In this paper we introduce a new theory for distributed compressed sensing (DCS) that enables new distributed coding algorithms for multi-signal ensembles that exploit both intra- and inter-signal correlation structures. The DCS theory rests on a new concept that we term the joint sparsity of a signal ensemble. We study three simple models for jointly sparse signals, propose algorithms for joint recov- ery of multiple signals from incoherent projections, and characterize theoretically and empirically the number of measurements per sensor required for accurate re- construction. In some sense DCS is a framework for distributed compression of sources with memory, which has remained a challenging problem in information theory for some time. DCS is immediately applicable to a range of problems in sensor networks and arrays.

paragraphs: The paper extends compressed sensing from individual sparse signals to collections of related signals. Its goal is to reconstruct multiple signals from small sets of linear projections while taking advantage of structure both within each signal and across the collection. The authors call this framework distributed compressed sensing.

The central concept is joint sparsity, which describes useful sparse structure at the level of a signal ensemble. The paper studies three simple models of that structure and proposes algorithms that recover several signals together from incoherent projections. Joint recovery makes the relationships among signals part of the reconstruction procedure.

The authors analyze, both theoretically and empirically, how many measurements each sensor needs for accurate reconstruction. This connects the structural models to concrete measurement requirements. The framework is presented as applicable to sensor networks and arrays, where multiple sources can carry related information. Its contribution is to organize distributed compression and recovery around shared sparse structure rather than treating each source entirely separately.
summary.tldr: Distributed compressed sensing uses joint sparsity to reconstruct related signals together and characterize the measurements required per sensor.

title: Recovery of Jointly Sparse Signals from Few Random Projections

abstract: Neurons can have rapidly changing spike train statistics dictated by the underlying network excitability or behavioural state of an animal. To estimate the time course of such state dynamics from single- or multi- ple neuron recordings, we have developed an algorithm that maximizes the likelihood of observed spike trains by optimizing the state lifetimes and the state-conditional interspike-interval (ISI) distributions. Our non- parametric algorithm is free of time-binning and spike-counting prob- lems and has the computational complexity of a Mixed-state Markov Model operating on a state sequence of length equal to the total num- ber of recorded spikes. As an example, we ﬁt a two-state model to paired recordings of premotor neurons in the sleeping songbird. We ﬁnd that the two state-conditional ISI functions are highly similar to the ones mea- sured during waking and singing, respectively.

Our non- parametric algorithm is free of time-binning and spike-counting prob- lems and has the computational complexity of a Mixed-state Markov Model operating on a state sequence of length equal to the total num- ber of recorded spikes. paragraphs: Neural firing patterns can change rapidly as network excitability or an animal's behavioral state changes. This paper develops a method for recovering the timing of such hidden state changes from recordings of one or more neurons. It uses the intervals between spikes to connect the observed activity with the underlying state dynamics.

The algorithm maximizes the likelihood of the recorded spike trains by jointly optimizing state lifetimes and the distribution of interspike intervals within each state. Its nonparametric formulation avoids the time-binning and spike-counting problems identified by the authors. Its computational complexity matches that of a mixed-state Markov model operating on a sequence whose length equals the total number of recorded spikes.

As an example, the authors fit a two-state model to paired recordings of premotor neurons in a sleeping songbird. The interval distributions associated with the two inferred states closely resemble those measured during waking and singing, respectively. This finding links distinct patterns recovered during sleep to patterns observed in those other conditions, through their spike-interval statistics.
summary.tldr: A likelihood-based algorithm infers hidden neural state dynamics directly from spike intervals, with a songbird example revealing distributions resembling waking and singing activity.

title: Efficient estimation of hidden state dynamics from spike trains

abstract: We present a computational Bayesian approach for Wiener diffusion models, which are prominent accounts of response time distributions in decision-making. We first develop a general closed-form analytic approximation to the response time distributions for one-dimensional diffusion processes, and derive the required Wiener diffusion as a special case. We use this result to undertake Bayesian modeling of benchmark data, using posterior sampling to draw inferences about the interesting psychological parameters. With the aid of the benchmark data, we show the Bayesian account has several advantages, including dealing naturally with the parameter variation needed to account for some key features of the data, and providing quantitative measures to guide decisions about model construction.

We first develop a general closed-form analytic approximation to the response time distributions for one-dimensional diffusion processes, and derive the required Wiener diffusion as a special case. We use this result to undertake Bayesian modeling of benchmark data, using posterior sampling to draw inferences about the interesting psychological parameters. With the aid of the benchmark data, we show the Bayesian account has several advantages, including dealing naturally with the parameter variation needed to account for some key features of the data, and providing quantitative measures to guide decisions about model construction.

paragraphs: Diffusion models describe decision-making through a process whose evolution produces a distribution of response times. This paper develops a computational Bayesian approach to Wiener diffusion models, a prominent member of that family. The aim is to infer psychologically meaningful parameters while accommodating the variation needed to explain observed response-time patterns.

The authors first construct a closed-form approximation to response-time distributions for one-dimensional diffusion processes. They then obtain the Wiener diffusion case from this broader result. This analytic approximation supplies a practical basis for Bayesian modeling: posterior sampling can use it to explore parameter values supported by benchmark observations.

On those benchmark data, the Bayesian account handles parameter variation that is needed to capture some key features of the observations. It also supplies quantitative measures to inform choices about model construction. The contribution therefore connects a mathematical approximation with a workable inference procedure, helping researchers assess both psychological parameters and decisions about how to build the model.
summary.tldr: An analytic response-time approximation makes Bayesian inference practical for diffusion models and helps guide model construction.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Diffusion Models of Decision-Making and Response Time

abstract: Stability is a desirable characteristic for linear dynamical systems, but it is often ignored by algorithms that learn these systems from data. We propose a novel method for learning stable linear dynamical systems: we formulate an approxima- tion of the problem as a convex program, start with a solution to a relaxed version of the program, and incrementally add constraints to improve stability. Rather than continuing to generate constraints until we reach a feasible solution, we test stability at each step; because the convex program is only an approximation of the desired problem, this early stopping rule can yield a higher-quality solution. We apply our algorithm to the task of learning dynamic textures from image sequences as well as to modeling biosurveillance drug-sales data. The constraint generation approach leads to noticeable improvement in the quality of simulated sequences. We compare our method to those of Lacy and Bernstein [1, 2], with positive results in terms of accuracy, quality of simulated sequences, and efﬁciency.
originalAbstract: Stability is a desirable characteristic for linear dynamical systems, but it is often ignored by algorithms that learn these systems from data. We propose a novel method for learning stable linear dynamical systems: we formulate an approxima- tion of the problem as a convex program, start with a solution to a relaxed version of the program, and incrementally add constraints to improve stability. Rather than continuing to generate constraints until we reach a feasible solution, we test stability at each step; because the convex program is only an approximation of the desired problem, this early stopping rule can yield a higher-quality solution. We apply our algorithm to the task of learning dynamic textures from image sequences as well as to modeling biosurveillance drug-sales data. The constraint generation approach leads to noticeable improvement in the quality of simulated sequences. We compare our method to those of Lacy and Bernstein [1, 2], with positive results in terms of accuracy, quality of simulated sequences, and efﬁciency.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning linear dynamical systems that remain stable, a property that learning algorithms often leave unenforced. The authors approximate the learning problem with a convex optimization program. They begin with a relaxed version and progressively add constraints intended to improve the stability of the learned system.

A central design choice is to test the system’s actual stability after each step. The algorithm can stop once stability is achieved, even if it has not satisfied every constraint of the approximate convex program. Because that program is only a proxy for the desired problem, enforcing all of its constraints can be unnecessarily restrictive. Early stopping can therefore produce a higher-quality solution.

The authors apply the method to dynamic textures learned from image sequences and to drug-sales data used in biosurveillance. They report noticeable improvements in simulated sequence quality. Comparisons with methods by Lacy and Bernstein are also positive for accuracy, simulation quality, and efficiency. These results support checking the desired system property directly while incrementally tightening an optimization approximation.
summary.tldr: Incrementally adding constraints and stopping when stability is achieved can improve learned linear dynamical systems and their simulated sequences.

title: A Constraint Generation Approach to Learning Stable Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: The relative merits of different population coding schemes have mostly been analyzed in the framework of stimulus reconstruction using Fisher Information. Here, we consider the case of stimulus discrimination in a two alternative forced choice paradigm and compute neurometric functions in terms of the minimal discrimination error and the Jensen-Shannon information to study neural population codes. We first explore the relationship between minimum discrimination error, Jensen-Shannon Information and Fisher Information and show that the discrimination framework is more informative about the coding accuracy than Fisher Information as it defines an error for any pair of possible stimuli. In particular, it includes Fisher Information as a special case. Second, we use the framework to study population codes of angular variables. Specifically, we assess the impact of different noise correlations structures on coding accuracy in long versus short decoding time windows. That is, for long time window we use the common Gaussian noise approximation. To address the case of short time windows we analyze the Ising model with identical noise correlation structure. In this way, we provide a new rigorous framework for assessing the functional consequences of noise correlation structures for the representational accuracy of neural population codes that is in particular applicable to short-time population coding.

Earlier analyses often emphasized stimulus reconstruction using Fisher information. Here, the authors construct neurometric functions using minimum discrimination error and Jensen-Shannon information, placing the comparison of stimulus pairs at the center of the analysis.

Its broader scope comes from assigning an error to any pair of possible stimuli. This offers a more informative account of coding accuracy than relying on Fisher information alone.

title: Neurometric function analysis of population codes

abstract: In matrix completion, we are given a matrix where the values of only some of the entries are present, and we want to reconstruct the missing ones. Much work has focused on the assumption that the data matrix has low rank. We propose a more general assumption based on denoising, so that we expect that the value of a missing entry can be predicted from the values of neighboring points. We propose a nonparametric version of denoising based on local, iterated averaging with mean-shift, possibly constrained to preserve local low-rank manifold structure. The few user parameters required (the denoising scale, number of neighbors and local dimensionality) and the number of iterations can be estimated by cross-validating the reconstruction error. Using our algorithms as a postprocessing step on an initial reconstruction (provided by e.g. a low-rank method), we show consistent improvements with synthetic, image and motion-capture data.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs entries missing from a partially observed table of values. Many methods assume the entire matrix has low rank, meaning its entries follow a relatively compact global structure. This paper introduces a broader perspective based on denoising: a missing value should be predictable from nearby points, allowing local relationships to guide reconstruction.

The proposed nonparametric procedure repeatedly averages information within local neighborhoods using mean-shift. It can also be constrained to preserve a locally low-rank manifold structure. That option combines neighborhood-based smoothing with a local geometric constraint. The denoising scale, neighborhood size, local dimensionality, and iteration count can be chosen by cross-validating reconstruction error.

The authors apply these algorithms after an initial reconstruction, which can come from a low-rank method. They report consistent improvements on synthetic data, images, and motion-capture data. These findings support denoising as a useful refinement stage: an initial estimate supplies completed values, and local structure provides additional information for improving them in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Local denoising improves initial matrix completions by using neighborhood relationships, with consistent gains on the reported datasets.

title: A Denoising View of Matrix Completion

abstract: Many real-world networks are described by both connectivity information and features for every node. To better model and understand these networks, we present structure preserving metric learning (SPML), an algorithm for learning a Mahalanobis distance metric from a network such that the learned distances are tied to the inherent connectivity structure of the network. Like the graph embedding algorithm structure preserving embedding, SPML learns a metric which is structure preserving, meaning a connectivity algorithm such as k-nearest neighbors will yield the correct connectivity when applied using the distances from the learned metric. We show a variety of synthetic and real-world experiments where SPML predicts link patterns from node features more accurately than standard techniques. We further demonstrate a method for optimizing SPML based on stochastic gradient descent which removes the running-time dependency on the size of the network and allows the method to easily scale to networks of thousands of nodes and millions of edges.

Like the graph embedding algorithm structure preserving embedding, SPML learns a metric which is structure preserving, meaning a connectivity algorithm such as k-nearest neighbors will yield the correct connectivity when applied using the distances from the learned metric. paragraphs: Many networks provide both connections between nodes and descriptive features for each node. The paper asks how those features can be compared in a way that reflects the network's connections. Its structure preserving metric learning method, SPML, learns a Mahalanobis distance metric tied to the connectivity already present in the network.

Structure preservation has a specific meaning here: applying a connectivity rule, such as nearest neighbors, using the learned distances yields the correct connections. The learning objective therefore links feature-based distance to network construction. This makes the distance function useful for understanding how node attributes relate to observed links and for predicting link patterns from those attributes.

Synthetic and real-world experiments show more accurate link-pattern prediction than standard techniques. The authors also develop a stochastic gradient descent optimization method that they describe as removing the running-time dependency on network size, enabling applications with thousands of nodes and millions of edges. The contribution pairs a connectivity-aware metric with an optimization approach intended to make that metric practical for large networks.
summary.tldr: SPML learns distances between node features that preserve network connectivity and improve link-pattern prediction in the reported experiments.

title: Learning a Distance Metric from a Network

abstract: Sudderth, Wainwright, and Willsky conjectured that the Bethe approximation corresponding to any fixed point of the belief propagation algorithm over an attractive, pairwise binary graphical model provides a lower bound on the true partition function. In this work, we resolve this conjecture in the affirmative by demonstrating that, for any graphical model with binary variables whose potential functions (not necessarily pairwise) are all log-supermodular, the Bethe partition function always lower bounds the true partition function. The proof of this result follows from a new variant of the “four functions” theorem that may be of independent interest.

The proof of this result follows from a new variant of the “four functions” theorem that may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The partition function normalizes a graphical model's probabilities, and the Bethe approach provides an approximation to it. This paper resolves a conjecture about the direction of that approximation's error. The conjecture concerned belief-propagation fixed points in attractive graphical models with binary variables and pairwise interactions.

The authors establish a broader result: for binary-variable graphical models whose potential functions are all log-supermodular, the Bethe partition function is always a lower bound on the true partition function. The potentials need not be pairwise, so the theorem also covers qualifying interactions involving more than two variables.

This matters because the approximation gains a guaranteed ordering relative to the exact quantity under the stated structural conditions. The result specifies which side of the true partition function the approximation occupies; it does not assert that the two quantities coincide. The proof uses a new variant of the four-functions theorem, which the authors suggest may have value beyond this particular graphical-model result.
summary.tldr: For binary graphical models with log-supermodular potentials, the Bethe partition function provably lower-bounds the true partition function.

title: The Bethe Partition Function of Log-supermodular Graphical Models

abstract: We propose a novel stochastic process that is with probability $\alpha_i$ being absorbed at current state $i$, and with probability $1-\alpha_i$ follows a random edge out of it. We analyze its properties and show its potential for exploring graph structures. We prove that under proper absorption rates, a random walk starting from a set $\mathcal{S}$ of low conductance will be mostly absorbed in $\mathcal{S}$. Moreover, the absorption probabilities vary slowly inside $\mathcal{S}$, while dropping sharply outside $\mathcal{S}$, thus implementing the desirable cluster assumption for graph-based learning. Remarkably, the partially absorbing process unifies many popular models arising in a variety of contexts, provides new insights into them, and makes it possible for transferring findings from one paradigm to another. Simulation results demonstrate its promising applications in graph-based learning.

We prove that under proper absorption rates, a random walk starting from a set $\mathcal{S}$ of low conductance will be mostly absorbed in $\mathcal{S}$. paragraphs: The paper introduces a random walk that can stop permanently at each graph node. At node i, it is absorbed with probability alpha_i; otherwise, it follows a randomly selected outgoing edge. The resulting absorption probabilities provide a way to explore graph structure by describing where walks are likely to end.

The authors prove that, with appropriate absorption rates, a walk starting in a low-conductance set is mostly absorbed within that set. Such a set has relatively weak connections to its surroundings. Absorption probabilities vary gradually inside the set but fall sharply outside it, producing the kind of within-cluster consistency and between-cluster separation desired in graph-based learning.

The process also unifies several popular models from different settings. This common formulation provides new interpretations and creates opportunities to transfer findings between those models. Simulations demonstrate promising graph-learning applications. The structural guarantee depends on choosing suitable absorption rates, so the stopping mechanism is part of what makes the walk respect a cluster's boundary.
summary.tldr: Random walks with suitable node-dependent stopping probabilities reveal cluster structure and unify several graph-learning models.

title: Learning with Partially Absorbing Random Walks

abstract: Discrete mixtures are used routinely in broad sweeping applications ranging from unsupervised settings to fully supervised multi-task learning. Indeed, finite mixtures and infinite mixtures, relying on Dirichlet processes and modifications, have become a standard tool. One important issue that arises in using discrete mixtures is low separation in the components; in particular, different components can be introduced that are very similar and hence redundant. Such redundancy leads to too many clusters that are too similar, degrading performance in unsupervised learning and leading to computational problems and an unnecessarily complex model in supervised settings. Redundancy can arise in the absence of a penalty on components placed close together even when a Bayesian approach is used to learn the number of components. To solve this problem, we propose a novel prior that generates components from a repulsive process, automatically penalizing redundant components. We characterize this repulsive prior theoretically and propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling algorithm for posterior computation. The methods are illustrated using synthetic examples and an iris data set.

paragraphs: Mixture models describe data using multiple components, but several components can end up nearly identical. This redundancy can create too many similar clusters, reduce unsupervised-learning performance, and add computational burden and unnecessary complexity in supervised applications. Learning the number of components through a Bayesian approach does not by itself prevent components from being placed close together.

The paper introduces a prior that generates mixture components through a repulsive process. Its purpose is to penalize redundant components automatically, making their separation part of the probabilistic model. This directly addresses overlap in component placement, rather than relying only on control over how many components the model contains.

The authors characterize the prior theoretically and develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior computation. Synthetic examples and the iris dataset illustrate the methods. The contribution is both a modeling mechanism and a way to perform inference with it: the prior expresses a preference against redundant components, and the sampler makes that preference usable in posterior analysis.
summary.tldr: A repulsive prior penalizes redundant mixture components, supported by theoretical characterization and a posterior sampling algorithm.

title: Repulsive Mixtures

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of online learning in a dynamic setting. We consider a social network in which each individual observes a private signal about the underlying state of the world and communicates with her neighbors at each time period. Unlike many existing approaches, the underlying state is dynamic, and evolves according to a geometric random walk. We view the scenario as an optimization problem where agents aim to learn the true state while suffering the smallest possible loss. Based on the decomposition of the global loss function, we introduce two update mechanisms, each of which generates an estimate of the true state. We establish a tight bound on the rate of change of the underlying state, under which individuals can track the parameter with a bounded variance. Then, we characterize explicit expressions for the steady state mean-square deviation(MSD) of the estimates from the truth, per individual. We observe that only one of the estimators recovers the optimal MSD, which underscores the impact of the objective function decomposition on the learning quality. Finally, we provide an upper bound on the regret of the proposed methods, measured as an average of errors in estimating the parameter in a finite time.

paragraphs: The paper studies a social network whose members repeatedly estimate a changing state of the world. Each person receives a private signal and communicates with neighbors at every time step. The underlying state follows a geometric random walk, so learning requires continual tracking rather than convergence toward one fixed unknown value.

The authors formulate tracking as optimization of a global loss and derive two update mechanisms from different decompositions of that objective. They establish a tight bound on how quickly the state can change while individuals still track it with bounded variance. They also derive explicit expressions for each person's steady-state mean-square deviation from the true state.

Only one of the two estimators achieves the optimal mean-square deviation. This shows that how the global objective is decomposed affects the quality of distributed learning, even when both mechanisms address the same tracking problem. The paper additionally bounds finite-time regret measured through average estimation errors, complementing its steady-state analysis with a guarantee over a finite observation period.
summary.tldr: Two distributed tracking rules reveal how objective decomposition affects accuracy when social-network agents learn a dynamically changing state.

title: Online Learning of Dynamic Parameters in Social Networks

abstract: We propose a boosting method, DirectBoost, a greedy coordinate descent algorithm that builds an ensemble classifier of weak classifiers through directly minimizing empirical classification error over labeled training examples; once the training classification error is reduced to a local coordinatewise minimum, DirectBoost runs a greedy coordinate ascent algorithm that continuously adds weak classifiers to maximize any targeted arbitrarily defined margins until reaching a local coordinatewise maximum of the margins in a certain sense. Experimental results on a collection of machine-learning benchmark datasets show that DirectBoost gives consistently better results than AdaBoost, LogitBoost, LPBoost with column generation and BrownBoost, and is noise tolerant when it maximizes an n'th order bottom sample margin.

Experimental results on a collection of machine-learning benchmark datasets show that DirectBoost gives consistently better results than AdaBoost, LogitBoost, LPBoost with column generation and BrownBoost, and is noise tolerant when it maximizes an n'th order bottom sample margin.

paragraphs: DirectBoost builds an ensemble by combining weak classifiers, with training organized around two objectives. First, it directly reduces the number of incorrectly classified training examples. This is empirical classification error, also called 0–1 loss, because each example contributes according to whether its predicted label is wrong.

The first phase uses greedy coordinate descent and stops at a local coordinatewise minimum. The algorithm then switches to greedy coordinate ascent, continuing to add weak classifiers while increasing a chosen margin objective. Margins describe how strongly examples are classified. The framework permits arbitrarily defined target margins, but its stopping claim concerns a local coordinatewise maximum in the authors' specified sense, rather than a global optimum.

Across a collection of benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently better results than AdaBoost, LogitBoost, LPBoost with column generation, and BrownBoost. They also report noise tolerance when optimizing a particular ordered bottom-sample margin. That qualification matters: the stated noise result is tied to the selected margin objective, not every possible margin definition.
summary.tldr: DirectBoost first greedily minimizes training classification error, then improves chosen margins, with favorable benchmark results and qualified noise tolerance.

title: Direct 0-1 Loss Minimization and Margin Maximization with Boosting

abstract: Partial monitoring is a general model for online learning with limited feedback: a learner chooses actions in a sequential manner while an opponent chooses outcomes. In every round, the learner suffers some loss and receives some feedback based on the action and the outcome. The goal of the learner is to minimize her cumulative loss. Applications range from dynamic pricing to label-efficient prediction to dueling bandits. In this paper, we assume that we are given some prior information about the distribution based on which the opponent generates the outcomes. We propose BPM, a family of new efficient algorithms whose core is to track the outcome distribution with an ellipsoid centered around the estimated distribution. We show that our algorithm provably enjoys near-optimal regret rate for locally observable partial-monitoring problems against stochastic opponents. As demonstrated with experiments on synthetic as well as real-world data, the algorithm outperforms previous approaches, even for very uninformed priors, with an order of magnitude smaller regret and lower running time.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring describes sequential decisions in which the learner receives only limited feedback about outcomes. Each chosen action incurs a loss and produces feedback determined jointly by that action and the opponent's outcome. The paper studies how prior information about the opponent's outcome distribution can help the learner keep cumulative loss low.

The proposed BPM family of algorithms tracks the outcome distribution using an ellipsoid centered on its current estimate. This representation allows the algorithms to organize uncertainty around what they have learned while incorporating prior information. The central computational task is therefore to maintain and use an evolving description of the distribution behind the observed feedback.

For locally observable partial-monitoring problems with stochastic opponents, the authors prove near-optimal regret rates. This guarantee applies to that specified class of problems and opponents. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report lower running time and regret an order of magnitude smaller than previous approaches, even with very uninformed priors. The findings suggest that the framework can remain useful when prior knowledge is weak.
summary.tldr: BPM uses prior information and ellipsoidal uncertainty estimates to learn efficiently from limited feedback, with near-optimal guarantees in a specified stochastic setting.

title: Efficient Partial Monitoring with Prior Information

abstract: Gaussian process regression can be accelerated by constructing a small pseudo-dataset to summarise the observed data. This idea sits at the heart of many approximation schemes, but such an approach requires the number of pseudo-datapoints to be scaled with the range of the input space if the accuracy of the approximation is to be maintained. This presents problems in time-series settings or in spatial datasets where large numbers of pseudo-datapoints are required since computation typically scales quadratically with the pseudo-dataset size. In this paper we devise an approximation whose complexity grows linearly with the number of pseudo-datapoints. This is achieved by imposing a tree or chain structure on the pseudo-datapoints and calibrating the approximation using a Kullback-Leibler (KL) minimisation. Inference and learning can then be performed efficiently using the Gaussian belief propagation algorithm. We demonstrate the validity of our approach on a set of challenging regression tasks including missing data imputation for audio and spatial datasets. We trace out the speed-accuracy trade-off for the new method and show that the frontier dominates those obtained from a large number of existing approximation techniques.

Maintaining accuracy across a wider input range, however, can require more pseudo-points. This is problematic for time-series and spatial data because computation in typical approaches grows quadratically with the pseudo-dataset size.

The paper constructs an approximation whose complexity grows linearly with the number of pseudo-points. It imposes a tree or chain structure on those points and calibrates the approximation through Kullback-Leibler minimization. These findings support the practical value of the structured approximation in the tested tasks, especially where retaining enough pseudo-points is important for accuracy over a broad input range.
summary.tldr: Tree-structured pseudo-data make Gaussian process approximation scale linearly in summary size and improve the reported speed-accuracy trade-off.

title: Tree-structured Gaussian Process Approximations

abstract: We show that several online combinatorial optimization problems that admit efficient no-regret algorithms become computationally hard in the sleeping setting where a subset of actions becomes unavailable in each round. Specifically, we show that the sleeping versions of these problems are at least as hard as PAC learning DNF expressions, a long standing open problem. We show hardness for the sleeping versions of Online Shortest Paths, Online Minimum Spanning Tree, Online k-Subsets, Online k-Truncated Permutations, Online Minimum Cut, and Online Bipartite Matching. The hardness result for the sleeping version of the Online Shortest Paths problem resolves an open problem presented at COLT 2015 [Koolen et al., 2015].

Specifically, we show that the sleeping versions of these problems are at least as hard as PAC learning DNF expressions, a long standing open problem. We show hardness for the sleeping versions of Online Shortest Paths, Online Minimum Spanning Tree, Online k-Subsets, Online k-Truncated Permutations, Online Minimum Cut, and Online Bipartite Matching. The hardness result for the sleeping version of the Online Shortest Paths problem resolves an open problem presented at COLT 2015 [Koolen et al., 2015].

paragraphs: The paper studies online combinatorial optimization when some actions become unavailable in each round. This is called the sleeping setting. The starting point is a collection of problems that have efficient no-regret algorithms when actions remain available. The authors ask what happens to computational tractability when availability changes during the sequence of decisions.

They show that the sleeping versions are at least as hard as PAC learning disjunctive normal form expressions, a longstanding open learning problem. This is a relative hardness result: an efficient solution to the sleeping problems would also address that difficult learning task. It therefore identifies a substantial computational barrier without proving an unconditional impossibility.

The result covers online shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, k-subsets, k-truncated permutations, minimum cuts, and bipartite matching. For shortest paths, it resolves a previously posed open question. Across these different structures, the shared lesson is that varying action availability can fundamentally change the difficulty of online learning, even when the corresponding always-available problem has efficient no-regret methods.
summary.tldr: Several online optimization problems become at least as hard as PAC learning DNF expressions when actions can become unavailable.

title: Hardness of Online Sleeping Combinatorial Optimization Problems

abstract: Spectral methods are popular in detecting global structures in the given data that can be represented as a matrix. However when the data matrix is sparse or noisy, classic spectral methods usually fail to work, due to localization of eigenvectors (or singular vectors) induced by the sparsity or noise. In this work, we propose a general method to solve the localization problem by learning a regularization matrix from the localized eigenvectors. Using matrix perturbation analysis, we demonstrate that the learned regularizations suppress down the eigenvalues associated with localized eigenvectors and enable us to recover the informative eigenvectors representing the global structure. We show applications of our method in several inference problems: community detection in networks, clustering from pairwise similarities, rank estimation and matrix completion problems. Using extensive experiments, we illustrate that our method solves the localization problem and works down to the theoretical detectability limits in different kinds of synthetic data. This is in contrast with existing spectral algorithms based on data matrix, non-backtracking matrix, Laplacians and those with rank-one regularizations, which perform poorly in the sparse case with noise.

In this work, we propose a general method to solve the localization problem by learning a regularization matrix from the localized eigenvectors. Using matrix perturbation analysis, we demonstrate that the learned regularizations suppress down the eigenvalues associated with localized eigenvectors and enable us to recover the informative eigenvectors representing the global structure. We show applications of our method in several inference problems: community detection in networks, clustering from pairwise similarities, rank estimation and matrix completion problems. Using extensive experiments, we illustrate that our method solves the localization problem and works down to the theoretical detectability limits in different kinds of synthetic data. This is in contrast with existing spectral algorithms based on data matrix, non-backtracking matrix, Laplacians and those with rank-one regularizations, which perform poorly in the sparse case with noise.

In sparse or noisy data, those vectors can become localized, concentrating on a small part of the data instead of representing the broader structure. The paper addresses this failure by learning a regularization matrix from the localized eigenvectors themselves.

Matrix perturbation analysis shows how the learned regularization suppresses eigenvalues associated with localized directions. This enables recovery of informative eigenvectors that represent global structure. The method uses the unwanted spectral behavior to construct a correction, linking the diagnosis of localization with the modification applied to the matrix.

Applications include network community detection, clustering from pairwise similarities, rank estimation, and matrix completion. Extensive experiments show successful handling of localization and performance reaching theoretical detectability limits in different synthetic settings. The authors contrast these findings with poor sparse-noisy performance from several existing spectral constructions. Reaching those limits is an experimental finding in the studied synthetic data, rather than a universal claim for every input matrix.
summary.tldr: Learning regularization from localized eigenvectors helps spectral methods recover global structure in sparse or noisy data.

title: Robust Spectral Detection of Global Structures in the Data by Learning a Regularization

abstract: Factorizing low-rank matrices has many applications in machine learning and statistics. For probabilistic models in the Bayes optimal setting, a general expression for the mutual information has been proposed using heuristic statistical physics computations, and proven in few specific cases. Here, we show how to rigorously prove the conjectured formula for the symmetric rank-one case. This allows to express the minimal mean-square-error and to characterize the detectability phase transitions in a large set of estimation problems ranging from community detection to sparse PCA. We also show that for a large set of parameters, an iterative algorithm called approximate message-passing is Bayes optimal. There exists, however, a gap between what currently known polynomial algorithms can do and what is expected information theoretically. Additionally, the proof technique has an interest of its own and exploits three essential ingredients: the interpolation method introduced in statistical physics by Guerra, the analysis of the approximate message-passing algorithm and the theory of spatial coupling and threshold saturation in coding. Our approach is generic and applicable to other open problems in statistical estimation where heuristic statistical physics predictions are available.

abstract: Deep learning has the potential to revolutionize quantum chemistry as it is ideally suited to learn representations for structured data and speed up the exploration of chemical space. While convolutional neural networks have proven to be the first choice for images, audio and video data, the atoms in molecules are not restricted to a grid. Instead, their precise locations contain essential physical information, that would get lost if discretized. Thus, we propose to use continuous-filter convolutional layers to be able to model local correlations without requiring the data to lie on a grid. We apply those layers in SchNet: a novel deep learning architecture modeling quantum interactions in molecules. We obtain a joint model for the total energy and interatomic forces that follows fundamental quantum-chemical principles. Our architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance for benchmarks of equilibrium molecules and molecular dynamics trajectories. Finally, we introduce a more challenging benchmark with chemical and structural variations that suggests the path for further work.

This paper introduces continuous-filter convolutional layers to model local relationships while allowing the input positions to remain off-grid.

The approach carries the local-pattern modeling idea of convolution into a setting where spatial coordinates are continuous. It produces a joint model of total energy and interatomic forces that follows fundamental quantum-chemical principles, linking two physically related quantities within one architecture.

summary.tldr: SchNet uses continuous-filter convolutions to model molecular energies and forces directly from atoms positioned off-grid.

title: SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling quantum interactions

abstract: Many online platforms act as intermediaries between a seller and a set of buyers. Examples of such settings include online retailers (such as Ebay) selling items on behalf of sellers to buyers, or advertising exchanges (such as AdX) selling pageviews on behalf of publishers to advertisers. In such settings, revenue sharing is a central part of running such a marketplace for the intermediary, and fixed-percentage revenue sharing schemes are often used to split the revenue among the platform and the sellers. In particular, such revenue sharing schemes require the platform to (i) take at most a constant fraction \alpha of the revenue from auctions and (ii) pay the seller at least the seller declared opportunity cost c for each item sold. A straightforward way to satisfy the constraints is to set a reserve price at c / (1 - \alpha) for each item, but it is not the optimal solution on maximizing the profit of the intermediary. While previous studies (by Mirrokni and Gomes, and by Niazadeh et al) focused on revenue-sharing schemes in static double auctions, in this paper, we take advantage of the repeated nature of the auctions. In particular, we introduce dynamic revenue sharing schemes where we balance the two constraints over different auctions to achieve higher profit and seller revenue. This is directly motivated by the practice of advertising exchanges where the fixed-percentage revenue-share should be met across all auctions and not in each auction. In this paper, we characterize the optimal revenue sharing scheme that satisfies both constraints in expectation. Finally, we empirically evaluate our revenue sharing scheme on real data.

paragraphs: An intermediary marketplace must divide auction revenue between itself and sellers. The paper considers two requirements: the platform keeps at most a specified fraction of revenue, and the seller receives at least its declared opportunity cost for an item sold. Enforcing both requirements separately in every auction can constrain the platform's profit.

A straightforward policy sets a reserve price by dividing the seller's declared cost by the fraction of revenue left after the platform's share. The authors explain that this policy is not optimal for intermediary profit. Their alternative uses repeated auctions, balancing the revenue-sharing requirements across different transactions. This matches the motivation from advertising exchanges, where the percentage agreement applies across auctions.

Allowing the requirements to balance across auctions creates opportunities for higher platform profit and seller revenue. The expectation qualification is central: the optimization concerns how payments and shares balance over repeated outcomes, rather than imposing the same guarantees independently on every transaction.
summary.tldr: Dynamic revenue sharing balances payment constraints across repeated auctions and characterizes an optimal scheme satisfying them in expectation.

title: Dynamic Revenue Sharing

abstract: Training large-scale image recognition models is computationally expensive. This raises the question of whether there might be simple ways to improve the test performance of an already trained model without having to re-train or fine-tune it with new data. Here, we show that, surprisingly, this is indeed possible. The key observation we make is that the layers of a deep network close to the output layer contain independent, easily extractable class-relevant information that is not contained in the output layer itself. We propose to extract this extra class-relevant information using a simple key-value cache memory to improve the classification performance of the model at test time. Our cache memory is directly inspired by a similar cache model previously proposed for language modeling (Grave et al., 2017). This cache component does not require any training or fine-tuning; it can be applied to any pre-trained model and, by properly setting only two hyper-parameters, leads to significant improvements in its classification performance. Improvements are observed across several architectures and datasets. In the cache component, using features extracted from layers close to the output (but not from the output layer itself) as keys leads to the largest improvements. Concatenating features from multiple layers to form keys can further improve performance over using single-layer features as keys. The cache component also has a regularizing effect, a simple consequence of which is that it substantially increases the robustness of models against adversarial attacks.

A model's existing internal representations therefore offer another source of evidence for making predictions.

It brings this extra information into classification at test time without training or fine-tuning the cache component. Features near the output work best as cache keys, and combining features from several layers can improve on using one layer alone. summary.tldr: A training-free cache uses information from a pretrained image classifier's internal layers to improve classification and observed adversarial robustness.

title: A Simple Cache Model for Image Recognition

abstract: Model compression is essential for serving large deep neural nets on devices with limited resources or applications that require real-time responses. For advanced NLP problems, a neural language model usually consists of recurrent layers (e.g., using LSTM cells), an embedding matrix for representing input tokens, and a softmax layer for generating output tokens. For problems with a very large vocabulary size, the embedding and the softmax matrices can account for more than half of the model size. For instance, the bigLSTM model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the One-Billion-Word (OBW) dataset with around 800k vocabulary, and its word embedding and softmax matrices use more than 6GBytes space, and are responsible for over 90\% of the model parameters. In this paper, we propose GroupReduce, a novel compression method for neural language models, based on vocabulary-partition (block) based low-rank matrix approximation and the inherent frequency distribution of tokens (the power-law distribution of words). We start by grouping words into $c$ blocks based on their frequency, and then refine the clustering iteratively by constructing weighted low-rank approximation for each block, where the weights are based the frequencies of the words in the block. The experimental results show our method can significantly outperform traditional compression methods such as low-rank approximation and pruning. On the OBW dataset, our method achieved 6.6x compression rate for the embedding and softmax matrices, and when combined with quantization, our method can achieve 26x compression rate without losing prediction accuracy.

These figures apply specifically to the targeted matrices, demonstrating the value of frequency-aware compression where model storage is concentrated.
summary.tldr: GroupReduce uses frequency-aware blockwise low-rank approximation to compress language-model matrices, reaching 26-fold compression with quantization in the reported experiment.

title: GroupReduce: Block-Wise Low-Rank Approximation for Neural Language Model Shrinking

abstract: Nearest-neighbor (NN) procedures are well studied and widely used in both supervised and unsupervised learning problems. In this paper we are concerned with investigating the performance of NN-based methods for anomaly detection. We first show through extensive simulations that NN methods compare favorably to some of the other state-of-the-art algorithms for anomaly detection based on a set of benchmark synthetic datasets. We further consider the performance of NN methods on real datasets, and relate it to the dimensionality of the problem. Next, we analyze the theoretical properties of NN-methods for anomaly detection by studying a more general quantity called distance-to-measure (DTM), originally developed in the literature on robust geometric and topological inference. We provide finite-sample uniform guarantees for the empirical DTM and use them to derive misclassification rates for anomalous observations under various settings. In our analysis we rely on Huber's contamination model and formulate mild geometric regularity assumptions on the underlying distribution of the data.

summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor anomaly detection receives empirical support and finite-sample error guarantees through distance-to-measure analysis.

title: Statistical Analysis of Nearest Neighbor Methods for Anomaly Detection

abstract: This paper considers the problem of efficient exploration of unseen environments, a key challenge in AI. We propose a learning to explore' framework where we learn a policy from a distribution of environments. At test time, presented with an unseen environment from the same distribution, the policy aims to generalize the exploration strategy to visit the maximum number of unique states in a limited number of steps. We particularly focus on environments with graph-structured state-spaces that are encountered in many important real-world applications like software testing and map building. We formulate this task as a reinforcement learning problem where the exploration' agent is rewarded for transitioning to previously unseen environment states and employ a graph-structured memory to encode the agent's past trajectory. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is extremely effective for exploration of spatial maps; and when applied on the challenging problems of coverage-guided software-testing of domain-specific programs and real-world mobile applications, it outperforms methods that have been hand-engineered by human experts.
