paragraphs: An exploration agent has limited time to discover an unfamiliar environment. This paper asks whether it can learn an exploration strategy from other environments and transfer that strategy to a new one. The objective is to visit as many distinct states as possible within a fixed number of steps, with training and test environments drawn from the same distribution.

The authors focus on environments whose states and transitions form a graph. They formulate exploration as reinforcement learning, rewarding the agent when it reaches a state it has not previously visited. A graph-structured memory records its past trajectory, giving the policy a representation of its exploration history.

The approach is evaluated on spatial maps and on coverage-guided testing of domain-specific programs and real-world mobile applications. The authors report strong map exploration performance and better software-testing performance than methods designed by human experts. These results support learning reusable exploration behavior across related environments. The transfer claim remains tied to unseen environments from the training distribution, rather than arbitrary environments with unrelated structure.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy with graph memory learns exploration strategies that transfer to unseen environments from the same distribution.

title: Learning Transferable Graph Exploration

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a widely used tool for modeling sequential data, yet they are often treated as inscrutable black boxes. Given a trained recurrent network, we would like to reverse engineer it--to obtain a quantitative, interpretable description of how it solves a particular task. Even for simple tasks, a detailed understanding of how recurrent networks work, or a prescription for how to develop such an understanding, remains elusive. In this work, we use tools from dynamical systems analysis to reverse engineer recurrent networks trained to perform sentiment classification, a foundational natural language processing task. Given a trained network, we find fixed points of the recurrent dynamics and linearize the nonlinear system around these fixed points. Despite their theoretical capacity to implement complex, high-dimensional computations, we find that trained networks converge to highly interpretable, low-dimensional representations. In particular, the topological structure of the fixed points and corresponding linearized dynamics reveal an approximate line attractor within the RNN, which we can use to quantitatively understand how the RNN solves the sentiment analysis task. Finally, we find this mechanism present across RNN architectures (including LSTMs, GRUs, and vanilla RNNs) trained on multiple datasets, suggesting that our findings are not unique to a particular architecture or dataset. Overall, these results demonstrate that surprisingly universal and human interpretable computations can arise across a range of recurrent networks.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a trained recurrent neural network actually carries out sentiment classification. Its goal is a quantitative account of the computation inside the network, going beyond treating the hidden state as an opaque representation. The authors use dynamical systems tools to examine the behavior of trained recurrent models.

They locate fixed points of the recurrent dynamics and approximate the nonlinear system locally around those points with linear dynamics. summary.tldr: Dynamical systems analysis reveals an approximate line attractor that explains sentiment computation across several recurrent architectures and datasets.

title: Reverse engineering recurrent networks for sentiment classification reveals line attractor dynamics

abstract: We consider a family of problems that are concerned about making predictions for the majority of unlabeled, graph-structured data samples based on a small proportion of labeled samples. Relational information among the data samples, often encoded in the graph/network structure, is shown to be helpful for these semi-supervised learning tasks. However, conventional graph-based regularization methods and recent graph neural networks do not fully leverage the interrelations between the features, the graph, and the labels. In this work, we propose a flexible generative framework for graph-based semi-supervised learning, which approaches the joint distribution of the node features, labels, and the graph structure. Borrowing insights from random graph models in network science literature, this joint distribution can be instantiated using various distribution families. For the inference of missing labels, we exploit recent advances of scalable variational inference techniques to approximate the Bayesian posterior. We conduct thorough experiments on benchmark datasets for graph-based semi-supervised learning. Results show that the proposed methods outperform state-of-the-art models under most settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction on graphs when only a small fraction of the data has labels. Each sample has its own features, but its relationships with other samples also provide information. The authors argue that existing graph regularization methods and graph neural networks do not fully capture how features, connections, and labels relate to one another.

Their approach models these three elements together through a joint probability distribution. This gives the method a way to express how the observed graph and features inform the missing labels. The framework is flexible because different distribution families can instantiate it, drawing on ideas from random graph models.

To predict unknown labels, the authors use scalable variational inference to approximate the Bayesian posterior. Their benchmark experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art models in most evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore both a modeling framework and empirical evidence that explicitly representing these interdependencies can improve graph-based prediction with limited labels.
summary.tldr: A generative framework jointly models graph connections, node features, and labels to improve prediction when labels are scarce.

title: A Flexible Generative Framework for Graph-based Semi-supervised Learning

abstract: Adversarial examples have attracted significant attention in machine learning, but the reasons for their existence and pervasiveness remain unclear. We demonstrate that adversarial examples can be directly attributed to the presence of non-robust features: features (derived from patterns in the data distribution) that are highly predictive, yet brittle and (thus) incomprehensible to humans. After capturing these features within a theoretical framework, we establish their widespread existence in standard datasets. Finally, we present a simple setting where we can rigorously tie the phenomena we observe in practice to a {\em misalignment} between the (human-specified) notion of robustness and the inherent geometry of the data.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why adversarial examples occur so broadly in machine learning. Its explanation centers on non-robust features: patterns in the data distribution that predict labels well but are brittle and incomprehensible to humans. Their predictive usefulness means that sensitivity to them can arise from learning real regularities in data.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for describing these features and establish that they are widespread in standard datasets. This connects adversarial vulnerability to the information a model can use for prediction. A feature can contribute to predictive success while failing to behave in a way that agrees with human expectations about robustness.

The paper also presents a simple setting in which the observed phenomena can be rigorously tied to a mismatch between human-specified robustness and the geometry of the data. This supports a concrete account of adversarial examples through non-robust features. The result makes the relationship between prediction and robustness central to understanding the phenomenon.
summary.tldr: Adversarial examples can arise from genuinely predictive but brittle data features that conflict with human notions of robustness.

title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features

abstract: While recent generative models for 2D images achieve impressive visual results, they clearly lack the ability to perform 3D reasoning. This heavily restricts the degree of control over generated objects as well as the possible applications of such models. In this work, we bridge this gap by leveraging recent advances in differentiable rendering. We design a framework that can generate triangle meshes and associated high-resolution texture maps, using only 2D supervision from single-view natural images. A key contribution of our work is the encoding of the mesh and texture as 2D representations, which are semantically aligned and can be easily modeled by a 2D convolutional GAN. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on Pascal3D+ Cars and CUB, both in an unconditional setting and in settings where the model is conditioned on class labels, attributes, and text. Finally, we propose an evaluation methodology that assesses the mesh and texture quality separately.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative framework that produces triangle meshes together with high-resolution texture maps using only two-dimensional supervision from single-view natural images. Its motivation is that visually convincing image generation alone provides limited control over an object's three-dimensional form. Generating explicit geometry and texture gives the model outputs that directly represent those aspects of an object.

The central design encodes both the mesh and its texture as two-dimensional representations with corresponding semantic structure. This allows a two-dimensional convolutional generative adversarial network to model them together. Differentiable rendering connects the generated three-dimensional objects to the image-based supervision, making the representation compatible with learning from the available natural images.

They also propose evaluating mesh quality separately from texture quality. That distinction helps assess the two outputs individually, so the evaluation can address the generated geometry as well as its surface appearance.
summary.tldr: Aligned two-dimensional encodings and differentiable rendering enable a convolutional GAN to generate textured 3D meshes from single-view image supervision.

title: Convolutional Generation of Textured 3D Meshes

abstract: Because of the lack of expertise, to gain benefits from their data, average users have to upload their private data to cloud servers they may not trust. Due to legal or privacy constraints, most users are willing to contribute only their encrypted data, and lack interests or resources to join deep neural network (DNN) training in cloud. To train a DNN on encrypted data in a completely non-interactive way, a recent work proposes a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)-based technique implementing all activations by \textit{Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan} (BGV)-based lookup tables. However, such inefficient lookup-table-based activations significantly prolong private training latency of DNNs. In this paper, we propose, Glyph, an FHE-based technique to fast and accurately train DNNs on encrypted data by switching between TFHE (Fast Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus) and BGV cryptosystems. Glyph uses logic-operation-friendly TFHE to implement nonlinear activations, while adopts vectorial-arithmetic-friendly BGV to perform multiply-accumulations (MACs). Glyph further applies transfer learning on DNN training to improve test accuracy and reduce the number of MACs between ciphertext and ciphertext in convolutional layers. Our experimental results show Glyph obtains state-of-the-art accuracy, and reduces training latency by 69%~99% over prior FHE-based privacy-preserving techniques on encrypted datasets.

This setting allows users to contribute encrypted information to cloud computation. These findings support matching different encrypted computations to cryptosystems with suitable strengths. Transfer learning provides a further way to reduce expensive encrypted operations while improving the reported predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Glyph combines two homomorphic encryption schemes and transfer learning to accelerate neural network training on encrypted data.

title: Glyph: Fast and Accurately Training Deep Neural Networks on Encrypted Data

abstract: We study the dynamics of optimization and the generalization properties of one-hidden layer neural networks with quadratic activation function in the overparametrized regime where the layer width m is larger than the input dimension d. We consider a teacher-student scenario where the teacher has the same structure as the student with a hidden layer of smaller width m*<=m. We describe how the empirical loss landscape is affected by the number n of data samples and the width m* of the teacher network. In particular we determine how the probability that there be no spurious minima on the empirical loss depends on n, d, and m*, thereby establishing conditions under which the neural network can in principle recover the teacher. We also show that under the same conditions gradient descent dynamics on the empirical loss converges and leads to small generalization error, i.e. it enables recovery in practice. Finally we characterize the time-convergence rate of gradient descent in the limit of a large number of samples. These results are confirmed by numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes one-hidden-layer networks with quadratic activations in an overparameterized setting where hidden-layer width exceeds input dimension. It uses a teacher–student setup: a teacher network generates the target relationship, and a student with the same architecture type and at least as much hidden width tries to recover it.

The authors examine how the number of training samples and the teacher's width shape the empirical loss landscape. In particular, they characterize how the probability of having no spurious minima depends on sample count, input dimension, and teacher width. This identifies conditions under which the optimization landscape permits recovery of the teacher rather than trapping learning at misleading minima.

Under the same conditions, the analysis shows that gradient descent converges and achieves small generalization error. This connects the possibility of recovery to a concrete learning procedure. The paper also characterizes convergence speed in the large-sample limit and confirms its results numerically. The conclusions concern the specified quadratic teacher–student setting, where optimization and generalization can be studied together.
summary.tldr: For overparameterized quadratic teacher–student networks, the paper identifies conditions connecting favorable loss landscapes, gradient-descent convergence, and generalization.

title: Optimization and Generalization of Shallow Neural Networks with Quadratic Activation Functions

abstract: Self-imitation learning motivated by lower-bound Q-learning is a novel and effective approach for off-policy learning. In this work, we propose a n-step lower bound which generalizes the original return-based lower-bound Q-learning, and introduce a new family of self-imitation learning algorithms. To provide a formal motivation for the potential performance gains provided by self-imitation learning, we show that n-step lower bound Q-learning achieves a trade-off between fixed point bias and contraction rate, drawing close connections to the popular uncorrected n-step Q-learning. We finally show that n-step lower bound Q-learning is a more robust alternative to return-based self-imitation learning and uncorrected n-step, over a wide range of benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Self-imitation learning uses an agent's own previous experience to guide further learning, including when that experience came from a different policy. This paper generalizes the lower-bound Q-learning motivation for self-imitation by introducing an n-step lower bound. That extension produces a family of algorithms rather than a single return-based learning rule.

The theoretical analysis explains a possible source of improved performance through a trade-off between fixed-point bias and contraction rate. Fixed-point bias concerns the value estimate toward which learning settles; contraction rate concerns how quickly repeated updates approach that target. The analysis shows how n-step lower-bound learning balances these properties and relates it closely to uncorrected n-step Q-learning.

Across a broad range of benchmark tasks, the authors find the method more robust than return-based self-imitation and uncorrected n-step learning. The theory motivates potential gains rather than guaranteeing that every task improves. The empirical results support the practical value of the generalized bound, while the bias-and-contraction analysis gives a clearer account of why revisiting past experience can help.
summary.tldr: An n-step lower bound generalizes self-imitation learning and offers a theoretically motivated trade-off that improves robustness in the evaluated tasks.

title: Self-Imitation Learning via Generalized Lower Bound Q-learning

abstract: We introduce a simple (one line of code) modification to the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) training algorithm that materially improves results with no increase in computational cost. When updating the generator parameters, we simply zero out the gradient contributions from the elements of the batch that the critic scores as `least realistic'. Through experiments on many different GAN variants, we show that this `top-k update' procedure is a generally applicable improvement. In order to understand the nature of the improvement, we conduct extensive analysis on a simple mixture-of-Gaussians dataset and discover several interesting phenomena. Among these is that, when gradient updates are computed using the worst-scoring batch elements, samples can actually be pushed further away from the their nearest mode. We also apply our method to state-of-the-art GAN models including BigGAN and improve state-of-the-art FID for conditional generation on CIFAR-10 from 9.21 to 8.57.

paragraphs: A GAN generator learns from feedback supplied by a critic about generated samples. This paper changes which samples contribute when the generator is updated. Instead of using every element of a batch, it sets the gradient contributions of the critic's least-realistic samples to zero, leaving the better-scoring samples to drive the update.

The modification is described as one line of code with no increase in computational cost. Experiments across many GAN variants support its broad applicability. To investigate why it helps, the authors analyze a mixture-of-Gaussians dataset and find that updates based on the worst-scoring samples can move samples farther from their nearest mode.

That observation shows why strongly criticized samples need not always provide useful generator updates. The authors also apply top-k training to leading GAN models, including BigGAN. For conditional CIFAR-10 generation, they improve the reported state-of-the-art FID from 9.21 to 8.57. The results support selectively using critic feedback as a simple way to improve GAN training.
summary.tldr: Updating GAN generators using only better-scoring batch samples improves results without increasing computational cost.

title: Top-k Training of GANs: Improving GAN Performance by Throwing Away Bad Samples

abstract: We consider the problem of online learning with dynamics, where a learner interacts with a stateful environment over multiple rounds. In each round of the interaction, the learner selects a policy to deploy and incurs a cost that depends on both the chosen policy and current state of the world. The state-evolution dynamics and the costs are allowed to be time-varying, in a possibly adversarial way. In this setting, we study the problem of minimizing policy regret and provide non-constructive upper bounds on the minimax rate for the problem. Our main results provide sufficient conditions for online learnability for this setup with corresponding rates. The rates are characterized by: 1) a complexity term capturing the expressiveness of the underlying policy class under the dynamics of state change, and 2) a dynamics stability term measuring the deviation of the instantaneous loss from a certain counterfactual loss. Further, we provide matching lower bounds which show that both the complexity terms are indeed necessary. Our approach provides a unifying analysis that recovers regret bounds for several well studied problems including online learning with memory, online control of linear quadratic regulators, online Markov decision processes, and tracking adversarial targets. In addition, we show how our tools help obtain tight regret bounds for a new problems (with non-linear dynamics and non-convex losses) for which such bounds were not known prior to our work.

This paper allows both state evolution and costs to vary over time, potentially adversarially. It studies policy regret, where evaluating decisions must account for the interaction between policies and the environment's evolving state.

It also gives tight bounds for new problems involving nonlinear dynamics and nonconvex losses. Because the upper bounds are non-constructive, the main contribution is a characterization of achievable learning rates rather than a directly specified general-purpose learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A minimax analysis characterizes online learning with changing dynamics through policy complexity and dynamical stability.

title: Online learning with dynamics: A minimax perspective

abstract: In this work, we consider a sequence of $J$ matrix multiplication jobs which needs to be distributed by a master across multiple worker nodes. For $i\in \{1,2,\ldots,J\}$, job-$i$ begins in round-$i$ and has to be completed by round-$(i+T)$. Previous works consider only the special case of $T=0$ and focus on coding across workers. We propose here two schemes with $T>0$, which feature coding across workers as well as the dimension of time. Our first scheme is a modification of the polynomial coding scheme introduced by Yu et al. and places no assumptions on the straggler model. Exploitation of the temporal dimension helps the scheme handle a larger set of straggler patterns than the polynomial coding scheme, for a given computational load per worker per round. The second scheme assumes a particular straggler model to further improve performance (in terms of encoding/decoding complexity). We develop theoretical results establishing (i) optimality of our proposed schemes for a certain class of straggler patterns and (ii) improved performance for the case of i.i.d. stragglers. These are further validated by experiments, where we implement our schemes to train neural networks.

paragraphs: Distributed matrix multiplication can be delayed by workers that finish slowly. This paper considers a sequence of jobs arriving in successive rounds, each with a deadline a fixed number of rounds later. That allowance creates an opportunity to organize redundant computation across time as well as across workers.

The authors propose two coding schemes that use this temporal flexibility. The first modifies polynomial coding without assuming a particular straggler model. For the same computational load per worker per round, it handles a broader collection of slow-worker patterns. The second assumes a specific straggler model and uses that additional structure to improve encoding and decoding complexity.

The theoretical results establish optimality for a particular class of straggler patterns and improved performance when stragglers are independent and identically distributed. Neural-network training experiments further validate the schemes. The central contribution is to show how a permitted delay between a job's arrival and deadline can become a useful resource for mitigating slow workers.
summary.tldr: Coding matrix multiplication across workers and time improves resilience to slow workers when jobs allow delayed completion.

title: Coded Sequential Matrix Multiplication For Straggler Mitigation

abstract: We introduce MARGE, a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model learned with an unsupervised multi-lingual multi-document paraphrasing objective. MARGE provides an alternative to the dominant masked language modeling paradigm, where we self-supervise the \emph{reconstruction} of target text by \emph{retrieving} a set of related texts (in many languages) and conditioning on them to maximize the likelihood of generating the original. We show it is possible to jointly learn to do retrieval and reconstruction, given only a random initialization. The objective noisily captures aspects of paraphrase, translation, multi-document summarization, and information retrieval, allowing for strong zero-shot performance on several tasks. For example, with no additional task-specific training we achieve BLEU scores of up to 35.8 for document translation. We further show that fine-tuning gives strong performance on a range of discriminative and generative tasks in many languages, making MARGE the most generally applicable pre-training method to date.

paragraphs: MARGE learns to generate text by retrieving related documents and using them to reconstruct a target document. The retrieved material can span multiple languages. This creates an unsupervised, multilingual, multi-document paraphrasing objective that offers an alternative to pre-training through masked language modeling.

The authors show that retrieval and reconstruction can be learned jointly from random initialization. The training objective approximately brings together abilities associated with paraphrasing, translation, summarization across documents, and information retrieval. Those connections are noisy rather than exact task supervision, but they allow a single pre-training procedure to develop capabilities useful across different language tasks.

Without additional task-specific training, MARGE achieves strong results on several tasks, including document translation with BLEU scores up to 35.8. Fine-tuning also produces strong performance across discriminative and generative tasks in multiple languages. The authors present this breadth as evidence for an especially general pre-training method. The reported findings show that retrieving related text can support both learning to reconstruct language and transferring the resulting model to varied tasks.
summary.tldr: MARGE jointly learns multilingual retrieval and text reconstruction, enabling strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance across language tasks.

title: Pre-training via Paraphrasing

abstract: Reinforcement learning has shown great promise for synthesizing realistic human behaviors by learning humanoid control policies from motion capture data. However, it is still very challenging to reproduce sophisticated human skills like ballet dance, or to stably imitate long-term human behaviors with complex transitions. The main difficulty lies in the dynamics mismatch between the humanoid model and real humans. That is, motions of real humans may not be physically possible for the humanoid model. To overcome the dynamics mismatch, we propose a novel approach, residual force control (RFC), that augments a humanoid control policy by adding external residual forces into the action space. During training, the RFC-based policy learns to apply residual forces to the humanoid to compensate for the dynamics mismatch and better imitate the reference motion. Experiments on a wide range of dynamic motions demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of convergence speed and the quality of learned motions. Notably, we showcase a physics-based virtual character empowered by RFC that can perform highly agile ballet dance moves such as pirouette, arabesque and jeté. Furthermore, we propose a dual-policy control framework, where a kinematic policy and an RFC-based policy work in tandem to synthesize multi-modal infinite-horizon human motions without any task guidance or user input. Our approach is the first humanoid control method that successfully learns from a large-scale human motion dataset (Human3.6M) and generates diverse long-term motions. Code and videos are available at https://www.ye-yuan.com/rfc.

Residual force control addresses that mismatch by adding external forces to the actions available to a reinforcement-learning controller. During training, the policy learns how to use those forces to better follow reference motion.

summary.tldr: Learned external residual forces help simulated humanoids imitate agile human motion and support diverse long-term motion synthesis.

title: Residual Force Control for Agile Human Behavior Imitation and Extended Motion Synthesis

abstract: Available 3D human pose estimation approaches leverage different forms of strong (2D/3D pose) or weak (multi-view or depth) paired supervision. Barring synthetic or in-studio domains, acquiring such supervision for each new target environment is highly inconvenient. To this end, we cast 3D pose learning as a self-supervised adaptation problem that aims to transfer the task knowledge from a labeled source domain to a completely unpaired target. We propose to infer image-to-pose via two explicit mappings viz. image-to-latent and latent-to-pose where the latter is a pre-learned decoder obtained from a prior-enforcing generative adversarial auto-encoder. Next, we introduce relation distillation as a means to align the unpaired cross-modal samples i.e., the unpaired target videos and unpaired 3D pose sequences. To this end, we propose a new set of non-local relations in order to characterize long-range latent pose interactions, unlike general contrastive relations where positive couplings are limited to a local neighborhood structure. Further, we provide an objective way to quantify non-localness in order to select the most effective relation set. We evaluate different self-adaptation settings and demonstrate state-of-the-art 3D human pose estimation performance on standard benchmarks.

This paper instead studies self-supervised adaptation from a labeled source domain to an entirely unpaired target domain. The target information consists of videos and three-dimensional pose sequences without corresponding video-to-pose pairs.

The model separates image-to-pose prediction into an image-to-latent mapping and a latent-to-pose mapping. The latter is a decoder learned beforehand using a generative adversarial autoencoder that enforces a prior. Relation distillation then aligns the unpaired visual and pose samples through relationships in their latent representations.

The authors also define an objective measure of non-localness to select effective relation sets. Evaluations across different self-adaptation settings achieve state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. The findings support using relationships among unpaired samples to transfer pose knowledge without collecting matched supervision for each target environment.
summary.tldr: Non-local relation distillation adapts 3D pose estimation to unpaired target videos and pose sequences by aligning long-range relationships in latent space.

title: Non-local Latent Relation Distillation for Self-Adaptive 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: The generalization of representations learned via contrastive learning depends crucially on what features of the data are extracted. However, we observe that the contrastive loss does not always sufficiently guide which features are extracted, a behavior that can negatively impact the performance on downstream tasks via “shortcuts", i.e., by inadvertently suppressing important predictive features. We find that feature extraction is influenced by the difficulty of the so-called instance discrimination task (i.e., the task of discriminating pairs of similar points from pairs of dissimilar ones). Although harder pairs improve the representation of some features, the improvement comes at the cost of suppressing previously well represented features. In response, we propose implicit feature modification (IFM), a method for altering positive and negative samples in order to guide contrastive models towards capturing a wider variety of predictive features. Empirically, we observe that IFM reduces feature suppression, and as a result improves performance on vision and medical imaging tasks.
originalAbstract: The generalization of representations learned via contrastive learning depends crucially on what features of the data are extracted. However, we observe that the contrastive loss does not always sufficiently guide which features are extracted, a behavior that can negatively impact the performance on downstream tasks via “shortcuts", i.e., by inadvertently suppressing important predictive features. We find that feature extraction is influenced by the difficulty of the so-called instance discrimination task (i.e., the task of discriminating pairs of similar points from pairs of dissimilar ones). Although harder pairs improve the representation of some features, the improvement comes at the cost of suppressing previously well represented features. In response, we propose implicit feature modification (IFM), a method for altering positive and negative samples in order to guide contrastive models towards capturing a wider variety of predictive features. Empirically, we observe that IFM reduces feature suppression, and as a result improves performance on vision and medical imaging tasks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning trains a representation by distinguishing similar pairs of examples from dissimilar pairs. Success at this training task does not necessarily mean the representation captures everything useful for later predictions. This paper investigates shortcuts in which the model suppresses important predictive features while still satisfying its contrastive objective.

The authors find that the difficulty of the pair-discrimination task influences which features survive. Making pairs harder can improve the representation of some features, but this improvement can come at the expense of features that were already represented well. The finding makes pair difficulty a tradeoff rather than a straightforward route to richer representations.

To address this behavior, the paper introduces implicit feature modification, or IFM. It alters positive and negative samples to steer the model toward retaining a broader variety of predictive information. Experiments on vision and medical imaging tasks show reduced feature suppression and improved downstream performance. These results support IFM as a way to counter the observed shortcut behavior, without establishing that contrastive learning becomes free of shortcuts in every setting.
summary.tldr: Implicit feature modification reduces observed contrastive-learning shortcuts by encouraging models to retain more predictive features.

title: Can contrastive learning avoid shortcut solutions?

abstract: We consider the setting of vector valued non-linear dynamical systems $X_{t+1} = \phi(A^{*} X_t) + \eta_t$, where $\eta_t$ is unbiased noise and $\phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a known link function that satisfies certain {\em expansivity property}. The goal is to learn $A^{*}$ from a single trajectory $X_1,\cdots , X_T$ of {\em dependent or correlated} samples.While the problem is well-studied in the linear case, where $\phi$ is identity, with optimal error rates even for non-mixing systems, existing results in the non-linear case hold only for mixing systems. In this work, we improve existing results for learning nonlinear systems in a number of ways: a) we provide the first offline algorithm that can learn non-linear dynamical systems without the mixing assumption, b) we significantly improve upon the sample complexity of existing results for mixing systems, c) in the much harder one-pass, streaming setting we study a SGD with Reverse Experience Replay (SGD-RER) method, and demonstrate that for mixing systems, it achieves the same sample complexity as our offline algorithm, d) we justify the expansivity assumption by showing that for the popular ReLU link function --- a non-expansive but easy to learn link function with i.i.d. samples --- any method would require exponentially many samples (with respect to dimension of $X_t$) from the dynamical system. We validate our results via. simulations and demonstrate that a naive application of SGD can be highly sub-optimal. Indeed, our work demonstrates that for correlated data, specialized methods designed for the dependency structure in data can significantly outperform standard SGD based methods.

The system applies an unknown matrix and a known nonlinear link function, then adds unbiased noise. The goal is to estimate the matrix under an expansivity property of the link function.

The authors provide an offline algorithm that does not require the system to be mixing, an assumption used by previous nonlinear results. For mixing systems, they also improve sample complexity. In the one-pass streaming setting, their stochastic gradient method with reverse experience replay matches the offline algorithm's sample complexity when mixing holds.

For the ReLU link, which lacks the required property, the authors show that learning from the dynamical system can require exponentially many samples in the state dimension, despite its tractability with independent samples. Simulations support the analysis and show that naive stochastic gradient descent can be highly suboptimal. The results explain why methods tailored to temporal dependence can outperform standard gradient training.
summary.tldr: Algorithms tailored to correlated trajectories improve nonlinear system learning, with offline guarantees beyond mixing and matching streaming rates under mixing.

title: Near-optimal Offline and Streaming Algorithms for Learning Non-Linear Dynamical Systems

abstract: Despite remarkable success in a variety of applications, it is well-known that deep learning can fail catastrophically when presented with out-of-distribution data. Toward addressing this challenge, we consider the \emph{domain generalization} problem, wherein predictors are trained using data drawn from a family of related training domains and then evaluated on a distinct and unseen test domain. We show that under a natural model of data generation and a concomitant invariance condition, the domain generalization problem is equivalent to an infinite-dimensional constrained statistical learning problem; this problem forms the basis of our approach, which we call Model-Based Domain Generalization. Due to the inherent challenges in solving constrained optimization problems in deep learning, we exploit nonconvex duality theory to develop unconstrained relaxations of this statistical problem with tight bounds on the duality gap. Based on this theoretical motivation, we propose a novel domain generalization algorithm with convergence guarantees. In our experiments, we report improvements of up to 30% over state-of-the-art domain generalization baselines on several benchmarks including ColoredMNIST, Camelyon17-WILDS, FMoW-WILDS, and PACS.

paragraphs: Domain generalization trains a predictor on related domains and evaluates it on a distinct domain it has never seen. This matters because strong performance on training-like data can coexist with severe failure under a distribution change. The paper develops an approach that explicitly connects generalization to a model of how data is generated.

Under that data-generation model and an associated invariance condition, the authors show that domain generalization is equivalent to an infinite-dimensional constrained learning problem. They then use nonconvex duality theory to derive unconstrained relaxations with tight bounds on the duality gap. These relaxations provide a more tractable foundation for the proposed learning algorithm, which has convergence guarantees.

Experiments report improvements of up to 30% over leading domain-generalization baselines across benchmarks including ColoredMNIST, Camelyon17-WILDS, FMoW-WILDS, and PACS. The theoretical equivalence depends on the stated modeling and invariance conditions, while the reported gains are empirical. Together, they connect a principled formulation of domain change with an algorithm that performs strongly in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Model-Based Domain Generalization derives a convergent algorithm from a conditional constrained-learning formulation and reports benchmark improvements of up to 30%.

title: Model-Based Domain Generalization

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) in the infinite width/channel limit have received much attention recently, as they provide a clear analytical window to deep learning via mappings to Gaussian Processes (GPs). Despite its theoretical appeal, this viewpoint lacks a crucial ingredient of deep learning in finite DNNs, laying at the heart of their success --- \textit{feature learning}. Here we consider DNNs trained with noisy gradient descent on a large training set and derive a self-consistent Gaussian Process theory accounting for \textit{strong} finite-DNN and feature learning effects. Applying this to a toy model of a two-layer linear convolutional neural network (CNN) shows good agreement with experiments. We further identify, both analytically and numerically, a sharp transition between a feature learning regime and a lazy learning regime in this model. Strong finite-DNN effects are also derived for a non-linear two-layer fully connected network. We have numerical evidence demonstrating that the assumptions required for our theory hold true in more realistic settings (Myrtle5 CNN trained on CIFAR-10).Our self-consistent theory provides a rich and versatile analytical framework for studying strong finite-DNN effects, most notably - feature learning.

paragraphs: Connections between infinitely wide neural networks and Gaussian processes make some aspects of deep learning easier to analyze. However, that perspective misses feature learning, a central behavior of finite networks. This paper develops a self-consistent Gaussian process theory that accounts for strong effects of finite network size, including changes in the features learned during training.

The analysis considers networks trained with noisy gradient descent on a large training set. Applied to a simplified two-layer linear convolutional network, the theory agrees well with experiments. In that model, the authors identify a sharp transition between a feature-learning regime and a lazy-learning regime, supporting the transition with both mathematical analysis and numerical results.

Numerical evidence from Myrtle5 trained on CIFAR-10 supports the theory's assumptions in a more realistic setting. Together, these results extend the analytical usefulness of Gaussian processes while distinguishing direct demonstrations in simplified models from evidence supporting applicability to larger networks.
summary.tldr: A self-consistent Gaussian process theory captures feature learning and other strong finite-network effects under the studied training conditions.

title: A self consistent theory of Gaussian Processes captures feature learning effects in finite CNNs

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of iterative machine teaching, where a teacher provides examples sequentially based on the current iterative learner. In contrast to previous methods that have to scan over the entire pool and select teaching examples from it in each iteration, we propose a label synthesis teaching framework where the teacher randomly selects input teaching examples (e.g., images) and then synthesizes suitable outputs (e.g., labels) for them. We show that this framework can avoid costly example selection while still provably achieving exponential teachability. We propose multiple novel teaching algorithms in this framework. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the value of our framework.

paragraphs: In iterative machine teaching, a teacher supplies training examples sequentially while taking the learner’s current state into account. Previous approaches can make this expensive by searching the entire example pool at every iteration. This paper asks whether the teacher can guide learning effectively without repeatedly performing that costly input-selection step.

The proposed framework randomly chooses an input example and then synthesizes an appropriate output for it. For an image input, that output could be a label. The teacher’s effort therefore shifts from finding a particular example to designing what the selected example should teach the current learner. The paper introduces several algorithms within this framework.

The authors prove that label synthesis can retain exponential teachability while avoiding the expensive example-selection procedure. They also report empirical evidence of the framework’s value. The result makes the teaching signal itself an important object of design: adapting the output can provide strong teaching capability even when the input is selected randomly rather than through a full search.
summary.tldr: Synthesizing labels for randomly selected inputs can avoid costly teaching-example searches while retaining provable exponential teachability.

title: Iterative Teaching by Label Synthesis

abstract: We introduce a novel measure for quantifying the error in input predictions. The error is based on a minimum-cost hyperedge cover in a suitably defined hypergraph and provides a general template which we apply to online graph problems. The measure captures errors due to absent predicted requests as well as unpredicted actual requests; hence, predicted and actual inputs can be of arbitrary size. We achieve refined performance guarantees for previously studied network design problems in the online-list model, such as Steiner tree and facility location. Further, we initiate the study of learning-augmented algorithms for online routing problems, such as the online traveling salesperson problem and the online dial-a-ride problem, where (transportation) requests arrive over time (online-time model). We provide a general algorithmic framework and we give error-dependent performance bounds that improve upon known worst-case barriers, when given accurate predictions, at the cost of slightly increased worst-case bounds when given predictions of arbitrary quality.

paragraphs: Online graph algorithms must make decisions as requests arrive, without knowing the full future input. Predictions can help, but evaluating their usefulness requires an error measure that handles both requests that were predicted but never arrive and requests that arrive unexpectedly. This paper proposes a general template that accommodates both, even when predicted and actual inputs have different sizes.

The measure uses a minimum-cost hyperedge cover in a specially constructed hypergraph. This gives the authors a way to connect discrepancies in predictions to algorithmic performance. They apply it to network design problems, including Steiner tree and facility location, and obtain more refined guarantees for the setting where requests are revealed in a list.

The paper also develops a framework for routing problems where transportation requests arrive over time, including traveling salesperson and dial-a-ride problems. Accurate predictions yield bounds better than established worst-case barriers. The tradeoff is a slight increase in worst-case bounds when predictions have arbitrary quality, making the benefit explicitly dependent on prediction accuracy.
summary.tldr: A general prediction-error measure supports improved online graph algorithms when predictions are accurate, with slightly worse worst-case bounds.

title: A Universal Error Measure for Input Predictions Applied to Online Graph Problems

abstract: Virtual, make-on-demand chemical libraries have transformed early-stage drug discovery by unlocking vast, synthetically accessible regions of chemical space. Recent years have witnessed rapid growth in these libraries from millions to trillions of compounds, hiding undiscovered, potent hits for a variety of therapeutic targets. However, they are quickly approaching a size beyond that which permits explicit enumeration, presenting new challenges for virtual screening. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Combinatorial Synthesis Library Variational Auto-Encoder (CSLVAE). The proposed generative model represents such libraries as a differentiable, hierarchically-organized database. Given a compound from the library, the molecular encoder constructs a query for retrieval, which is utilized by the molecular decoder to reconstruct the compound by first decoding its chemical reaction and subsequently decoding its reactants. Our design minimizes autoregression in the decoder, facilitating the generation of large, valid molecular graphs. Our method performs fast and parallel batch inference for ultra-large synthesis libraries, enabling a number of important applications in early-stage drug discovery. Compounds proposed by our method are guaranteed to be in the library, and thus synthetically and cost-effectively accessible. Importantly, CSLVAE can encode out-of-library compounds and search for in-library analogues. In experiments, we demonstrate the capabilities of the proposed method in the navigation of massive combinatorial synthesis libraries.

title: An efficient graph generative model for navigating ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries

abstract: Deep learning has achieved many breakthroughs in modern classification tasks. Numerous architectures have been proposed for different data structures but when it comes to the loss function, the cross-entropy loss is the predominant choice. Recently, several alternative losses have seen revived interests for deep classifiers. In particular, empirical evidence seems to promote square loss but a theoretical justification is still lacking. In this work, we contribute to the theoretical understanding of square loss in classification by systematically investigating how it performs for overparametrized neural networks in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime. Interesting properties regarding the generalization error, robustness, and calibration error are revealed. We consider two cases, according to whether classes are separable or not. In the general non-separable case, fast convergence rate is established for both misclassification rate and calibration error. When classes are separable, the misclassification rate improves to be exponentially fast. Further, the resulting margin is proven to be lower bounded away from zero, providing theoretical guarantees for robustness. We expect our findings to hold beyond the NTK regime and translate to practical settings. To this end, we conduct extensive empirical studies on practical neural networks, demonstrating the effectiveness of square loss in both synthetic low-dimensional data and real image data. Comparing to cross-entropy, square loss has comparable generalization error but noticeable advantages in robustness and model calibration.

title: Understanding Square Loss in Training Overparametrized Neural Network Classifiers

abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) has been proven to be effective for tasks with sparse rewards, for it can improve the agent's exploration efficiency by discovering high-quality hierarchical structures (e.g., subgoals or options). However, automatically discovering high-quality hierarchical structures is still a great challenge. Previous HRL methods can only find the hierarchical structures in simple environments, as they are mainly achieved through the randomness of agent's policies during exploration. In complicated environments, such a randomness-driven exploration paradigm can hardly discover high-quality hierarchical structures because of the low exploration efficiency. In this paper, we propose CDHRL, a causality-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework, to build high-quality hierarchical structures efficiently in complicated environments. The key insight is that the causalities among environment variables are naturally fit for modeling reachable subgoals and their dependencies; thus, the causality is suitable to be the guidance in building high-quality hierarchical structures. Roughly, we build the hierarchy of subgoals based on causality autonomously, and utilize the subgoal-based policies to unfold further causality efficiently. Therefore, CDHRL leverages a causality-driven discovery instead of a randomness-driven exploration for high-quality hierarchical structure construction. The results in two complex environments, 2D-Minecraft and Eden, show that CDHRL can discover high-quality hierarchical structures and significantly enhance exploration efficiency.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning organizes behavior around intermediate goals, which can help an agent explore when rewards are sparse. The difficult part is discovering useful intermediate goals and their dependencies. This paper argues that relying primarily on randomness during exploration makes that discovery inefficient in complicated environments.

The proposed CDHRL framework uses causal relationships among environment variables to guide construction of a subgoal hierarchy. These relationships provide information about which subgoals are reachable and how achieving one may depend on others. Its broader methodological significance is the use of causal dependencies to organize exploration: the agent's emerging understanding of the environment helps determine what it should attempt next.
summary.tldr: CDHRL uses causal dependencies to discover subgoal hierarchies and improves exploration in two complex reinforcement-learning environments.

title: Causality-driven Hierarchical Structure Discovery for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A fundamental procedure in the analysis of massive datasets is the construction of similarity graphs. Such graphs play a key role for many downstream tasks, including clustering, classification, graph learning, and nearest neighbor search. For these tasks, it is critical to build graphs which are sparse yet still representative of the underlying data. The benefits of sparsity are twofold: firstly, constructing dense graphs is infeasible in practice for large datasets, and secondly, the runtime of downstream tasks is directly influenced by the sparsity of the similarity graph. In this work, we present Stars: a highly scalable method for building extremely sparse graphs via two-hop spanners, which are graphs where similar points are connected by a path of length at most two. Stars can construct two-hop spanners with significantly fewer similarity comparisons, which are a major bottleneck for learning based models where comparisons are expensive to evaluate. Theoretically, we demonstrate that Stars builds a graph in nearly-linear time, where approximate nearest neighbors are contained within two-hop neighborhoods. In practice, we have deployed Stars for multiple data sets allowing for graph building at the Tera-Scale, i.e., for graphs with hundreds of billions of nodes and tens of trillions of edges. We evaluate the performance of Stars for clustering and graph learning, and demonstrate 10~1000-fold improvements in pairwise similarity comparisons and significant running time speedups with negligible quality loss.

Sparsity matters both when building the graph and when running later algorithms on it. Stars aims to preserve useful neighborhood structure while greatly reducing edges and expensive similarity comparisons.

These results indicate that preserving short paths between related points can make enormous similarity graphs useful without requiring dense direct connections.
summary.tldr: Stars builds extremely sparse similarity graphs using two-hop connections, enabling massive-scale construction with far fewer comparisons.

title: Stars: Tera-Scale Graph Building for Clustering and Learning

abstract: Drug design is a crucial step in the drug discovery cycle. Recently, various deep learning-based methods design drugs by generating novel molecules from scratch, avoiding traversing large-scale drug libraries. However, they depend on scarce experimental data or time-consuming docking simulation, leading to overfitting issues with limited training data and slow generation speed. In this study, we propose the zero-shot drug design method DESERT (Drug dEsign by SkEtching and geneRaTing). Specifically, DESERT splits the design process into two stages: sketching and generating, and bridges them with the molecular shape. The two-stage fashion enables our method to utilize the large-scale molecular database to reduce the need for experimental data and docking simulation. Experiments show that DESERT achieves a new state-of-the-art at a fast speed.

In this study, we propose the zero-shot drug design method DESERT (Drug dEsign by SkEtching and geneRaTing). Specifically, DESERT splits the design process into two stages: sketching and generating, and bridges them with the molecular shape. The two-stage fashion enables our method to utilize the large-scale molecular database to reduce the need for experimental data and docking simulation. Experiments show that DESERT achieves a new state-of-the-art at a fast speed.

paragraphs: Generating new molecules from scratch offers an alternative to searching large drug libraries. However, the paper identifies two obstacles for existing deep-learning approaches: dependence on scarce experimental data and reliance on time-consuming docking simulations. Limited training data can lead to overfitting, while simulation requirements can slow the generation process.

DESERT divides design into two stages, called sketching and generating, and uses molecular shape to connect them. This separation allows the method to use a large molecular database, reducing its need for experimental data and docking simulation. Shape serves as the shared representation linking the stages, making database information useful within the proposed zero-shot design process.

The experiments report state-of-the-art performance together with fast generation. The stated contribution is the two-stage organization and its ability to reduce dependence on costly or scarce inputs while producing new molecular candidates. These findings concern computational drug design: the abstract’s performance claim supports the generation approach and its speed, without establishing that generated candidates have demonstrated therapeutic effectiveness.
summary.tldr: DESERT connects molecular sketching and generation through shape to reduce reliance on experimental data and docking simulations.

title: Zero-Shot 3D Drug Design by Sketching and Generating

abstract: We study stochastic monotone inclusion problems, which widely appear in machine learning applications, including robust regression and adversarial learning. We propose novel variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with recursive variance reduction. In the cocoercive---and more generally Lipschitz-monotone---setup, our algorithm attains $\epsilon$ norm of the operator with $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^3})$ stochastic operator evaluations, which significantly improves over state of the art $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^4})$ stochastic operator evaluations required for existing monotone inclusion solvers applied to the same problem classes. We further show how to couple one of the proposed variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with a scheduled restart scheme to solve stochastic monotone inclusion problems with ${\mathcal{O}}(\frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{\epsilon^2})$ stochastic operator evaluations under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions.

paragraphs: Stochastic monotone inclusion problems arise in applications including robust regression and adversarial learning. Their solvers work with stochastic operator evaluations, and the paper measures computational effort by how many such evaluations are needed to reach a specified accuracy. The goal is to reduce that evaluation cost.

The authors introduce variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with recursive variance reduction. Under cocoercivity, and more generally in the Lipschitz-monotone setting, the method reaches an operator norm of epsilon using O(1/epsilon³) evaluations. Existing solvers cited for these same problem classes require O(1/epsilon⁴). The improved exponent means the stated evaluation bound grows more slowly as the desired tolerance becomes smaller.

A further result combines one variant with scheduled restarts. Under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions, the evaluation requirement becomes O(log(1/epsilon)/epsilon²). These stronger assumptions are part of that faster guarantee. The paper thus gives improved complexity results at two levels of problem structure, showing how variance reduction and, when justified, restarts can reduce the stochastic evaluations needed for accuracy.
summary.tldr: Variance-reduced stochastic Halpern methods improve evaluation complexity, with faster guarantees under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions.

title: Stochastic Halpern Iteration with Variance Reduction for Stochastic Monotone Inclusions

abstract: Recently, tensor network (TN) decompositions have gained prominence in computer vision and contributed promising results to high-order data recovery tasks. However, current TN models are rather being developed towards more intricate structures to pursue incremental improvements, which instead leads to a dramatic increase in rank numbers, thus encountering laborious hyper-parameter selection, especially for higher-order cases. In this paper, we propose a novel TN decomposition, dubbed tensor wheel (TW) decomposition, in which a high-order tensor is represented by a set of latent factors mapped into a specific wheel topology. Such decomposition is constructed starting from analyzing the graph structure, aiming to more accurately characterize the complex interactions inside objectives while maintaining a lower hyper-parameter scale, theoretically alleviating the above deficiencies. Furthermore, to investigate the potentiality of TW decomposition, we provide its one numerical application, i.e., tensor completion (TC), yet develop an efficient proximal alternating minimization-based solving algorithm with guaranteed convergence. Experimental results elaborate that the proposed method is significantly superior to other tensor decomposition-based state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world data, implying the merits of TW decomposition. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhongchengwu/code_TWDec.

paragraphs: Tensor decompositions represent high-dimensional arrays through interacting smaller factors. More elaborate tensor-network structures can improve recovery of missing data, but they also introduce many rank settings to choose. The paper addresses this growing hyperparameter burden, particularly when the data have many dimensions.

Tensor wheel decomposition arranges latent factors in a wheel-shaped network. The design starts from analysis of the graph structure, aiming to capture complex interactions while keeping the number of hyperparameters lower. The authors argue theoretically that this organization alleviates the difficulties associated with increasingly intricate tensor-network models.

To demonstrate the decomposition, the paper applies it to tensor completion, the recovery of missing entries. It develops an efficient solver based on proximal alternating minimization and provides a convergence guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real data report significantly better performance than other state-of-the-art tensor-decomposition methods. These findings support the wheel topology as a useful representation for the tested recovery problems, pairing its structural design with a concrete optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Tensor wheel decomposition uses a wheel-shaped factor network to limit hyperparameter complexity and improve tensor completion in reported experiments.

title: Tensor Wheel Decomposition and Its Tensor Completion Application

abstract: In this paper we study the problem of testing of constrained samplers over high-dimensional distributions with $(\varepsilon,\eta,\delta)$ guarantees. Samplers are increasingly used in a wide range of safety-critical ML applications, and hence the testing problem has gained importance. For $n$-dimensional distributions, the existing state-of-the-art algorithm, $\mathsf{Barbarik2}$, has a worst case query complexity of exponential in $n$ and hence is not ideal for use in practice. Our primary contribution is an exponentially faster algorithm, $\mathsf{Barbarik3}$, that has a query complexity linear in $n$ and hence can easily scale to larger instances. We demonstrate our claim by implementing our algorithm and then comparing it against $\mathsf{Barbarik2}$. Our experiments on the samplers $\mathsf{wUnigen3}$ and $\mathsf{wSTS}$, find that $\mathsf{Barbarik3}$ requires $10\times$ fewer samples for $\mathsf{wUnigen3}$ and $450\times$ fewer samples for $\mathsf{wSTS}$ as compared to $\mathsf{Barbarik2}$.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test constrained samplers for high-dimensional distributions with formal guarantees expressed through epsilon, eta, and delta. Such testing matters when samplers are used in safety-critical machine-learning applications. The central practical obstacle is the number of queries required to test a sampler as the distribution's dimension grows.

The previous algorithm, Barbarik2, has worst-case query complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. The proposed Barbarik3 reduces that dependence to linear growth. This is an exponential improvement in dimensional scaling, making the testing procedure substantially more suitable for larger instances under the paper's testing framework.

The authors implement Barbarik3 and compare it with Barbarik2 on two samplers. Barbarik3 uses ten times fewer samples for wUnigen3 and 450 times fewer for wSTS in these experiments. These results provide concrete evidence alongside the complexity analysis: the new algorithm improves the theoretical scaling and also substantially reduces sample requirements in the evaluated cases.
summary.tldr: Barbarik3 reduces sampler-testing query complexity from exponential to linear in dimension, with substantial sample savings in two evaluated samplers.

title: On Scalable Testing of Samplers

abstract: In human networks, nodes belonging to a marginalized group often have a disproportionate rate of unknown or missing features. This, in conjunction with graph structure and known feature biases, can cause graph feature imputation algorithms to predict values for unknown features that make the marginalized group's feature values more distinct from the the dominant group's feature values than they are in reality. We call this distinction the discrimination risk. We prove that a higher discrimination risk can amplify the unfairness of a machine learning model applied to the imputed data. We then formalize a general graph feature imputation framework called mean aggregation imputation and theoretically and empirically characterize graphs in which applying this framework can yield feature values with a high discrimination risk. We propose a simple algorithm to ensure mean aggregation-imputed features provably have a low discrimination risk, while minimally sacrificing reconstruction error (with respect to the imputation objective). We evaluate the fairness and accuracy of our solution on synthetic and real-world credit networks.

paragraphs: Filling in missing attributes in a human network can change how groups appear in the data. Marginalized groups may have more missing features, and network structure together with biases in observed features can cause imputation to exaggerate differences between groups. The paper calls this artificial increase in distinctness discrimination risk.

The authors prove that higher discrimination risk can amplify unfairness in a model trained or applied on the completed data. They formalize mean aggregation imputation as a general framework and study, theoretically and empirically, which graph conditions can make its inferred features carry high discrimination risk. This connects a data preparation operation to possible downstream fairness consequences.

They then propose a simple algorithm that guarantees low discrimination risk for mean-aggregation-imputed features while minimally sacrificing reconstruction error under the imputation objective. Evaluation considers fairness and accuracy on synthetic and real credit networks. The contribution makes group distortion an explicit target during imputation, alongside the usual objective of reconstructing missing feature values.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how graph feature imputation can exaggerate group differences and proposes an algorithm with provably low discrimination risk.

title: On the Discrimination Risk of Mean Aggregation Feature Imputation in Graphs

abstract: This paper uncovers a simple but rather surprising connection: it shows that the well-known convex-concave procedure (CCCP) and its generalization to constrained problems are both special cases of the Frank-Wolfe (FW) method. This connection not only provides insight of deep (in our opinion) pedagogical value, but also transfers the recently discovered convergence theory of nonconvex Frank-Wolfe methods immediately to CCCP, closing a long-standing gap in its non-asymptotic convergence theory. We hope the viewpoint uncovered by this paper spurs the transfer of other advances made for FW to both CCCP and its generalizations.
originalAbstract: This paper uncovers a simple but rather surprising connection: it shows that the well-known convex-concave procedure (CCCP) and its generalization to constrained problems are both special cases of the Frank-Wolfe (FW) method. This connection not only provides insight of deep (in our opinion) pedagogical value, but also transfers the recently discovered convergence theory of nonconvex Frank-Wolfe methods immediately to CCCP, closing a long-standing gap in its non-asymptotic convergence theory. We hope the viewpoint uncovered by this paper spurs the transfer of other advances made for FW to both CCCP and its generalizations.

paragraphs: The paper establishes a connection between two optimization methods usually presented separately: the convex-concave procedure, or CCCP, and Frank-Wolfe. It shows that CCCP can be understood as a special case of Frank-Wolfe. The same relationship also covers a generalization of CCCP for constrained problems, giving the connection a broader reach than the original procedure alone.

The immediate payoff is theoretical. Recent convergence results for nonconvex Frank-Wolfe methods can be transferred to CCCP through this relationship. In particular, this closes a longstanding gap in CCCP's non-asymptotic convergence theory: understanding what can be guaranteed after a finite amount of computation, rather than only describing behavior as the number of iterations grows indefinitely.

The contribution therefore gives an established algorithm a different mathematical foundation and a route to existing guarantees. It also offers a unified way to teach and reason about these methods. The authors suggest that other advances in Frank-Wolfe could eventually benefit CCCP and its generalizations; that broader transfer is a proposed research direction beyond the convergence connection established here.
summary.tldr: Showing that CCCP and its constrained generalization are special cases of Frank-Wolfe transfers finite-iteration convergence theory to CCCP.

title: CCCP is Frank-Wolfe in disguise

abstract: We study {\it model reusability evaluation} (MRE) for source pre-trained models: evaluating their transfer learning performance to new target tasks. In special, we focus on the setting under which the target training datasets are small, making it difficult to produce reliable MRE scores using them. Under this situation, we propose {\it synergistic learning} for building the task-model metric, which can be realized by collecting a set of pre-trained models and asking a group of data providers to participate. We provide theoretical guarantees to show that the learned task-model metric distances can serve as trustworthy MRE scores, and propose synergistic learning algorithms and models for general learning tasks. Experiments show that the MRE models learned by synergistic learning can generate significantly more reliable MRE scores than existing approaches for small-data transfer learning.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained model for a new task requires estimating how well its knowledge will transfer. This paper studies that evaluation problem when the target task has little training data. Small datasets make it difficult to obtain reliable scores, so the model-selection decision itself becomes an important learning challenge.

The proposed solution, synergistic learning, builds a learned metric relating tasks and models. It can be implemented by assembling a collection of pretrained models and involving a group of data providers. This broader collection supplies the setting for learning the task-model relationship used to evaluate reusability.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees supporting the learned metric distances as trustworthy reusability scores, together with algorithms and models for general learning tasks. Experiments show significantly more reliable scores than existing approaches in small-data transfer settings. The main contribution concerns evaluating transfer potential: it makes the relationship between a candidate model and a target task something to learn across available resources, rather than relying solely on a small target dataset to produce the evaluation.
summary.tldr: Synergistic learning builds a task-model metric that improves pretrained-model reusability estimates when target datasets are small.

title: Pre-Trained Model Reusability Evaluation for Small-Data Transfer Learning

abstract: The task of Human-Object Interaction (HOI) detection targets fine-grained visual parsing of humans interacting with their environment, enabling a broad range of applications. Prior work has demonstrated the benefits of effective architecture design and integration of relevant cues for more accurate HOI detection. However, the design of an appropriate pre-training strategy for this task remains underexplored by existing approaches. To address this gap, we propose $\textit{Relational Language-Image Pre-training}$ (RLIP), a strategy for contrastive pre-training that leverages both entity and relation descriptions. To make effective use of such pre-training, we make three technical contributions: (1) a new $\textbf{Par}$allel entity detection and $\textbf{Se}$quential relation inference (ParSe) architecture that enables the use of both entity and relation descriptions during holistically optimized pre-training; (2) a synthetic data generation framework, Label Sequence Extension, that expands the scale of language data available within each minibatch; (3) ambiguity-suppression mechanisms, Relation Quality Labels and Relation Pseudo-Labels, to mitigate the influence of ambiguous/noisy samples in the pre-training data. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the benefits of these contributions, collectively termed RLIP-ParSe, for improved zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuning HOI detection performance as well as increased robustness to learning from noisy annotations. Code will be available at https://github.com/JacobYuan7/RLIP.

paragraphs: Human-object interaction detection identifies how people interact with objects in an image. This requires understanding both the entities and their relationships. RLIP investigates pretraining designed specifically for that combination, using contrastive learning with language descriptions of entities and relations to prepare the model for interaction detection.

Its ParSe architecture detects entities in parallel and then infers relations sequentially, allowing both kinds of descriptions to participate in jointly optimized pretraining. A synthetic data procedure called Label Sequence Extension increases the amount of language data available within each minibatch. Together, these components organize how visual entities and relational language enter the learning process.

The framework also introduces Relation Quality Labels and Relation Pseudo-Labels to reduce the influence of ambiguous or noisy pretraining examples. Experiments show benefits from the combined RLIP-ParSe system in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned interaction detection, as well as improved robustness when learning from noisy annotations. The findings support pretraining that explicitly represents relationships, while also addressing the amount and ambiguity of the language supervision used.
summary.tldr: RLIP pretrains on entity and relation descriptions to improve human-object interaction detection across multiple supervision settings.

title: RLIP: Relational Language-Image Pre-training for Human-Object Interaction Detection

abstract: Most recurrent neural networks (RNNs) do not include a fundamental constraint of real neural circuits: Dale's Law, which implies that neurons must be excitatory (E) or inhibitory (I). Dale's Law is generally absent from RNNs because simply partitioning a standard network's units into E and I populations impairs learning. However, here we extend a recent feedforward bio-inspired EI network architecture, named Dale's ANNs, to recurrent networks, and demonstrate that good performance is possible while respecting Dale's Law. This begs the question: What makes some forms of EI network learn poorly and others learn well? And, why does the simple approach of incorporating Dale's Law impair learning? Historically the answer was thought to be the sign constraints on EI network parameters, and this was a motivation behind Dale's ANNs. However, here we show the spectral properties of the recurrent weight matrix at initialisation are more impactful on network performance than sign constraints. We find that simple EI partitioning results in a singular value distribution that is multimodal and dispersed, whereas standard RNNs have an unimodal, more clustered singular value distribution, as do recurrent Dale's ANNs. We also show that the spectral properties and performance of partitioned EI networks are worse for small networks with fewer I units, and we present normalised SVD entropy as a measure of spectrum pathology that correlates with performance. Overall, this work sheds light on a long-standing mystery in neuroscience-inspired AI and computational neuroscience, paving the way for greater alignment between neural networks and biology.
