The authors extend the biologically inspired Dale’s ANNs architecture to recurrent networks and demonstrate that good performance remains possible while respecting this constraint.

They then investigate why some excitatory-inhibitory designs learn better than others. Their results identify the initial recurrent weight matrix’s spectral properties as more influential than parameter sign constraints. Simple population partitioning produces a dispersed singular-value distribution with multiple modes. Standard recurrent networks and recurrent Dale’s ANNs instead have more concentrated distributions with a single mode.

The spectral problems and performance losses are worse in small partitioned networks with fewer inhibitory units. The authors also introduce normalized SVD entropy as a measure of spectral pathology and find that it correlates with performance. These findings redirect attention toward initialization and matrix structure when incorporating biological constraints, showing that the learning difficulty is not adequately explained by sign restrictions alone.
summary.tldr: Recurrent networks can learn well under Dale’s Law, with initial spectral properties explaining performance better than sign constraints alone.

title: Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective

abstract: Due to the inability to interact with the environment, offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods face the challenge of estimating the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) points. Existing methods for addressing this issue either control policy to exclude the OOD action or make the $Q$ function pessimistic. However, these methods can be overly conservative or fail to identify OOD areas accurately. To overcome this problem, we propose a Constrained Policy optimization with Explicit Behavior density (CPED) method that utilizes a flow-GAN model to explicitly estimate the density of behavior policy. By estimating the explicit density, CPED can accurately identify the safe region and enable exploration within the region, resulting in less conservative learning policies. We further provide theoretical results for both the flow-GAN estimator and performance guarantee for CPED by showing that CPED can find the optimal $Q$-function value. Empirically, CPED outperforms existing alternatives on various standard offline reinforcement learning tasks, yielding higher expected returns.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy without collecting new experience from the environment. This makes actions outside the recorded data distribution difficult to value reliably. Existing approaches restrict actions or deliberately lower estimated values, but these safeguards can be excessively conservative or fail to locate unsupported regions accurately.

CPED addresses this problem by explicitly estimating the density of the behavior policy using a flow-GAN model. This estimate identifies a region supported by the recorded behavior, within which the learned policy can explore alternatives. Here, the safe region refers to support for offline learning decisions; its role is to permit improvement while controlling exposure to unreliable value estimates.

The paper provides theoretical results for the density estimator and a performance guarantee showing that CPED can find the optimal Q-function value. Experiments on standard offline reinforcement learning tasks report higher expected returns than existing alternatives. Together, these results support using an explicit account of behavior density to make policy constraints less conservative.
summary.tldr: CPED estimates behavior-policy density explicitly to support less conservative offline policy improvement within a data-supported region.

title: Constrained Policy Optimization with Explicit Behavior Density For Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: It is well-known that modern computer vision systems often exhibit behaviors misaligned with those of humans: from adversarial attacks to image corruptions, deeplearning vision models suffer in a variety of settings that humans capably handle. Inlight of these phenomena, here we introduce another, orthogonal perspective studying the human-machine vision gap. We revisit the task of recovering images underdegradation, first introduced over 30 years ago in the Recognition-by-Componentstheory of human vision. Specifically, we study the performance and behavior ofneural networks on the seemingly simple task of classifying regular polygons atvarying orders of degradation along their perimeters. To this end, we implement theAutomated Shape Recoverability Testfor rapidly generating large-scale datasetsof perimeter-degraded regular polygons, modernizing the historically manual creation of image recoverability experiments. We then investigate the capacity ofneural networks to recognize and recover such degraded shapes when initializedwith different priors. Ultimately, we find that neural networks’ behavior on thissimple task conflicts with human behavior, raising a fundamental question of therobustness and learning capabilities of modern computer vision models

paragraphs: This paper studies a human-machine vision gap through a deliberately simple task: recognizing regular polygons when parts of their boundaries have been degraded. The question is whether neural networks can identify and recover shapes from incomplete visual evidence in ways consistent with human behavior. This offers another perspective alongside familiar failures involving adversarial inputs or image corruption.

The authors build the Automated Shape Recoverability Test to generate large datasets of polygons with varying degrees of perimeter degradation. The system modernizes a previously manual approach to image recoverability experiments associated with Recognition-by-Components theory. It makes it possible to investigate shape recognition systematically across many degraded examples and networks initialized with different priors.

The reported finding is that neural network behavior on this task conflicts with human behavior. The significance lies in the simplicity of the visual objects: a mismatch appears even when the task concerns basic geometric shapes. These results raise questions about robustness and learned visual recovery, without establishing that every network fails in the same way.
summary.tldr: Automated tests of degraded polygon recognition reveal neural network behavior that conflicts with human shape perception.

title: Degraded Polygons Raise Fundamental Questions of Neural Network Perception

abstract: Black-box optimization has gained great attention for its success in recent applications. However, scaling up to high-dimensional problems with good query efficiency remains challenging. This paper proposes a novel Rank-1 Lattice Targeted Sampling (RLTS) technique to address this issue. Our RLTS benefits from random rank-1 lattice Quasi-Monte Carlo, which enables us to perform fast local exact Gaussian processes (GP) training and inference with $O(n \log n)$ complexity w.r.t. $n$ batch samples. Furthermore, we developed a fast coordinate searching method with $O(n \log n)$ time complexity for fast targeted sampling. The fast computation enables us to plug our RLTS into the sampling phase of stochastic optimization methods. This improves the query efficiency while scaling up to higher dimensional problems than Bayesian optimization. Moreover, to construct rank-1 lattices efficiently, we proposed a closed-form construction. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmark test functions and black-box prompt fine-tuning for large language models demonstrate the query efficiency of our RLTS technique.
originalAbstract: Black-box optimization has gained great attention for its success in recent applications. However, scaling up to high-dimensional problems with good query efficiency remains challenging. This paper proposes a novel Rank-1 Lattice Targeted Sampling (RLTS) technique to address this issue. Our RLTS benefits from random rank-1 lattice Quasi-Monte Carlo, which enables us to perform fast local exact Gaussian processes (GP) training and inference with $O(n \log n)$ complexity w.r.t. $n$ batch samples. Furthermore, we developed a fast coordinate searching method with $O(n \log n)$ time complexity for fast targeted sampling. The fast computation enables us to plug our RLTS into the sampling phase of stochastic optimization methods. This improves the query efficiency while scaling up to higher dimensional problems than Bayesian optimization. Moreover, to construct rank-1 lattices efficiently, we proposed a closed-form construction. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmark test functions and black-box prompt fine-tuning for large language models demonstrate the query efficiency of our RLTS technique.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good inputs when an objective is accessed through evaluations. As the number of input dimensions grows, choosing useful evaluations efficiently becomes challenging. This paper introduces Rank-1 Lattice Targeted Sampling, or RLTS, to improve the sampling stage of stochastic optimization methods.

RLTS uses randomized rank-1 lattice Quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. The structure enables local exact Gaussian-process training and inference in O(n log n) time for a batch of n samples. The authors also develop a coordinate search procedure with the same time complexity and a closed-form way to construct the lattices. These components make targeted sampling computationally practical within the broader optimization process.

The paper reports that incorporating RLTS improves query efficiency while reaching higher-dimensional problems than Bayesian optimization. Experiments cover challenging benchmark functions and black-box prompt fine-tuning for large language models. The findings concern both the cost of deciding where to sample and the usefulness of the resulting evaluations: faster sampling computations support a more query-efficient search in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: RLTS uses structured lattice samples to make targeted black-box search computationally fast and empirically more query-efficient.

title: Fast Rank-1 Lattice Targeted Sampling for Black-box Optimization

abstract: Empirical risk minimization (ERM) of neural networks is prone to over-reliance on spurious correlations and poor generalization on minority groups. The recent deep feature reweighting (DFR) technique achieves state-of-the-art group robustness via simple last-layer retraining, but it requires held-out group and class annotations to construct a group-balanced reweighting dataset. In this work, we examine this impractical requirement and find that last-layer retraining can be surprisingly effective with no group annotations (other than for model selection) and only a handful of class annotations. We first show that last-layer retraining can greatly improve worst-group accuracy even when the reweighting dataset has only a small proportion of worst-group data. This implies a "free lunch" where holding out a subset of training data to retrain the last layer can substantially outperform ERM on the entire dataset with no additional data, annotations, or computation for training. To further improve group robustness, we introduce a lightweight method called selective last-layer finetuning (SELF), which constructs the reweighting dataset using misclassifications or disagreements. Our experiments present the first evidence that model disagreement upsamples worst-group data, enabling SELF to nearly match DFR on four well-established benchmarks across vision and language tasks with no group annotations and less than 3% of the held-out class annotations.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained to minimize average error can rely on spurious correlations and perform poorly on minority groups. Retraining only the final layer can improve group robustness, but the DFR approach requires group and class labels for a balanced held-out dataset. This paper investigates how much of that annotation requirement can be removed.

The authors find that final-layer retraining can substantially improve worst-group accuracy even when relatively few retraining examples come from the worst-performing group. Holding out part of the original training data for this purpose can outperform training with all the data, without additional data, annotations, or training computation. Their broader low-annotation setup still uses group annotations for model selection.

The proposed SELF method selects retraining examples through misclassifications or model disagreements. Experiments provide evidence that disagreement enriches the selected set with worst-group examples. Across four vision and language benchmarks, SELF nearly matches DFR while using less than 3% of the held-out class annotations and no group annotations for constructing the retraining set. The findings make final-layer retraining more practical under limited labeling resources.
summary.tldr: Selective final-layer retraining nearly matches DFR's group robustness with far fewer labels, while still using group annotations for model selection.

title: Towards Last-layer Retraining for Group Robustness with Fewer Annotations

abstract: We propose a novel neural network-based approach to modeling protein dynamics using an implicit representation of a protein’s surface in 3D and time. Our method utilizes the zero-level set of signed distance functions (SDFs) to represent protein surfaces, enabling temporally and spatially continuous representations of protein dynamics. Our experimental results demonstrate that our model accurately captures protein dynamic trajectories and can interpolate and extrapolate in 3D and time. Importantly, this is the first study to introduce this method and successfully model large-scale protein dynamics. This approach offers a promising alternative to current methods, overcoming the limitations of first-principles-based and deep learning methods, and provides a more scalable and efficient approach to modeling protein dynamics. Additionally, our surface representation approach simplifies calculations and allows identifying movement trends and amplitudes of protein domains, making it a useful tool for protein dynamics research. Codes are available at https://github.com/Sundw-818/DSR, and we have a project webpage that shows some video results, https://sundw-818.github.io/DSR/.

paragraphs: DSR models protein motion through a continuous representation of the protein’s surface in space and time. The approach uses a neural network to represent a signed distance function, whose zero-valued locations define the surface. Including time in this representation lets the same model describe how that surface changes as the protein moves.

This formulation supports evaluating the representation across spatial locations and times, rather than limiting the description to separate surface snapshots. The authors report that their model accurately captures protein trajectories and can interpolate and extrapolate in both space and time. They describe the work as the first successful application of this approach to large-scale protein dynamics.

The surface representation also simplifies calculations used to identify movement directions and amplitudes of protein domains. This connects the learned geometry to quantities useful for studying protein motion. The paper presents DSR as a promising, more scalable and efficient alternative to existing first-principles and deep learning approaches, with its experimental results supporting the proposed representation’s usefulness for dynamics research.
summary.tldr: DSR represents moving protein surfaces with neural signed distance functions, enabling continuous modeling and analysis across space and time.

title: DSR: Dynamical Surface Representation as Implicit Neural Networks for Protein

abstract: Machine learning models are often personalized based on information that is protected, sensitive, self-reported, or costly to acquire. These models use information about people, but do not facilitate nor inform their *consent*. Individuals cannot opt out of reporting information that a model needs to personalize their predictions nor tell if they benefit from personalization in the first place. We introduce a new family of prediction models, called participatory systems, that let individuals opt into personalization at prediction time. We present a model-agnostic algorithm to learn participatory systems for supervised learning tasks where models are personalized with categorical group attributes. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study of participatory systems in clinical prediction tasks, comparing them to common approaches for personalization and imputation. Our results show that participatory systems can facilitate and inform consent in a way that improves performance and privacy across all groups who report personal data.

paragraphs: Personalized prediction often depends on information that is sensitive, protected, self-reported, or costly to collect. Yet people may have little ability to decline disclosure or determine whether personalization helps them. This paper treats those choices as part of the prediction system itself, introducing participatory systems that let individuals opt into personalization when a prediction is made.

The authors provide a model-agnostic learning algorithm for supervised tasks in which personalization uses categorical group attributes. This scope makes the method applicable across underlying prediction models while specifying the kind of personal information it handles. The central design goal is to support consent and help people understand the benefit of sharing information.

An empirical study evaluates participatory systems on clinical prediction tasks against common personalization and imputation approaches. The results show that these systems can facilitate informed consent while improving performance and privacy across all groups that report personal data. The contribution connects user participation with predictive modeling, demonstrating that decisions about disclosure can be incorporated into the operation of a learned classifier.
summary.tldr: Participatory classifiers let people opt into personalization at prediction time, with reported improvements in performance and privacy for groups sharing data.

title: Participatory Personalization in Classification

abstract: A popular heuristic method for improving clustering results is to apply dimensionality reduction before running clustering algorithms.It has been observed that spectral-based dimensionality reduction tools, such as PCA or SVD, improve the performance of clustering algorithms in many applications. This phenomenon indicates that spectral method not only serves as a dimensionality reduction tool, but also contributes to the clustering procedure in some sense. It is an interesting question to understand the behavior of spectral steps in clustering problems.As an initial step in this direction, this paper studies the power of vanilla-SVD algorithm in the stochastic block model (SBM). We show that, in the symmetric setting, vanilla-SVD algorithm recovers all clusters correctly. This result answers an open question posed by Van Vu (Combinatorics Probability and Computing, 2018) in the symmetric setting.

paragraphs: Clustering pipelines often reduce dimensionality before assigning data points to groups. Spectral tools such as PCA and singular value decomposition frequently improve the resulting clusters, suggesting that they do more than compress the data. This paper investigates that additional contribution by studying a basic SVD algorithm in the stochastic block model, a mathematical setting for graph clustering.

The central result is exact recovery of all clusters by vanilla SVD in the symmetric setting studied by the authors. Recovering every cluster correctly is a stronger conclusion than merely obtaining a useful low-dimensional representation or improving an average clustering score. It directly connects the spectral step to the underlying group structure in this setting.

The result resolves a previously posed open question for the symmetric case. Its significance is theoretical: it gives a concrete account of the clustering power of a familiar dimensionality-reduction tool. The symmetric stochastic block model is the stated scope of the conclusion, so the result should be understood within that setting rather than extended to arbitrary clustering problems.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that vanilla SVD correctly recovers all clusters in the studied symmetric stochastic block model.

title: On the Power of SVD in the Stochastic Block Model

abstract: Weak supervision enables efficient development of training sets by reducing the need for ground truth labels. However, the techniques that make weak supervision attractive---such as integrating any source of signal to estimate unknown labels---also entail the danger that the produced pseudolabels are highly biased. Surprisingly, given everyday use and the potential for increased bias, weak supervision has not been studied from the point of view of fairness. We begin such a study, starting with the observation that even when a fair model can be built from a dataset with access to ground-truth labels, the corresponding dataset labeled via weak supervision can be arbitrarily unfair. To address this, we propose and empirically validate a model for source unfairness in weak supervision, then introduce a simple counterfactual fairness-based technique that can mitigate these biases. Theoretically, we show that it is possible for our approach to simultaneously improve both accuracy and fairness---in contrast to standard fairness approaches that suffer from tradeoffs. Empirically, we show that our technique improves accuracy on weak supervision baselines by as much as 32\% while reducing demographic parity gap by 82.5\%. A simple extension of our method aimed at maximizing performance produces state-of-the-art performance in five out of ten datasets in the WRENCH benchmark.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines imperfect signals to generate training labels, reducing dependence on manually established ground truth. Those signals can also introduce bias. The paper shows that a dataset capable of supporting a fair model with true labels can become arbitrarily unfair when labeled through weak supervision. This makes the labeling process itself a fairness concern.

The authors propose a model of unfairness in supervision sources and validate it empirically. They then develop a mitigation technique based on counterfactual fairness. Their theoretical analysis establishes that the approach can improve accuracy and fairness simultaneously. This is a possibility demonstrated by the analysis, rather than a guarantee that every application avoids tradeoffs.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of as much as 32% over weak-supervision baselines while reducing the demographic parity gap by 82.5%. An extension aimed at maximizing performance achieves state-of-the-art results on five of ten WRENCH datasets. Together, these findings indicate that correcting source bias can improve the quality of inferred labels in ways that benefit both predictive performance and measured fairness.
summary.tldr: A counterfactual fairness technique mitigates bias in weak supervision and can improve accuracy and fairness together.

title: Mitigating Source Bias for Fairer Weak Supervision

abstract: Reward shaping is an effective technique for integrating domain knowledge into reinforcement learning (RL). However, traditional approaches like potential-based reward shaping totally rely on manually designing shaping reward functions, which significantly restricts exploration efficiency and introduces human cognitive biases.While a number of RL methods have been proposed to boost exploration by designing an intrinsic reward signal as exploration bonus. Nevertheless, these methods heavily rely on the count-based episodic term in their exploration bonus which falls short in scalability. To address these limitations, we propose a general end-to-end potential-based exploration bonus for deep RL via potentials of state discrepancy, which motivates the agent to discover novel states and provides them with denser rewards without manual intervention. Specifically, we measure the novelty of adjacent states by calculating their distance using the bisimulation metric-based potential function, which enhances agent's exploration and ensures policy invariance. In addition, we offer a theoretical guarantee on our inverse dynamic bisimulation metric, bounding the value difference and ensuring that the agent explores states with higher TD error, thus significantly improving training efficiency. The proposed approach is named \textbf{LIBERTY} (exp\textbf{L}oration v\textbf{I}a \textbf{B}isimulation m\textbf{E}t\textbf{R}ic-based s\textbf{T}ate discrepanc\textbf{Y}) which is comprehensively evaluated on the MuJoCo and the Arcade Learning Environments. Extensive experiments have verified the superiority and scalability of our algorithm compared with other competitive methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can explore more effectively when they receive informative rewards beyond the original task reward. However, manually designed shaping rewards introduce dependence on human choices, while exploration bonuses based heavily on episodic counts can face scalability problems. LIBERTY proposes a learned, end-to-end exploration bonus based on differences between states.

The method measures novelty between adjacent states using a potential function built from a bisimulation metric. This state discrepancy provides denser rewards and encourages discovery of novel states without manual reward design. The authors also state that their construction preserves policy invariance, connecting exploration assistance to a formal property of potential-based shaping.

The theoretical analysis bounds value differences using the proposed inverse dynamic bisimulation metric and establishes exploration of states with higher temporal-difference error. These are states where learning has a larger discrepancy to resolve. Evaluations in MuJoCo and the Arcade Learning Environments report superior performance and scalability relative to competitive methods. The contribution combines a learned exploration signal with theoretical support for the behavior that signal encourages.
summary.tldr: LIBERTY learns a state-discrepancy exploration bonus with policy-invariance guarantees and reports improved exploration performance and scalability.

title: Efficient Potential-based Exploration in Reinforcement Learning using Inverse Dynamic Bisimulation Metric

abstract: Large language models(LLMs) have sparked a new wave of exciting AI applications. Hosting these models at scale requires significant memory resources. One crucial memory bottleneck for the deployment stems from the context window. It is commonly recognized that model weights are memory hungry; however, the size of key-value embedding stored during the generation process (KV cache) can easily surpass the model size. The enormous size of the KV cache puts constraints on the inference batch size, which is crucial for high throughput inference workload. Inspired by an interesting observation of the attention scores, we hypothesize the persistence of importance: only pivotal tokens, which had a substantial influence at one step, will significantly influence future generations. Based on our empirical verification and theoretical analysis around this hypothesis, we propose scissorhands, a system that maintains the memory usage of the KV cache at a fixed budget without finetuning the model. In essence, Scissorhands manages the KV cache by storing the pivotal tokens with a higher probability. We validate that scissorhands reduces the inference memory usage of the KV cache by up to 5$\times$ without compromising model quality. We further demonstrate that scissorhands can be combined with 4-bit quantization, traditionally used to compress model weights, to achieve up to 20$\times$ compression.

paragraphs: Language-model generation stores key and value embeddings from the context in a KV cache. This cache can exceed the memory occupied by model weights and restrict how many requests can be processed together. Scissorhands addresses this growing inference-memory cost by deciding which stored tokens are most worth retaining.

The method builds on a persistence-of-importance hypothesis: tokens that strongly influence one generation step are expected to remain influential later. The authors provide empirical verification and theoretical analysis around this hypothesis. Their system keeps the cache within a fixed memory budget, giving pivotal tokens a higher probability of being stored, without fine-tuning the model.

The reported evaluations achieve up to fivefold reduction in KV-cache memory without compromising model quality. Combining the method with 4-bit quantization yields up to twentyfold compression. These are demonstrated maximum gains rather than guarantees for every workload. The contribution shows how attention-based importance can guide selective memory retention during generation and complement compression through lower numerical precision.
summary.tldr: Scissorhands retains likely important tokens within a fixed KV-cache budget, demonstrating up to fivefold memory reduction without model fine-tuning.

title: Scissorhands: Exploiting the Persistence of Importance Hypothesis for LLM KV Cache Compression at Test Time

abstract: Federated learning (FL) provides a distributed training paradigm where multiple clients can jointly train a global model without sharing their local data. However, recent studies have shown that FL offers an additional surface for backdoor attacks. For instance, an attacker can compromise a subset of clients and thus corrupt the global model to misclassify an input with a backdoor trigger as the adversarial target. Existing defenses for FL against backdoor attacks usually detect and exclude the corrupted information from the compromised clients based on a static attacker model. However, such defenses are inadequate against dynamic attackers who strategically adapt their attack strategies. To bridge this gap, we model the strategic interactions between the defender and dynamic attackers as a minimax game. Based on the analysis of the game, we design an interactive defense mechanism FedGame. We prove that under mild assumptions, the global model trained with FedGame under backdoor attacks is close to that trained without attacks. Empirically, we compare FedGame with multiple state-of-the-art baselines on several benchmark datasets under various attacks. We show that FedGame can effectively defend against strategic attackers and achieves significantly higher robustness than baselines. Our code is available at: https://github.com/AI-secure/FedGame.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model without exchanging their local datasets. Compromised clients can nevertheless introduce a backdoor, causing inputs with a particular trigger to receive an attacker-chosen prediction. Defenses that detect and exclude suspicious contributions using a fixed attacker model can struggle when attackers strategically change their behavior.

FedGame treats this interaction as a minimax game between the defender and adaptive attackers. The authors use analysis of that game to design an interactive defense mechanism. This makes strategic adaptation part of the defense problem, rather than treating malicious behavior as a fixed pattern that only needs to be identified.

The paper provides a conditional theoretical guarantee: under assumptions described as mild, the model trained with FedGame during backdoor attacks remains close to the model trained without attacks. Experiments on several benchmark datasets and attacks report substantially stronger robustness than the compared defenses. These findings support the approach against the strategic attackers studied, while the theoretical closeness result retains its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: FedGame models adaptive backdoor attackers and a federated learning defender as a minimax game, yielding conditional guarantees and improved empirical robustness.

title: FedGame: A Game-Theoretic Defense against Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning

abstract: Automated seizure detection is of great importance to epilepsy diagnosis and treatment. An emerging method used in seizure detection, stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), can provide detailed and stereoscopic brainwave information. However, modeling SEEG in clinical scenarios will face challenges like huge domain shift between different patients and dramatic pattern evolution among different brain areas. In this study, we propose a Pretraining-based model for Patient-independent seizure detection (PPi) to address these challenges. Firstly, we design two novel self-supervised tasks which can extract rich information from abundant SEEG data while preserving the unique characteristics between brain signals recorded from different brain areas. Then two techniques channel background subtraction and brain region enhancement are proposed to effectively tackle the domain shift problem. Extensive experiments show that PPi outperforms the SOTA baselines on two public datasets and a real-world clinical dataset collected by ourselves, which demonstrates the effectiveness and practicability of PPi. Finally, visualization analysis illustrates the rationality of the two domain generalization techniques.

paragraphs: SEEG provides detailed recordings of brain activity for seizure detection, but a model must cope with substantial differences between patients and between brain areas. PPi addresses these two sources of variation through pretraining and domain-generalization techniques. Its aim is seizure detection that can work across patients while retaining meaningful regional differences in brain signals.

The model uses two self-supervised tasks to learn from abundant SEEG data. These tasks are designed to extract useful information without erasing the distinctive characteristics of signals recorded in different brain regions. The authors then introduce channel background subtraction and brain region enhancement to address shifts between patients. Together, these components connect broad signal learning with explicit treatment of the variation that complicates transfer.

Experiments on two public datasets and an additional clinical dataset collected by the authors show improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Visualization analysis also supports the rationale for the two domain-generalization techniques. The reported evidence establishes effectiveness across those evaluated datasets and supports the practical promise of combining region-sensitive pretraining with methods aimed at patient-to-patient variation.
summary.tldr: PPi combines self-supervised SEEG pretraining with domain-generalization techniques to improve seizure detection across patients in three evaluated datasets.

title: PPi: Pretraining Brain Signal Model for Patient-independent Seizure Detection

abstract: The proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm stands as one of the most prosperous methods in the field of reinforcement learning (RL). Despite its success, the theoretical understanding of PPO remains deficient. Specifically, it is unclear whether PPO or its optimistic variants can effectively solve linear Markov decision processes (MDPs), which are arguably the simplest models in RL with function approximation. To bridge this gap, we propose an optimistic variant of PPO for episodic adversarial linear MDPs with full-information feedback, and establish a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{3/4}H^2K^{3/4})$ regret for it. Here $d$ is the ambient dimension of linear MDPs, $H$ is the length of each episode, and $K$ is the number of episodes. Compared with existing policy-based algorithms, we achieve the state-of-the-art regret bound in both stochastic linear MDPs and adversarial linear MDPs with full information. Additionally, our algorithm design features a novel multi-batched updating mechanism and the theoretical analysis utilizes a new covering number argument of value and policy classes, which might be of independent interest.

Additionally, our algorithm design features a novel multi-batched updating mechanism and the theoretical analysis utilizes a new covering number argument of value and policy classes, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: PPO is widely successful in reinforcement learning, but its theoretical foundations leave important questions open. This paper asks whether an optimistic version can learn effectively in linear Markov decision processes, a basic setting for studying reinforcement learning with function approximation. The authors develop a variant for episodic problems with adversarial rewards and full-information feedback.

The algorithm uses a new mechanism that organizes updates into multiple batches. Its analysis also introduces a covering-number argument for value and policy classes: a way of controlling the complexity of the collections of predictions and behaviors considered. Together, these ingredients support a regret guarantee of roughly d^(3/4) H² K^(3/4), suppressing logarithmic factors.

Here d describes the linear model dimension, H the episode length, and K the number of episodes. The sublinear dependence on K means average regret decreases as experience accumulates. The authors report the strongest regret bound among existing policy-based algorithms in the stated stochastic and full-information adversarial settings. This establishes a guarantee for their particular optimistic variant under these conditions.
summary.tldr: An optimistic PPO variant achieves improved theoretical regret guarantees in linear decision processes using batched updates and a new complexity analysis.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of Optimistic Proximal Policy Optimization in Linear Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Covariate shift occurs prevalently in practice, where the input distributions of the source and target data are substantially different. Despite its practical importance in various learning problems, most of the existing methods only focus on some specific learning tasks and are not well validated theoretically and numerically. To tackle this problem, we propose a unified analysis of general nonparametric methods in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) under covariate shift. Our theoretical results are established for a general loss belonging to a rich loss function family, which includes many commonly used methods as special cases, such as mean regression, quantile regression, likelihood-based classification, and margin-based classification. Two types of covariate shift problems are the focus of this paper and the sharp convergence rates are established for a general loss function to provide a unified theoretical analysis, which concurs with the optimal results in literature where the squared loss is used. Extensive numerical studies on synthetic and real examples confirm our theoretical findings and further illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Covariate shift arises when source and target data have different input distributions. Methods for handling it are often studied separately for particular learning tasks, leaving a fragmented theoretical picture. This paper develops a unified analysis of nonparametric learning in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, aiming to cover a broad range of prediction objectives.

The analysis applies to a rich family of loss functions. It includes mean regression, quantile regression, likelihood-based classification, and margin-based classification as special cases. This breadth matters because it brings several distinct ways of defining prediction error into one framework for understanding learning under changed input distributions.

The authors study two types of covariate-shift problems and establish sharp convergence rates for the general loss setting. Their results agree with known optimal results when the loss is squared error, connecting the broader framework to an established case. Numerical studies on synthetic and real examples support the theory and demonstrate the proposed method’s effectiveness across the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: A unified kernel-learning analysis establishes sharp convergence rates under covariate shift for a broad family of regression and classification losses.

title: Towards a Unified Analysis of Kernel-based Methods Under Covariate Shift

abstract: We study core-set construction algorithms for the task of Diversity Maximization under fairness/partition constraint. Given a set of points $P$ in a metric space partitioned into $m$ groups, and given $k_1,\ldots,k_m$, the goal of this problem is to pick $k_i$ points from each group $i$ such that the overall diversity of the $k=\sum_i k_i$ picked points is maximized. We consider two natural diversity measures: sum-of-pairwise distances and sum-of-nearest-neighbor distances, and show improved core-set construction algorithms with respect to these measures. More precisely, we show the first constant factor core-set w.r.t. sum-of-pairwise distances whose size is independent of the size of the dataset and the aspect ratio. Second, we show the first core-set w.r.t. the sum-of-nearest-neighbor distances. Finally, we run several experiments showing the effectiveness of our core-set approach. In particular, we apply constrained diversity maximization to summarize a set of timed messages that takes into account the messages' recency. Specifically, the summary should include more recent messages compared to older ones. This is a real task in one of the largest communication platforms, affecting the experience of hundreds of millions daily active users. By utilizing our core-set method for this task, we achieve a 100x speed-up while losing the diversity by only a few percent. Moreover, our approach allows us to improve the space usage of the algorithm in the streaming setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select a diverse summary while satisfying prescribed representation requirements. Data points belong to groups, and the summary must contain a specified number from each group. Diversity is measured either by adding all pairwise distances among selected points or by adding each selected point's distance to its nearest selected neighbor.

The authors construct core-sets: smaller collections that support the constrained selection problem. For pairwise-distance diversity, they provide the first constant-factor core-set whose size does not depend on dataset size or aspect ratio. For nearest-neighbor diversity, they provide the first core-set result. These guarantees address how much data must be retained to support diverse selection under group quotas.

Experiments include summarizing timed messages with quotas that favor recent messages. In this application, the core-set method achieves a 100-fold speedup while reducing diversity by only a few percent. The approach also improves space usage in a streaming setting. These results show how a mathematical summary of the selection problem can make a practical summarization task substantially cheaper.
summary.tldr: New core-sets accelerate diverse subset selection under group quotas, including a message-summary application with a 100-fold speedup and a small diversity loss.

title: Core-sets for Fair and Diverse Data Summarization

abstract: In supervised learning, the question of data quality and curation has been sidelined in recent years in favor of increasingly more powerful and expressive models that can ingest internet-scale data. However, in offline learning for robotics, we simply lack internet scale data, and so high quality datasets are a necessity. This is especially true in imitation learning (IL), a sample efficient paradigm for robot learning using expert demonstrations. Policies learned through IL suffer from state distribution shift at test time due to compounding errors in action prediction, which leads to unseen states that the policy cannot recover from.Instead of designing new algorithms to address distribution shift, an alternative perspective is to develop new ways of assessing and curating datasets. There is growing evidence that the same IL algorithms can have substantially different performance across different datasets. This calls for a formalism for defining metrics of "data quality" that can further be leveraged for data curation.In this work, we take the first step toward formalizing data quality for imitation learning through the lens of distribution shift: a high quality dataset encourages the policy to stay in distribution at test time. We propose two fundamental properties that are necessary for a high quality datasets: i) action divergence: the mismatch between the expert and learned policy at certain states; and ii) transition diversity: the noise present in the system for a given state and action. We investigate the combined effect of these two key properties in imitation learning theoretically, and we empirically analyze models trained on a variety of different data sources. We show that state diversity is not always beneficial, and we demonstrate how action divergence and transition diversity interact in practice.

paragraphs: A robot trained to imitate demonstrations can make small action errors that accumulate. Those errors carry it into states unlike the training data, where it may struggle to recover. This paper studies dataset quality through that distribution-shift problem: useful demonstrations should help a learned policy remain within the distribution it can handle.

The authors identify two central properties for assessing quality. Action divergence measures disagreement between expert actions and the learned policy at particular states. Transition diversity describes noise in what happens after a given state and action. Studying them together connects errors in the policy's choices with variability in the environment's response, rather than judging a dataset solely by the range of states it contains.

The paper develops a theoretical analysis of their combined effects and examines models trained on different data sources. It finds that greater state diversity is not always beneficial and shows how action divergence and transition diversity interact in practice. This gives dataset curation a more targeted objective than simply collecting broader coverage.
summary.tldr: The paper connects imitation-learning data quality to action mismatch and transition noise, showing that more diverse states do not always improve learning.

title: Data Quality in Imitation Learning

abstract: Efficient computation of graph diffusion equations (GDEs), such as Personalized PageRank, Katz centrality, and the Heat kernel, is crucial for clustering, training neural networks, and many other graph-related problems. Standard iterative methods require accessing the whole graph per iteration, making them time-consuming for large-scale graphs. While existing local solvers approximate diffusion vectors through heuristic local updates, they often operate sequentially and are typically designed for specific diffusion types, limiting their applicability. Given that diffusion vectors are highly localizable, as measured by the participation ratio, this paper introduces a novel framework for approximately solving GDEs using a local diffusion process. This framework reveals the suboptimality of existing local solvers. Furthermore, our approach effectively localizes standard iterative solvers by designing simple and provably sublinear time algorithms. These new local solvers are highly parallelizable, making them well-suited for implementation on GPUs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in quickly obtaining approximate diffusion vectors, achieving up to a hundred-fold speed improvement, and its applicability to large-scale dynamic graphs. Our framework could also facilitate more efficient local message-passing mechanisms for GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion computations underpin tools such as Personalized PageRank, Katz centrality, and the heat kernel. Standard iterative methods revisit the entire graph at each step, which becomes expensive on large graphs. Existing local methods reduce that work, but often rely on sequential heuristics tailored to one particular kind of diffusion.

The paper develops a more general framework around the local concentration of diffusion vectors, measured through the participation ratio. A local diffusion process makes it possible to approximate these vectors without treating every part of the graph equally. The framework exposes shortcomings of existing local solvers and turns standard iterative methods into local algorithms with provably sublinear running time.

These are results for approximate diffusion computation, where locality can reduce the work needed. The authors additionally suggest that the framework could support more efficient local message passing in graph neural networks.
summary.tldr: A general local-diffusion framework yields parallelizable approximate graph solvers with sublinear-time guarantees and reported speedups of up to a hundred-fold.

title: Faster Local Solvers for Graph Diffusion Equations

abstract: What data or environments to use for training to improve downstream performance is a longstanding and very topical question in reinforcement learning. In particular, Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) methods have gained recent attention as their adaptive curricula promise to enable agents to be robust to in- and out-of-distribution tasks.This work investigates how existing UED methods select training environments, focusing on task prioritisation metrics.Surprisingly, despite methods aiming to maximise regret in theory, the practical approximations do not correlate with regret but with success rate.As a result, a significant portion of an agent's experience comes from environments it has already mastered, offering little to no contribution toward enhancing its abilities. Put differently, current methods fail to predict intuitive measures of *learnability*. Specifically, they are unable to consistently identify those scenarios that the agent can sometimes solve, but not always.Based on our analysis, we develop a method that directly trains on scenarios with high learnability. This simple and intuitive approach outperforms existing UED methods in several binary-outcome environments, including the standard domain of Minigrid and a novel setting closely inspired by a real-world robotics problem. We further introduce a new adversarial evaluation procedure for directly measuring robustness, closely mirroring the conditional value at risk (CVaR).We open-source all our code and present visualisations of final policies here: https://github.com/amacrutherford/sampling-for-learnability.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning depends partly on which environments an agent encounters during training. Unsupervised Environment Design adapts this curriculum to improve performance and robustness. This paper examines the practical metrics used to prioritize environments, asking whether they actually select tasks with useful opportunities for learning.

The authors find that existing approximations intended to track regret correlate with success rate instead. Consequently, agents spend substantial experience on environments they have already mastered. These metrics also fail to consistently identify scenarios the agent solves sometimes but not reliably, which the paper treats as an intuitive indicator of learnability.

Based on this analysis, the authors directly prioritize scenarios with high learnability. The approach outperforms existing methods in several binary-outcome environments, including Minigrid and a new setting inspired by a robotics problem. They also introduce an adversarial robustness evaluation resembling conditional value at risk. Together, the contributions connect curriculum selection more closely to remaining learning opportunities and provide an additional procedure for assessing the resulting policies' robustness.
summary.tldr: Prioritizing environments an agent can sometimes solve improves curriculum learning over regret approximations that favor already-mastered tasks.

title: No Regrets: Investigating and Improving Regret Approximations for Curriculum Discovery

abstract: Machine learning applied to blockchain graphs offers significant opportunities for enhanced data analysis and applications. However, the potential of this field is constrained by the lack of a large-scale, cross-chain dataset that includes hierarchical graph-level data. To address this issue, we present novel datasets that provide detailed label information at the token level and integrate interactions between tokens across multiple blockchain platforms. We model transactions within each token as local graphs and the relationships between tokens as global graphs, collectively forming a "Graphs of Graphs" (GoG) approach. This innovative approach facilitates a deeper understanding of systemic structures and hierarchical interactions, which are essential for applications such as link prediction, anomaly detection, and token classification. We conduct a series of experiments demonstrating that this dataset delivers new insights and challenges for exploring GoG within the blockchain domain. Our work promotes advancements and opens new avenues for research in both the blockchain and graph communities. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Xtra-Computing/Cryptocurrency-Graphs-of-graphs.

paragraphs: Blockchain analysis involves relationships at more than one level: transactions occur within tokens, while tokens also interact across platforms. This paper introduces datasets designed to represent both levels together. It addresses the lack of large-scale cross-chain data with hierarchical graph information and detailed labels at the token level.

The proposed Graphs of Graphs representation treats transactions within each token as a local graph. Relationships among tokens form a global graph whose components carry their own internal structure. Combining these views makes it possible to study token-level activity alongside broader interactions, preserving information that belongs to different levels of the system.

The authors conduct experiments showing that the datasets create new insights and research challenges for hierarchical blockchain analysis. They identify link prediction, anomaly detection, and token classification as relevant applications. The main contribution is therefore a data resource and representation approach for studying systemic structure, providing a basis for research that connects local transaction patterns with relationships across tokens and chains.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces cross-chain blockchain datasets that connect local transaction graphs through a global graph of token relationships.

title: Multi-Chain Graphs of Graphs: A New Approach to Analyzing Blockchain Datasets

abstract: Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation (ZS-OGN) enables robots to navigate toward objects of unseen categories without prior training. Traditional approaches often leverage categorical semantic information for navigation guidance, which struggles when only partial objects are observed or detailed and functional representations of the environment are lacking. To resolve the above two issues, we propose \textit{Geometric-part and Affordance Maps} (GAMap), a novel method that integrates object parts and affordance attributes for navigation guidance. Our method includes a multi-scale scoring approach to capture geometric-part and affordance attributes of objects at different scales. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the HM3D and Gibson benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements in Success Rates and Success weighted by Path Length, underscoring the efficacy of our geometric-part and affordance-guided navigation approach in enhancing robot autonomy and versatility, without any additional task-specific training or fine-tuning with the semantics of unseen objects and/or the locomotions of the robot.

paragraphs: GAMap addresses navigation toward objects from categories a robot has not received task-specific training to find. Guidance based mainly on category semantics can struggle when the robot sees only part of an object. It can also lack the detailed geometric and functional information needed to interpret the surroundings.

The method constructs Geometric-part and Affordance Maps that incorporate object parts and attributes related to what objects afford. A multi-scale scoring approach captures these cues at different scales. This expands navigation guidance beyond a category-level description, using both the visible structure of objects and information about their functions to guide the search.

Experiments on HM3D and Gibson report improvements in success rate and success weighted by path length. These findings indicate benefits for both reaching the target and the path-sensitive measure of navigation success. The approach achieves the reported gains without additional task-specific training or fine-tuning on unseen-object semantics or robot locomotion. Its contribution is to make geometric and functional cues useful for navigation in that zero-shot setting.
summary.tldr: GAMap uses multi-scale object-part and affordance information to improve navigation toward unseen object categories without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: GAMap: Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation with Multi-Scale Geometric-Affordance Guidance

abstract: Empirical data can often be considered as samples from a set of probability distributions. Kernel methods have emerged as a natural approach for learning to classify these distributions. Although numerous kernels between distributions have been proposed, applying kernel methods to distribution regression tasks remains challenging, primarily because selecting a suitable kernel is not straightforward. Surprisingly, the question of learning a data-dependent distribution kernel has received little attention. In this paper, we propose a novel objective for the unsupervised learning of data-dependent distribution kernel, based on the principle of entropy maximization in the space of probability measure embeddings. We examine the theoretical properties of the latent embedding space induced by our objective, demonstrating that its geometric structure is well-suited for solving downstream discriminative tasks. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the learned kernel across different modalities.

paragraphs: Some learning problems treat each collection of observations as samples from a probability distribution. The object to compare or predict from is then a distribution, rather than a single observation. Kernel methods provide a way to compare such objects, but choosing an appropriate distribution kernel can be difficult, particularly for regression.

This paper proposes learning a data-dependent distribution kernel without supervision. Its objective maximizes entropy in the space of probability-measure embeddings, where distributions are represented for comparison. This turns kernel selection into a learning problem guided by the arrangement of distribution representations, rather than requiring a suitable kernel to be chosen beforehand.

The authors analyze the latent space produced by this objective and show that its geometry is well suited to downstream discriminative tasks. They also demonstrate the learned kernel’s performance across different modalities. The contribution links an unsupervised representation-learning principle to the needs of later prediction tasks, providing both theoretical motivation for the resulting geometry and empirical evidence of usefulness.
summary.tldr: An entropy-maximization objective learns distribution kernels without supervision, producing embedding geometry suited to downstream discrimination.

title: Learning to Embed Distributions via Maximum Kernel Entropy

abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is crucial in today's cybersecurity landscape, providing essential insights to understand and mitigate the ever-evolving cyber threats. The recent rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in this domain, but concerns about their reliability, accuracy, and hallucinations persist. While existing benchmarks provide general evaluations of LLMs, there are no benchmarks that address the practical and applied aspects of CTI-specific tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce CTIBench, a benchmark designed to assess LLMs' performance in CTI applications. CTIBench includes multiple datasets focused on evaluating knowledge acquired by LLMs in the cyber-threat landscape. Our evaluation of several state-of-the-art models on these tasks provides insights into their strengths and weaknesses in CTI contexts, contributing to a better understanding of LLM capabilities in CTI.

paragraphs: Cyber threat intelligence uses knowledge about threats to help people understand and mitigate security risks. Language models could support this work, but their usefulness depends on reliable, accurate answers rather than plausible-looking mistakes. The paper argues that general language-model benchmarks do not adequately assess the practical demands of this particular field.

CTIBench supplies a dedicated evaluation benchmark containing multiple datasets for cyber threat intelligence tasks. Its focus is the knowledge models have acquired about the cyber-threat landscape and how that knowledge performs in applied CTI settings. This gives researchers a way to examine domain-specific capabilities instead of inferring them from performance on unrelated general evaluations.

The authors evaluate several state-of-the-art models and use the results to identify strengths and weaknesses within CTI. The stated contribution is a clearer basis for assessing model capabilities in this domain. By organizing evaluation around CTI applications, the benchmark makes reliability concerns more directly testable and helps distinguish broad language ability from performance on the security tasks being assessed.
summary.tldr: CTIBench evaluates language models on cyber threat intelligence tasks to reveal domain-specific strengths and weaknesses.

title: CTIBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Cyber Threat Intelligence

abstract: This paper examines two extensions of multi-armed bandit problems: multi-armed bandits with expert advice and contextual linear bandits. For the former problem, multi-armed bandits with expert advice, the previously known best upper and lower bounds have been $O(\sqrt{KT \log \frac{N}{K} })$ and $\Omega( \sqrt{KT \frac{ \log N }{\log K }} )$, respectively. Here, $K$, $N$, and $T$ represent the numbers of arms, experts, and rounds, respectively. We provide a lower bound of $\Omega( \sqrt{KT \log \frac{N}{K}} )$ for the setup in which the player chooses an expert before observing the advices in each round. For the latter problem, contextual linear bandits, we provide an algorithm that achieves $O ( \sqrt{d T \log ( K \min\{ 1, \frac{S}{d} \} )} )$ together with a matching lower bound, where $d$ and $S$ represent the dimensionality of feature vectors and the size of the context space, respectively.

paragraphs: Bandit problems study repeated decisions where an algorithm must learn while choosing among available actions. Regret measures the resulting shortfall against a comparison strategy. This paper sharpens worst-case regret guarantees for two variants: bandits using expert advice and contextual linear bandits, where decisions depend on feature information.

For expert advice, earlier upper and lower bounds did not match. The paper proves a lower bound of order sqrt(KT log(N/K)), with K arms, N experts, and T rounds. This matches the previously known upper-bound rate for the specified setup in which the player selects an expert before seeing that round’s advice. The order of information and choice is an essential part of this result.

For contextual linear bandits, the authors give an algorithm and a matching lower bound at order sqrt(dT log(K min{1, S/d})), where d is feature dimension and S is context-space size. Matching bounds identify the optimal worst-case rate in the analyzed setting, clarifying how these problem dimensions affect achievable learning performance.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes matching regret rates for contextual linear bandits and closes a bound gap in a specified expert-advice setting.

title: On the Minimax Regret for Contextual Linear Bandits and Multi-Armed Bandits with Expert Advice

abstract: Scale has become a main ingredient in obtaining strong machine learning models. As a result, understanding a model's scaling properties is key to effectively designing both the right training setup as well as future generations of architectures. In this work, we argue that scale and training research has been needlessly complex due to reliance on the cosine schedule, which prevents training across different lengths for the same model size. We investigate the training behavior of a direct alternative --- constant learning rate and cooldowns --- and find that it scales predictably and reliably similar to cosine. Additionally, we show that stochastic weight averaging yields improved performance along the training trajectory, without additional training costs, across different scales. Importantly, with these findings we demonstrate that scaling experiments can be performed with significantly reduced compute and GPU hours by utilizing fewer but reusable training runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/epfml/schedules-and-scaling/.

paragraphs: Scaling studies compare how model performance changes with training resources, so the ability to evaluate different training durations matters. This paper argues that reliance on cosine learning-rate schedules makes those studies unnecessarily expensive. Because the schedule is tied to a chosen duration, exploring several durations at the same model size requires less reusable training.

The authors investigate a constant learning rate followed by cooldown periods as a direct alternative. They find that this approach scales predictably and reliably, similarly to cosine scheduling. They also study stochastic weight averaging, which combines model weights from training, and report improved performance along the training trajectory across scales without additional training costs.

Together, these findings allow scaling experiments to use fewer, reusable training runs and substantially reduce compute and GPU hours. The contribution concerns the design of the experimental process as much as model optimization. A schedule that supports reuse can make it cheaper to study how performance depends on training duration and to inform decisions about future training setups and architectures.
summary.tldr: Constant learning rates with cooldowns enable reusable scaling runs, while weight averaging improves performance without additional training costs.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations

abstract: Foundation models are becoming valuable tools in medicine. Yet despite their promise, the best way to leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex medical tasks remains an open question. We introduce a novel multi-agent framework, named **M**edical **D**ecision-making **Agents** (**MDAgents**) that helps to address this gap by automatically assigning a collaboration structure to a team of LLMs. The assigned solo or group collaboration structure is tailored to the medical task at hand, a simple emulation inspired by the way real-world medical decision-making processes are adapted to tasks of different complexities. We evaluate our framework and baseline methods using state-of-the-art LLMs across a suite of real-world medical knowledge and clinical diagnosis benchmarks, including a comparison ofLLMs’ medical complexity classification against human physicians. MDAgents achieved the **best performance in seven out of ten** benchmarks on tasks requiring an understanding of medical knowledge and multi-modal reasoning, showing a significant **improvement of up to 4.2\%** ($p$ < 0.05) compared to previous methods' best performances. Ablation studies reveal that MDAgents effectively determines medical complexity to optimize for efficiency and accuracy across diverse medical tasks. Notably, the combination of moderator review and external medical knowledge in group collaboration resulted in an average accuracy **improvement of 11.8\%**. Our code can be found at https://github.com/mitmedialab/MDAgents.

paragraphs: MDAgents organizes language models into a collaboration structure selected for the medical task being considered. Depending on task complexity, it assigns either solo work or group collaboration. The approach takes inspiration from how medical decision-making processes vary with the difficulty of a case, making the choice of collaboration structure part of the framework.

The evaluation covers medical knowledge and clinical diagnosis benchmarks, including tasks requiring multimodal reasoning. It also compares language models' judgments of medical complexity with those of physicians. MDAgents achieves the best performance on seven of ten benchmarks, with improvements of up to 4.2% over the best previous results and reported statistical significance at p below 0.05.

Ablation studies support the framework's ability to assess complexity in ways that improve efficiency and accuracy across the evaluated tasks. Within group collaboration, combining moderator review with external medical knowledge produces an average accuracy improvement of 11.8%. These findings suggest that both task-dependent organization and the information and review processes inside a group contribute to the reported benchmark gains.
summary.tldr: MDAgents adapts solo or group language-model collaboration to medical task complexity and achieves the best results on seven of ten evaluated benchmarks.

title: MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making

abstract: One-shot Federated learning (FL) is a powerful technology facilitating collaborative training of machine learning models in a single round of communication. While its superiority lies in communication efficiency and privacy preservation compared to iterative FL, one-shot FL often compromises model performance. Prior research has primarily focused on employing data-free knowledge distillation to optimize data generators and ensemble models for better aggregating local knowledge into the server model. However, these methods typically struggle with data heterogeneity, where inconsistent local data distributions can cause teachers to provide misleading knowledge. Additionally, they may encounter scalability issues with complex datasets due to inherent two-step information loss: first, during local training (from data to model), and second, when transferring knowledge to the server model (from model to inversed data). In this paper, we propose FedSD2C, a novel and practical one-shot FL framework designed to address these challenges. FedSD2C introduces a distiller to synthesize informative distillates directly from local data to reduce information loss and proposes sharing synthetic distillates instead of inconsistent local models to tackle data heterogeneity. Our empirical results demonstrate that FedSD2C consistently outperforms other one-shot FL methods with more complex and real datasets, achieving up to 2.6 $\times$ the performance of the best baseline. Code: https://github.com/Carkham/FedSD2C

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning combines knowledge from distributed clients using a single communication round. This saves communication but often reduces model performance. Existing approaches commonly transfer knowledge through local models and generated data. When clients have different data distributions, their models can provide inconsistent guidance, while the successive transfers can discard information.

FedSD2C changes what clients communicate. A distiller synthesizes informative examples directly from each client's local data, and these synthetic distillates are shared instead of the local models. This targets two problems together: information loss from passing through a trained model before reconstructing data, and misleading guidance caused by heterogeneous local teachers.

Experiments on more complex and real datasets show that FedSD2C consistently outperforms the compared one-shot federated learning methods. The strongest reported result reaches up to 2.6 times the performance of the best baseline; this is a maximum reported gain, not a uniform improvement across all evaluations. The findings support direct synthetic data communication as an effective way to preserve useful local information within a single-round collaboration.
summary.tldr: FedSD2C communicates synthetic examples distilled directly from local data to improve single-round federated learning under data heterogeneity.

title: One-shot Federated Learning via Synthetic Distiller-Distillate Communication

abstract: In this work, we propose Asynchronous Perception Machine (APM), a computationally-efficient architecture for test-time-training (TTT). APM can process patches of an image one at a time in any order asymmetrically and still encode semantic-awareness in the net. We demonstrate APM's ability to recognize out-of-distribution images without dataset-specific pre-training, augmentation or any-pretext task. APM offers competitive performance over existing TTT approaches. To perform TTT, APM just distills test sample's representation once. APM possesses a unique property: it can learn using just this single representation and starts predicting semantically-aware features.APM demostrates potential applications beyond test-time-training: APM can scale up to a dataset of 2D images and yield semantic-clusterings in a single forward pass. paragraphs: Asynchronous Perception Machine, or APM, is an architecture for efficiently adapting a model when it encounters a test image. It processes image patches individually and can accept them in any order while retaining awareness of meaningful image content. This flexibility is central to its proposed approach to perception and test-time training.

For adaptation, APM distills the test sample's representation once and learns from that single representation to predict semantically meaningful features. The authors demonstrate recognition of out-of-distribution images without dataset-specific pretraining, augmentation, or a pretext task. They report competitive performance against existing test-time-training approaches, supporting the possibility of adaptation through a comparatively compact procedure.

The paper also explores behavior beyond individual test samples. APM can produce semantic groupings across a dataset of two-dimensional images in one forward pass. The authors interpret their empirical findings as initial support for GLOM's idea of perception as a field. They present this as progress toward a shared connectionist implementation of interpolation and perception, with broader applications remaining a potential direction.
summary.tldr: APM adapts from a single distilled test-image representation while processing patches in arbitrary order and retaining semantic awareness.

title: Asynchronous Perception Machine for Efficient Test Time Training

abstract: We investigate the extent to which contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) can engage in exploration, a core capability in reinforcement learning and decision making. We focus on native performance of existing LLMs, without training interventions. We deploy LLMs as agents in simple multi-armed bandit environments, specifying the environment description and interaction history entirely in-context, i.e., within the LLM prompt. We experiment with GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama2, using a variety of prompt designs, and find that the models do not robustly engage in exploration without substantial interventions: i) Only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought reasoning and an externally summarized interaction history; ii) All other configurations did not result in robust exploratory behavior, including those with chain-of-thought reasoning but unsummarized history. While these findings can be interpreted positively, they suggest that external summarization—which may not be possible in more complex settings—is essential for desirable LLM behavior. We conclude that non-trivial algorithmic interventions, such as fine-tuning or dataset curation, may be required to empower LLM-based decision making agents in complex settings.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether existing language models can explore effectively using only information supplied in their prompts. Exploration involves gathering information through choices, a central requirement for decision-making agents. The authors test native model behavior without additional training, using simple multi-armed bandit environments described entirely through prompts and interaction histories.

The experiments examine GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama2 under several prompt designs. Only one tested configuration shows satisfactory exploration: GPT-4 using chain-of-thought reasoning together with an externally summarized interaction history. Other configurations fail to explore robustly, including ones that use chain-of-thought reasoning but retain an unsummarized history.

The result makes the organization of experience a consequential part of the tested agent setup. Reasoning prompts alone did not reliably produce the desired behavior; the successful configuration also depended on external summarization. The authors note that such summarization may be unavailable in more complex settings. They consequently suggest that interventions such as fine-tuning or dataset curation may be needed for more capable decision-making agents, rather than claiming that these experiments establish an absolute inability to explore.
summary.tldr: Across the tested settings, only GPT-4 with chain-of-thought reasoning and externally summarized history explored satisfactorily without additional training.

title: Can large language models explore in-context?

abstract: We introduce a general framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) using generative diffusion models. In particular, we focus on the scenarios where we do not have the full knowledge of the scene necessary to apply classical solvers. Most existing forward or inverse PDE approaches perform poorly when the observations on the data or the underlying coefficients are incomplete, which is a common assumption for real-world measurements. In this work, we propose DiffusionPDE that can simultaneously fill in the missing information and solve a PDE by modeling the joint distribution of the solution and coefficient spaces. We show that the learned generative priors lead to a versatile framework for accurately solving a wide range of PDEs under partial observation, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art methods for both forward and inverse directions.
