paragraphs: Solving a partial differential equation often requires information about the system that measurements do not fully provide. Missing observations or unknown coefficients can prevent direct use of classical solvers and weaken existing learned approaches. DiffusionPDE focuses on this incomplete-information setting, treating reconstruction of the missing quantities as part of the solving problem.

The method uses a generative diffusion model to learn the joint distribution of equation solutions and coefficients. Modeling them together provides a learned prior over how these quantities relate. The framework can then fill in missing information while solving the equation, rather than requiring a complete description of the system before the process begins.

The authors report accurate results across a broad range of PDEs under partial observation, with significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both forward and inverse problems. The stated contribution is a common generative framework for these two directions. Its findings support learning relationships between solutions and coefficients as a useful way to handle incomplete measurements.
summary.tldr: DiffusionPDE jointly models solutions and coefficients to solve PDEs while reconstructing information missing from observations.

title: DiffusionPDE: Generative PDE-Solving under Partial Observation

abstract: Recently, research on denoising diffusion models has expanded its application to the field of image restoration. Traditional diffusion-based image restoration methods utilize degraded images as conditional input to effectively guide the reverse generation process, without modifying the original denoising diffusion process. However, since the degraded images already include low-frequency information, starting from Gaussian white noise will result in increased sampling steps. We propose Resfusion, a general framework that incorporates the residual term into the diffusion forward process, starting the reverse process directly from the noisy degraded images. The form of our inference process is consistent with the DDPM. We introduced a weighted residual noise, named resnoise, as the prediction target and explicitly provide the quantitative relationship between the residual term and the noise term in resnoise. By leveraging a smooth equivalence transformation, Resfusion determine the optimal acceleration step and maintains the integrity of existing noise schedules, unifying the training and inference processes. The experimental results demonstrate that Resfusion exhibits competitive performance on ISTD dataset, LOL dataset and Raindrop dataset with only five sampling steps. Furthermore, Resfusion can be easily applied to image generation and emerges with strong versatility. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/nkicsl/Resfusion.

paragraphs: A degraded image already contains useful low-frequency information about the image to be restored. Conventional diffusion restoration methods condition generation on that image but still begin from Gaussian white noise. Resfusion changes the diffusion process so restoration can start directly from a noisy version of the degraded image, using information already present.

The framework introduces a residual term into forward diffusion and trains the model to predict a weighted combination of residual and noise, called resnoise. The authors specify the quantitative relationship between its components. A smooth equivalence transformation determines an acceleration step while preserving existing noise schedules and keeping training and inference aligned.

Although its starting point changes, the inference process retains the DDPM form. Experiments report competitive restoration performance on ISTD, LOL, and Raindrop using only five sampling steps. The paper also describes applying the framework to image generation. Its central finding is that incorporating the degraded image into the diffusion construction can support effective restoration with a short sampling process.
summary.tldr: Resfusion incorporates residual information into diffusion and achieves competitive image restoration with five sampling steps.

title: Resfusion: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Image Restoration Based on Prior Residual Noise

abstract: A challenging problem in seeking to bring multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) techniques into real-world applications, such as autonomous driving and drone swarms, is how to control multiple agents safely and cooperatively to accomplish tasks. Most existing safe MARL methods learn the centralized value function by introducing a global state to guide safety cooperation. However, the global coupling arising from agents’ safety constraints and the exponential growth of the state-action space size limit their applicability in instant communication or computing resource-constrained systems and larger multi-agent systems. In this paper, we develop a novel scalable and theoretically-justified multi-agent constrained policy optimization method. This method utilizes the rigorous bounds of the trust region method and the bounds of the truncated advantage function to provide a new local policy optimization objective for each agent. Also, we prove that the safety constraints and the joint policy improvement can be met when each agent adopts a sequential update scheme to optimize a $\kappa$-hop policy. Then, we propose a practical algorithm called Scalable MAPPO-Lagrangian (Scal-MAPPO-L). The proposed method’s effectiveness is verified on a collection of benchmark tasks, and the results support our theory that decentralized training with local interactions can still improve reward performance and satisfy safe constraints.

paragraphs: Safe multi-agent reinforcement learning must improve collective task performance while respecting safety constraints. Many existing methods use a centralized value function informed by a global state. This becomes difficult as joint state and action spaces expand and safety constraints couple agents together, especially when communication and computing resources are limited.

The paper develops a local policy objective for each agent using trust-region bounds and bounds on a truncated advantage function. These bounds provide the basis for limiting how much information each update needs. The authors prove that safety constraints and joint policy improvement can be achieved when agents sequentially update policies using information within a κ-hop neighborhood.

They turn the approach into Scalable MAPPO-Lagrangian, a practical algorithm evaluated on benchmark tasks. The results support the theoretical claim that decentralized training with local interactions can improve rewards while satisfying safety constraints. The sequential update scheme and neighborhood-based policies are central conditions of the stated guarantee, connecting scalability to a specific form of coordinated local optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper develops local multi-agent policy updates with safety and improvement guarantees under a sequential neighborhood-based update scheme.

title: Scalable Constrained Policy Optimization for Safe Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The recent rise of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) has significantly improved multi-step reasoning performance, but often at the cost of generating excessively long reasoning chains. This paper revisits the efficiency of such reasoning processes through an information-theoretic lens, revealing a fundamental trade-off between reasoning length and semantic efficiency. We propose two metrics—InfoBias and InfoGain—to quantify divergence from ideal reasoning paths and stepwise information contribution, respectively. Empirical analyses show that longer reasoning chains tend to exhibit higher information bias and diminishing information gain, especially for incorrect answers. Motivated by these findings, we introduce an entropy-based Adaptive Think strategy that dynamically halts reasoning once confidence is sufficiently high, improving efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy. Compared to the Vanilla Think approach (default mode), our strategy yields a 1.10% improvement in average accuracy and a 50.80% reduction in token usage on QwQ-32B across six benchmark tasks spanning diverse reasoning types and difficulty levels, demonstrating superior efficiency and reasoning performance. These results underscore the promise of entropy-based methods for enhancing both accuracy and cost-effiiciency in large language model deployment.

paragraphs: Long reasoning chains can improve multistep problem solving, but additional text does not always add useful information. This paper examines that tension through information theory. It introduces InfoBias to measure divergence from ideal reasoning paths and InfoGain to measure the information contributed by individual steps, making reasoning efficiency a question of content as well as length.

The empirical analysis finds that longer chains tend to accumulate more information bias while providing diminishing information gains, particularly when the final answer is wrong. These are observed tendencies rather than a claim that every long chain is unhelpful. Motivated by them, the authors develop Adaptive Think, an entropy-based strategy that stops reasoning when confidence becomes sufficiently high.

On QwQ-32B across six benchmarks covering different reasoning types and difficulty levels, Adaptive Think improves average accuracy by 1.10% and reduces token usage by 50.80% relative to the default Vanilla Think approach. The results show that adaptive stopping can preserve competitive accuracy while substantially reducing generated reasoning, and can improve accuracy in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Think uses entropy-based stopping to reduce reasoning tokens while improving average accuracy in the reported QwQ-32B evaluation.

title: Think or Not? Exploring Thinking Efficiency in Large Reasoning Models via an Information-Theoretic Lens

abstract: We introduce a novel class of score-based diffusion processes that operate directly in the representation space of Lie groups. Leveraging the framework of Generalized Score Matching, we derive a class of Langevin dynamics that decomposes as a direct sum of Lie algebra representations, enabling the modeling of any target distribution on any (non-Abelian) Lie group. Standard score-matching emerges as a special case of our framework when the Lie group is the translation group. We prove that our generalized generative processes arise as solutions to a new class of paired stochastic differential equations (SDEs), introduced here for the first time. We validate our approach through experiments on diverse data types, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications such as $\text{SO}(3)$-guided molecular conformer generation and modeling ligand-specific global $\text{SE}(3)$ transformations for molecular docking, showing improvement in comparison to Riemannian diffusion on the group itself. We show that an appropriate choice of Lie group enhances learning efficiency by reducing the effective dimensionality of the trajectory space and enables the modeling of transitions between complex data distributions.

paragraphs: This paper develops diffusion models that operate in representation spaces of Lie groups, mathematical structures used to describe transformations. The approach allows the transformation structure to shape generation directly. Its framework includes non-Abelian groups, where the order of transformations matters, and recovers ordinary score matching when the chosen group describes translations.

Using generalized score matching, the authors derive Langevin dynamics that split into components corresponding to Lie algebra representations. They also prove that the generative processes solve a new class of paired stochastic differential equations. The theoretical framework supports modeling any target distribution on any non-Abelian Lie group, giving the construction broad scope beyond a single application.

Experiments include rotation-guided molecular conformer generation using SO(3) and ligand-specific rigid transformations using SE(3) for molecular docking. The approach improves on Riemannian diffusion performed on the group itself in these applications. The authors further show that an appropriate group choice can reduce the effective dimensionality of generation trajectories, improve learning efficiency, and support transitions between complex distributions.
summary.tldr: Diffusion in Lie-group representation spaces provides a general transformation-aware framework and improves molecular generation and docking results over diffusion on the group itself.

title: Diffusion Generative Modeling on Lie Group Representations

abstract: Graph Transformer (GT) has recently emerged as a promising neural network architecture for learning graph-structured data. However, its global attention mechanism with quadratic complexity concerning the graph scale prevents wider application to large graphs. Effectively representing graph information while ensuring learning efficiency remains challenging, as our analysis reveals that current GT designs targeting scalability still suffer from the computational bottleneck related to graph-scale operations. In this work, we tackle the GT scalability issue by proposing HubGT, a scalable Graph Transformer boosted by fully decoupled graph processing and simplified learning. HubGT represents the graph by a novel hierarchical scheme exploiting hub labels, which is shown to be more informative than plain adjacency by offering global connections while promoting locality, and is particularly suitable for handling complex graph patterns such as heterophily. We also design algorithms for efficiently constructing and querying the hub label hierarchy tailored for the GT attention training in scalable deployments. Notably, the precomputation and training processes of HubGT achieve complexities linear to the number of graph edges and nodes, respectively, while the training stage completely removes graph-related computations, leading to favorable mini-batch capability and GPU utilization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HubGT is efficient in terms of computational enhancement and mini-batch capability over existing GT designs on large-scale benchmarks, while achieving top-tier effectiveness on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs.

paragraphs: Graph transformers use global attention to learn from graph structure, but its quadratic cost makes large graphs difficult to handle. The paper argues that even designs intended to scale can retain expensive operations tied to the whole graph. HubGT tackles this bottleneck by separating graph processing from training and simplifying the work performed during learning.

Its representation uses a hierarchy built from hub labels. The hierarchy provides information about global connections while retaining locality, and the authors show it is more informative than plain adjacency. It is also suited to heterophilous graphs, where connected nodes can differ. Dedicated construction and query algorithms make this representation usable for transformer attention.

HubGT’s precomputation scales linearly with edge count, while training scales linearly with node count. Graph-related computations are removed from the training stage, supporting mini-batches and favorable GPU utilization. Experiments on large benchmarks report improved computational efficiency and mini-batch capability alongside top-tier effectiveness on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs.
summary.tldr: HubGT precomputes a hub-label hierarchy to remove graph processing from training and scale graph transformers efficiently.

title: HubGT: Fast Graph Transformer with Decoupled Hierarchy Labeling

abstract: The urban environment is characterized by complex spatio-temporal dynamics arising from diverse human activities and interactions. Effectively modeling these dynamics is essential for understanding and optimizing urban systems. In this work, we introduce UrbanDiT, a foundation model for open-world urban spatio-temporal learning that successfully scales up diffusion transformers in this field. UrbanDiT pioneers a unified model that integrates diverse data sources and types while learning universal spatio-temporal patterns across different cities and scenarios. This allows the model to unify both multi-data and multi-task learning, and effectively support a wide range of spatio-temporal applications. Its key innovation lies in the elaborated prompt learning framework, which adaptively generates both data-driven and task-specific prompts, guiding the model to deliver superior performance across various urban applications. UrbanDiT offers three advantages: 1) It unifies diverse data types, such as grid-based and graph-based data, into a sequential format; 2) With task-specific prompts, it supports a wide range of tasks, including bi-directional spatio-temporal prediction, temporal interpolation, spatial extrapolation, and spatio-temporal imputation; and 3) It generalizes effectively to open-world scenarios, with its powerful zero-shot capabilities outperforming nearly all baselines with training data. UrbanDiT sets up a new benchmark for foundation models in the urban spatio-temporal domain. Code and datasets are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/UrbanDiT}.

paragraphs: UrbanDiT is a foundation model for urban data that changes across space and time. The paper aims to combine learning across cities, data sources, and applications within one diffusion-transformer model. This shared approach is intended to capture patterns that remain useful across different urban settings and prediction tasks.

The model converts different data structures, including grids and graphs, into a common sequential format. Its prompt-learning framework then generates guidance based on both the data and the requested task. These prompts let the same model support prediction in both temporal directions, interpolation between times, extrapolation across space, and filling missing spatial or temporal observations.

The authors report effective generalization to new scenarios, with zero-shot performance exceeding nearly all evaluated baselines that have training data. This is a comparison within the reported evaluation, rather than a guarantee for every city or application. The contribution connects a common data representation with adaptive task guidance, allowing one model to address multiple forms of urban spatiotemporal learning.
summary.tldr: UrbanDiT combines urban data formats and tasks in one prompted diffusion transformer, with strong reported zero-shot generalization.

title: Diffusion Transformers as Open-World Spatiotemporal Foundation Models

abstract: We propose MoGe-2, an advanced open-domain geometry estimation model that recovers a metric-scale 3D point map of a scene from a single image. Our method builds upon the recent monocular geometry estimation approach, MoGe, which predicts affine-invariant point maps with unknown scales. We explore effective strategies to extend MoGe for metric geometry prediction without compromising the relative geometry accuracy provided by the affine-invariant point representation. Additionally, we discover that noise and errors in real data diminish fine-grained detail in the predicted geometry. We address this by developing a data refinement approach that filters and completes real data using sharp synthetic labels, significantly enhancing the granularity of the reconstructed geometry while maintaining the overall accuracy. We train our model on a large corpus of mixed datasets and conducted comprehensive evaluations, demonstrating its superior performance in achieving accurate relative geometry, precise metric scale, and fine-grained detail recovery -- capabilities that no previous methods have simultaneously achieved.

paragraphs: MoGe-2 reconstructs a scene’s three-dimensional point map from a single image, with the added goal of recovering metric scale. Its predecessor, MoGe, predicts affine-invariant point maps whose scale is unknown. The new work explores how to add real-scale geometry prediction while preserving the accurate relative geometry supported by that representation.

The paper also identifies training-data quality as a cause of lost detail. Noise and errors in real data can blur fine structures in predicted geometry. To address this, the authors introduce a refinement process that filters and completes real data using sharp synthetic labels. This improves the granularity of reconstruction while maintaining overall geometric accuracy.

After training on a large mixture of datasets, MoGe-2 is evaluated for relative geometry, metric scale, and fine detail. The authors report superior performance across these capabilities and describe their simultaneous achievement as a distinction from previous methods. The contribution combines an extension of the geometric representation’s capabilities with a targeted improvement to the supervision used for learning.
summary.tldr: MoGe-2 estimates metric-scale 3D geometry from one image while preserving relative accuracy and improving detail through refined training data.

title: MoGe-2: Accurate Monocular Geometry with Metric Scale and Sharp Details

abstract: In real-word scenarios, person re-identification (ReID) expects to identify a person-of-interest via the descriptive query, regardless of whether the query is a single modality or a combination of multiple modalities. However, existing methods and datasets remain constrained to limited modalities, failing to meet this requirement. Therefore, we investigate a new challenging problem called Omni Multi-modal Person Re-identification (OM-ReID), which aims to achieve effective retrieval with varying multi-modal queries. To address dataset scarcity, we construct ORBench, the first high-quality multi-modal dataset comprising 1,000 unique identities across five modalities: RGB, infrared, color pencil, sketch, and textual description. This dataset also has significant superiority in terms of diversity, such as the painting perspectives and textual information. It could serve as an ideal platform for follow-up investigations in OM-ReID. Moreover, we propose ReID5o, a novel multi-modal learning framework for person ReID. It enables synergistic fusion and cross-modal alignment of arbitrary modality combinations in a single model, with a unified encoding and multi-expert routing mechanism proposed. Extensive experiments verify the advancement and practicality of our ORBench. A range of models have been compared on it, and our proposed ReID5o gives the best performance.

paragraphs: Person re-identification queries can arrive in different forms, including images, drawings, or text, and may combine several of them. This paper studies retrieval under such varying combinations. Its proposed task, Omni Multi-modal Person Re-identification, expands beyond methods and datasets restricted to a small set of input modalities.

The authors introduce ORBench, containing 1,000 identities represented through RGB images, infrared images, color-pencil depictions, sketches, and textual descriptions. The dataset also emphasizes variation in drawing perspectives and textual information. This gives researchers a shared setting for testing how retrieval models handle different kinds and combinations of evidence about the same person.

Their ReID5o framework uses unified encoding and routing among multiple experts to align modalities and combine their information in a single model. It supports arbitrary combinations of the available modalities. Among the models compared on ORBench, ReID5o performs best. The paper therefore contributes both a broader evaluation setting and a model designed specifically for flexible multimodal queries.
summary.tldr: ReID5o supports flexible combinations of five query modalities, with ORBench providing a 1,000-identity evaluation dataset.

title: ReID5o: Achieving Omni Multi-modal Person Re-identification in a Single Model

abstract: Advancements in direct-integration fine-tuning frameworks have underscored their potential to enhance the performance of labeled scenarios and tasks. To enhance the generalization of different categories in the same dataset, some methods have added visual loss to these frameworks for unlabeled scenarios. However, the performance of these methods through visual loss does not improve significantly in domain generalization and cross-dataset generalization tasks. This may be attributed to the uncoordinated learning of the two-modalities alignment and visual loss. To mitigate this issue of uncoordinated learning, we propose a novel method called Levelling Paradigm (LePa) to improve performance for unlabeled tasks or scenarios. The proposed LePa, designed as a plug-in module, dynamically constrains and coordinates multiple objective functions, thereby improving the generalization of these baseline methods. Comprehensive experiments have shown that our design can effectively address generalized scenarios and tasks.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning frameworks that work well with labeled data do not necessarily transfer their gains to unlabeled settings. Some approaches add a visual loss to improve generalization across categories within a dataset. According to this paper, those additions have produced limited improvements when the challenge shifts to new domains or different datasets.

The authors suggest that the difficulty may come from uncoordinated learning between the objective that aligns two modalities and the visual objective. Their proposed Levelling Paradigm, or LePa, is a plug-in module that dynamically constrains and coordinates multiple objectives. It changes how the training goals interact, rather than simply adding another goal to optimize.

The reported experiments show improved generalization for the baseline methods equipped with LePa across the studied scenarios and tasks. The practical contribution is a way to adapt existing frameworks for unlabeled learning by coordinating their objectives. The proposed explanation for earlier methods' weak transfer remains qualified: uncoordinated learning is presented as a possible cause, while LePa's benefits are supported by the experiments.
summary.tldr: LePa dynamically coordinates training objectives to improve existing methods' generalization in unlabeled scenarios.

title: An Effective Levelling Paradigm for Unlabeled Scenarios

abstract: The parameter size of modern large language models (LLMs) can be scaled up to the trillion-level via the sparsely-activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) technique to avoid excessive increase of the computational costs. To further improve training efficiency, pipelining computation and communication has become a promising solution for distributed MoE training. However, existing work primarily focuses on scheduling tasks within the MoE layer, such as expert computing and all-to-all (A2A) communication, while neglecting other key operations including multi-head attention (MHA) computing, gating, and all-reduce communication. In this paper, we propose FlowMoE, a scalable framework for scheduling multi-type task pipelines. First, FlowMoE constructs a unified pipeline to consistently scheduling MHA computing, gating, expert computing, and A2A communication. Second, FlowMoE introduces a tensor chunk-based priority scheduling mechanism to overlap the all-reduce communication with all computing tasks. We implement FlowMoE as an adaptive and generic framework atop PyTorch. Extensive experiments with 675 typical MoE layers and four real-world MoE models across two GPU clusters demonstrate that our proposed FlowMoE framework outperforms state-of-the-art MoE training frameworks, reducing training time by14%-57%, energy consumption by 10%-39%, and memory usage by 7%-32%. FlowMoE’s code is anonymously available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FlowMoE.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models can grow to very large parameter counts while activating only part of the model, avoiding a proportional increase in computation. Training them across GPUs still requires coordinating computation and communication. FlowMoE addresses that coordination by scheduling a broader set of training operations together.

The paper identifies a gap in earlier scheduling approaches: they concentrate mainly on expert computation and all-to-all communication within the MoE layer. FlowMoE builds a unified pipeline that also includes multi-head attention computation and gating. Bringing these operations into the same schedule lets the framework coordinate work that earlier approaches largely left outside their scheduling scope.

FlowMoE also introduces a priority scheduling mechanism based on tensor chunks. This mechanism overlaps all-reduce communication with computing tasks, allowing communication and computation to proceed concurrently. The authors implement the combined approach as an adaptive, general framework built on PyTorch.

The reported evaluation covers 675 typical MoE layers and four real-world MoE models on two GPU clusters. Compared with state-of-the-art MoE training frameworks, FlowMoE reduces training time by 14%–57%, energy consumption by 10%–39%, and memory usage by 7%–32%. These measured improvements support the value of coordinating multiple operation types, with benefits spanning speed, energy, and memory in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FlowMoE coordinates more computation and communication tasks in distributed Mixture-of-Experts training, reducing training time, energy consumption, and memory usage in its reported evaluations.

title: FlowMoE: A Scalable Pipeline Scheduling Framework for Distributed Mixture-of-Experts Training

abstract: Robustness to modeling errors and uncertainties remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we address this challenge by leveraging diffusion models to train robust RL policies. Diffusion models have recently gained popularity in model-based RL due to their ability to generate full trajectories "all at once", mitigating the compounding errors typical of step-by-step transition models. Moreover, they can be conditioned to sample from specific distributions, making them highly flexible. We leverage conditional sampling to learn policies that are robust to uncertainty in environment dynamics. Building on the established connection between Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) optimization and robust RL, we introduce Adversarial Diffusion for Robust Reinforcement Learning (AD-RRL). AD-RRL guides the diffusion process to generate worst-case trajectories during training, effectively optimizing the CVaR of the cumulative return. Empirical results across standard benchmarks show that AD-RRL achieves superior robustness and performance compared to existing robust RL methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies can struggle when an environment behaves differently from the model used during training. This paper addresses that uncertainty by training policies on unfavorable trajectories generated with a diffusion model. The aim is to improve behavior under difficult dynamics, rather than relying only on trajectories that reflect typical outcomes.

Diffusion models provide two useful capabilities here. They can generate complete trajectories together, mitigating the accumulating errors associated with predicting each transition separately. They can also condition generation toward particular distributions. AD-RRL uses that conditional generation to guide the diffusion process toward worst-case trajectories during policy training.

The training objective connects to Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, which focuses on the unfavorable part of the return distribution. Through an established connection between CVaR optimization and robust reinforcement learning, the generated trajectories support policies that account for dynamics uncertainty. Across standard benchmarks, the authors report better robustness and performance than existing robust reinforcement learning methods. These findings support adversarial trajectory generation as an effective empirical approach to robust policy training.
summary.tldr: AD-RRL guides diffusion models toward worst-case training trajectories to improve reinforcement learning robustness under uncertain environment dynamics.

title: Adversarial Diffusion for Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We prove rich algebraic structures of the solution space for 2-layer neural networks with quadratic activation and $L_2$ loss, trained on reasoning tasks in Abelian group (e.g., modular addition). Such a rich structure enables \emph{analytical} construction of global optimal solutions from partial solutions that only satisfy part of the loss, despite its high nonlinearity. We coin the framework as \ours{} (\emph{\underline{Co}mposing \underline{G}lobal \underline{S}olutions}). Specifically, we show that the weight space over different numbers of hidden nodes of the 2-layer network is equipped with a semi-ring algebraic structure, and the loss function to be optimized consists of \emph{sum potentials}, which are ring homomorphisms, allowing partial solutions to be composed into global ones by ring addition and multiplication. Our experiments show that around $95\%$ of the solutions obtained by gradient descent match exactly our theoretical constructions. Although the global solutions constructed only required a small number of hidden nodes, our analysis on gradient dynamics shows that overparameterization asymptotically decouples training dynamics and is beneficial. We further show that training dynamics favors simpler solutions under weight decay, and thus high-order global solutions such as perfect memorization are unfavorable. The code is open sourced\footnote{\url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters/tree/yuandong3/ssl/real-dataset}}.

paragraphs: This paper studies a specific mathematical setting: two-layer neural networks with quadratic activations and an L2 loss, trained on reasoning tasks over Abelian groups such as modular addition. It proves that their solution space has an algebraic structure that makes it possible to construct globally optimal solutions analytically from pieces that satisfy only parts of the loss.

The construction treats weight spaces with different hidden-layer sizes as a semiring, an algebraic system supporting addition and multiplication. Components of the loss called sum potentials preserve relevant algebraic operations. Consequently, combining partial solutions through these operations can produce complete solutions despite the original optimization problem’s nonlinearity. This provides a concrete description of how solutions fit together.

In experiments, about 95% of solutions found by gradient descent exactly match the theoretical constructions. Although compact networks can represent the constructed solutions, the analysis shows that overparameterization asymptotically separates training dynamics in a beneficial way. With weight decay, training favors simpler solutions and disfavors higher-order solutions such as perfect memorization. These conclusions concern the network and task setting analyzed.
summary.tldr: For a specific class of reasoning networks, algebraic operations combine partial solutions into global optima and help explain training behavior.

title: Composing Global Solutions to Reasoning Tasks via Algebraic Objects in Neural Nets

abstract: LLM developers deploy technical mitigations to prevent _fine-tuning misuse attacks_, attacks in which adversaries evade safeguards by fine-tuning the model using a public API. Previous work has established several successful attacks against specific fine-tuning API defences; however, prior attacks training and/or inference samples can be easily flagged as suspicious. In this work, we show that defences of fine-tuning APIs that seek to detect individual harmful training or inference samples ('pointwise' detection) are _fundamentally limited_ in their ability to prevent fine-tuning attacks. We demonstrate a class of 'pointwise-undetectable' attacks that repurpose semantic or syntactic variations in benign model outputs to covertly transmit dangerous knowledge. Our attacks are composed solely of unsuspicious benign samples that can be collected from the model before fine-tuning, meaning training and inference samples are all individually benign and low-perplexity. We test our attacks against the OpenAI fine-tuning API, finding they succeed in eliciting answers to harmful multiple-choice questions, and that they evade an enhanced monitoring system we design that successfully detects other fine-tuning attacks. Our results showing fundamental limitations of defending against pointwise attacks suggest focusing research efforts on mitigations towards multi-point defences.

paragraphs: This paper examines a weakness in defenses that inspect fine-tuning or inference samples individually. Such pointwise checks try to recognize harmful content one sample at a time. The authors show how misuse can instead depend on relationships among apparently benign samples, making individual harmlessness insufficient for identifying the broader behavior.

The demonstrated attack class uses semantic or syntactic variation in benign outputs to carry dangerous knowledge covertly. Its training and inference samples can be collected from the model before fine-tuning and are individually benign and low-perplexity. The key issue is that the meaning carried by the overall arrangement is not captured by judging each sample independently.

Tests against the OpenAI fine-tuning API elicit answers to harmful multiple-choice questions. The attacks also evade an enhanced monitoring system that detects other fine-tuning attacks. These results establish limitations of the pointwise defensive approach studied, rather than showing that every form of defense must fail. The authors consequently direct attention toward multi-point defenses that can examine relationships across samples.
summary.tldr: Individually benign samples can support fine-tuning misuse, exposing fundamental limits of defenses that inspect samples in isolation.

title: Fundamental Limitations in Pointwise Defences of LLM Finetuning APIs

abstract: Speech signal analysis poses significant challenges, particularly in tasks such as speech quality evaluation and profiling, where the goal is to predict multiple perceptual and objective metrics. For instance, metrics like PESQ (Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality), STOI (Short-Time Objective Intelligibility), and MOS (Mean Opinion Score) each capture different aspects of speech quality. However, these metrics often have different scales, assumptions, and dependencies, making joint estimation non-trivial. To address these issues, we introduce ARECHO (Autoregressive Evaluation via Chain-based Hypothesis Optimization), a chain-based, versatile evaluation system for speech assessment grounded in autoregressive dependency modeling. ARECHO is distinguished by three key innovations: (1) a comprehensive speech information tokenization pipeline; (2) a dynamic classifier chain that explicitly captures inter-metric dependencies; and (3) a two-step confidence-oriented decoding algorithm that enhances inference reliability. Experiments demonstrate that ARECHO significantly outperforms the baseline framework across diverse evaluation scenarios, including enhanced speech analysis, speech generation evaluation, and noisy speech evaluation. Furthermore, its dynamic dependency modeling improves interpretability by capturing inter-metric relationships. Across tasks, ARECHO offers reference-free evaluation using its dynamic classifier chain to support subset queries (single or multiple metrics) and reduces error propagation via confidence-oriented decoding.

paragraphs: Speech quality cannot be captured by a single score. Measures such as PESQ, STOI, and MOS describe different perceptual or objective aspects, and their scales and assumptions differ. ARECHO addresses the challenge of predicting several such measures together while accounting for relationships among them.

The system first converts speech information into tokens. A dynamic classifier chain then estimates metrics through an autoregressive process, explicitly modeling dependencies between predictions. A two-step decoding procedure uses confidence to improve reliability and reduce the propagation of errors through that chain. This makes the relationships between scores part of the evaluation mechanism rather than leaving each prediction isolated.

The authors report significant improvements over their baseline across enhanced, generated, and noisy speech evaluation. ARECHO works without a reference recording and supports requests for either individual metrics or selected groups of metrics. Its dependency modeling also improves interpretability by exposing relationships among measures, making the framework useful for examining several aspects of speech within one evaluation system.
summary.tldr: ARECHO jointly estimates speech metrics through a dynamic prediction chain that models their dependencies and uses confidence to reduce errors.

title: ARECHO: Autoregressive Evaluation via Chain-Based Hypothesis Optimization for Speech Multi-Metric Estimation

abstract: We study the Hamiltonian flow for optimization (HF-opt), which simulates the Hamiltonian dynamics for some integration time and resets the velocity to $0$ to decrease the objective function; this is the optimization analogue of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm for sampling. For short integration time, HF-opt has the same convergence rates as gradient descent for minimizing strongly and weakly convex functions. We show that by randomizing the integration time in HF-opt, the resulting randomized Hamiltonian flow (RHF) achieves accelerated convergence rates in continuous time, similar to the rates for accelerated gradient flow. We study a discrete-time implementation of RHF as the randomized Hamiltonian gradient descent (RHGD) algorithm. We prove that RHGD achieves the same accelerated convergence rates as Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent (AGD) for minimizing smooth strongly and weakly convex functions. We provide numerical experiments to demonstrate that RHGD is competitive with classical accelerated methods such as AGD across all settings and outperforms them in certain regimes.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian flow offers a physics-inspired way to minimize an objective: simulate motion for a period, then reset velocity to zero so the objective decreases. With short simulation periods, this procedure converges at the same rates as gradient descent on strongly and weakly convex functions. The paper asks whether changing the duration of these motion segments can yield acceleration.

The key change is to randomize the integration time. The authors prove that this randomized Hamiltonian flow achieves accelerated convergence in continuous time, with rates similar to accelerated gradient flow. They then turn the continuous process into a discrete algorithm called randomized Hamiltonian gradient descent, making the approach available as an iterative optimization method.

The contribution connects randomized simulation timing to both theoretical acceleration and an implementable algorithm, without claiming that it always outperforms existing accelerated methods.
summary.tldr: Randomizing Hamiltonian integration time yields an optimization algorithm that matches Nesterov’s accelerated rates under the stated smoothness and convexity conditions.

title: Hamiltonian Descent Algorithms for Optimization: Accelerated Rates via Randomized Integration Time

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted across diverse domains of software engineering, such as code generation, program repair, and vulnerability detection. These applications require understanding beyond surface-level code patterns: value propagation, control flow, and interdependence between program elements. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end outcomes, such as whether code is correctly repaired or generated, leaving the models' ability of program semantic reasoning underexplored.This work presents CoRe, a high-quality, human-verified benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs on fundamental static analysis tasks. CoRe includes 12,553 task instances spanning data dependency, control dependency, and information flow across programs written in C/C++, Java, and Python. To ensure semantic diversity and reasoning complexity, we propose a semantics-aware diverse sampling strategy that selects targets and task instances based on structural coverage and dependency depth. We evaluate 10 state-of-the-art LLMs and show that, while they perform well at identifying dependencies, models still struggle with tasks that require deeper semantic understanding and multi-step reasoning.We further conduct qualitative analyses to uncover key challenges, such as complex control structures and backward dependency patterns, offering insights into improving LLMs’ code reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: A model can produce or repair code successfully without an evaluation revealing how well it understands the program's internal relationships. CoRe examines that understanding directly through static analysis tasks. These tasks focus on how values propagate, how control decisions affect execution, and how information moves between program elements.

The human-verified benchmark contains 12,553 instances covering data dependency, control dependency, and information flow in C/C++, Java, and Python. Its sampling strategy considers program structure and dependency depth when choosing instances. This gives the evaluation semantic variety while including relationships that require following multiple steps, rather than concentrating only on readily visible connections.

Across ten evaluated language models, dependency identification is comparatively successful, but deeper semantic reasoning remains challenging. Qualitative analysis identifies complex control structures and backward dependency patterns as particular difficulties. The benchmark therefore provides a more focused view of code understanding than end-to-end success alone: it helps distinguish recognizing a dependency from reasoning through the chain of program behavior that establishes it.
summary.tldr: CoRe tests program dependencies and information flow directly, revealing weaknesses in language models' deeper, multi-step code reasoning.

title: CoRe: Benchmarking LLMs’ Code Reasoning Capabilities through Static Analysis Tasks

abstract: Gating mechanisms have been widely utilized, from early models like LSTMs and Highway Networks to recent state space models, linear attention, and also softmax attention. Yet, existing literature rarely examines the specific effects of gating. In this work, we conduct comprehensive experiments to systematically investigate gating-augmented softmax attention variants. Specifically, we perform a comprehensive comparison over 30 variants of 15B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models and 1.7B dense models trained on a 3.5 trillion token dataset. Our central finding is that a simple modification—applying a head-specific sigmoid gate after the Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA)—consistently improves performance. This modification also enhances training stability, tolerates larger learning rates, and improves scaling properties. By comparing various gating positions and computational variants, we attribute this effectiveness to two key factors: (1) introducing non-linearity upon the low-rank mapping in the softmax attention, and (2) applying query-dependent sparse gating scores to modulate the SDPA output. Notably, we find this sparse gating mechanism mitigates `massive activation`, `attention sink` and enhances long-context extrapolation performance. We also release related codes (https://github.com/qiuzh20/gated_attention}) and models (https://huggingface.co/QwQZh/gated_attention) to facilitate future research. Furthermore, the most effective SDPA output gating is used in the Qwen3-Next models (https://huggingface.co/collections/Qwen/qwen3-next).

The change also improves training stability, supports larger learning rates, and strengthens scaling behavior. Comparisons across gate placements and computations help isolate the mechanisms associated with these improvements.

The authors attribute the benefits to added nonlinearity in attention's low-rank mapping and sparse gating scores that depend on the query. They report reduced massive activations and attention sinks, along with better long-context extrapolation. The results make a specific architectural recommendation, and the abstract states that the most effective output-gating design is used in Qwen3-Next.
summary.tldr: Head-specific sigmoid gates after attention improve tested language models through added nonlinearity and query-dependent sparsity.

title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free

abstract: Deep neural networks with short residual connections have demonstrated remarkable success across domains, but increasing depth often introduces computational redundancy without corresponding improvements in representation quality. We introduce Auto-Compressing Networks (ACNs), an architectural variant where additive long feedforward connections from each layer to the output replace traditional short residual connections. By analyzing the distinct dynamics induced by this modification, we reveal a unique property we coin as *auto-compression*—the ability of a network to organically compress information during training with gradient descent, through architectural design alone. Through auto-compression, information is dynamically "pushed" into early layers during training, enhancing their representational quality and revealing potential redundancy in deeper ones. We theoretically show that this property emerges from layer-wise training patterns found only in ACNs, where layers are dynamically utilized during training based on task requirements. We also find that ACNs exhibit enhanced noise robustness compared to residual networks, superior performance in low-data settings, improved transfer learning capabilities, and mitigate catastrophic forgetting suggesting that they learn representations that generalize better despite using fewer parameters. Our results demonstrate up to 18\% reduction in catastrophic forgetting and 30-80\% architectural compression while maintaining accuracy across vision transformers, MLP-mixers, and BERT architectures. These findings establish ACNs as a practical approach to developing efficient neural architectures that automatically adapt their computational footprint to task complexity, while learning robust representations suitable for noisy real-world tasks and continual learning scenarios.

The paper studies how this architectural change alters gradient-descent training, addressing the possibility that additional depth introduces computation without a corresponding improvement in representations.

The central property is auto-compression: during training, useful information moves into earlier layers, improving their representations and exposing redundancy deeper in the network. The authors theoretically connect this behavior to layer-specific training patterns in ACNs. summary.tldr: Auto-Compressing Networks use long connections to concentrate information in early layers, enabling substantial compression while maintaining tested accuracy.

title: Auto-Compressing Networks

abstract: Spike sorting is an essential process in neural recording, which identifies and separates electrical signals from individual neurons recorded by electrodes in the brain, enabling researchers to study how specific neurons communicate and process information. Although there exist a number of spike sorting methods which have contributed to significant neuroscientific breakthroughs, many are heuristically designed, making it challenging to verify their correctness due to the difficulty of obtaining ground truth labels from real-world neural recordings. In this work, we explore a data-driven, deep learning-based approach. We begin by creating a large-scale dataset through electrophysiology simulations using biologically realistic computational models. We then present SimSort, a pretraining framework for spike sorting. Trained solely on simulated data, SimSort demonstrates zero-shot generalizability to real-world spike sorting tasks, yielding consistent improvements over existing methods across multiple benchmarks. These results highlight the potential of simulation-driven pretraining to enhance the robustness and scalability of spike sorting in experimental neuroscience.

paragraphs: Brain electrodes record electrical activity that must be separated into signals associated with individual neurons. This process, called spike sorting, helps researchers study how neurons communicate and process information. Assessing sorting methods is difficult because real recordings rarely provide the ground-truth labels needed to establish which neuron produced each signal.

The authors explore a data-driven alternative to heuristically designed sorting methods. They first generate a large electrophysiology dataset using biologically realistic computational models. SimSort then uses that simulated dataset for deep-learning-based pretraining, placing simulation at the center of the training approach.

Despite being trained solely on simulated data, SimSort demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world spike-sorting tasks. It consistently improves over existing methods across multiple evaluated benchmarks. These findings show that simulation-trained representations can transfer to experimental recordings in the tested settings. They support simulation-driven pretraining as a promising route toward more robust and scalable spike sorting, especially where obtaining real training labels is difficult.
summary.tldr: SimSort learns spike sorting entirely from biologically realistic simulations and shows zero-shot improvements on real-world benchmarks.

title: SimSort: A Data-Driven Framework for Spike Sorting by Large-Scale Electrophysiology Simulation

abstract: Dataset distillation seeks to synthesize a compact distilled dataset, enabling models trained on it to achieve performance comparable to models trained on the full dataset. Recent methods for large-scale datasets focus on matching global distributional statistics (e.g., mean and variance), but overlook critical instance-level characteristics and intraclass variations, leading to suboptimal generalization. We address this limitation by reformulating dataset distillation as an Optimal Transport (OT) distance minimization problem, enabling fine-grained alignment at both global and instance levels throughout the pipeline. OT offers a geometrically faithful framework for distribution matching. It effectively preserves local modes, intra-class patterns, and fine-grained variations that characterize the geometry of complex, high-dimensional distributions. Our method comprises three components tailored for preserving distributional geometry: (1) OT-guided diffusion sampling, which aligns latent distributions of real and distilled images; (2) label-image-aligned soft relabeling, which adapts label distributions based on the complexity of distilled image distributions; and (3) OT-based logit matching, which aligns the output of student models with soft-label distributions. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and large-scale datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in an efficient manner, achieving at least 4\% accuracy improvement under IPC=10 settings for each architecture on ImageNet-1K.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain the usefulness of a much larger dataset. The paper argues that matching only broad statistics, such as means and variances, can miss differences between individual examples and variation within a class. Those details matter because they help define the structure a model must learn.

The method frames distillation as minimizing an optimal transport distance, aligning distributions at both global and individual-example levels. It applies this idea throughout the pipeline: transport-guided diffusion sampling aligns image latent distributions, soft relabeling adapts label distributions to the complexity of generated images, and transport-based logit matching aligns student outputs with those soft labels.

Experiments across multiple architectures and large datasets report consistent improvements over leading approaches with efficient operation. On ImageNet-1K with ten images per class, the abstract reports at least a 4% accuracy improvement for each tested architecture. The findings support preserving distributional geometry across image generation, labeling, and model training, so the compact dataset carries more than aggregate class statistics.
summary.tldr: The method uses optimal transport throughout dataset distillation to preserve fine-grained variation and improve training from compact synthetic datasets.

title: Optimizing Distributional Geometry Alignment with Optimal Transport for Generative Dataset Distillation

abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is a fundamental task in artificial intelligence, with far-reaching implications for decision-making, predictions, and interventions. Despite significant advances, existing methods can be broadly categorized as constraint-based or score-based approaches. Constraint-based methods offer rigorous causal discovery but are often hindered by small sample sizes, while score-based methods provide flexible optimization but typically forgo explicit conditional independence testing. This work explores a third avenue: developing differentiable $d$-separation scores, obtained through a percolation theory using soft logic. This enables the implementation of a new type of causal discovery method: gradient-based optimization of conditional independence constraints. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the robust performance of our approach in low-sample regimes, surpassing traditional constraint-based and score-based baselines on a real-world dataset. Code implementing the proposed method is publicly available at [https://github.com/PurdueMINDS/DAGPA](https://github.com/PurdueMINDS/DAGPA).

paragraphs: Causal discovery seeks to infer causal structure from observational data. Constraint-based methods use conditional independence relationships, but can struggle when samples are scarce. Score-based approaches offer flexible optimization, yet typically do not explicitly test those relationships. This paper develops a way to bring independence constraints into a differentiable optimization process.

The central construction is a differentiable score for d-separation, the graph property used to express conditional independence implications. The authors derive these scores through percolation theory and soft logic. Making the scores differentiable allows gradient-based optimization to work directly with conditional independence constraints, connecting a structural reasoning approach with numerical optimization.

The resulting method offers a third route alongside the usual constraint-based and score-based categories. Empirical evaluations report robust performance when little data is available, including results surpassing traditional methods from both categories on a real-world dataset. These findings support the usefulness of optimizing independence constraints in low-sample settings, where conventional constraint-based discovery is often difficult.
summary.tldr: Differentiable d-separation scores enable gradient-based causal discovery that directly optimizes conditional independence constraints.

title: Differentiable Constraint-Based Causal Discovery

abstract: Parameter-efficient training, based on low-rank optimization, has become a highly successful tool for fine-tuning large deep-learning models. However, these methods fail at low-rank pre-training tasks where maintaining the low-rank structure and the objective remains a challenging task. We propose the Quadratic Reweighted Rank Regularizer dubbed Q3R, which leads to a novel low-rank inducing training strategy inspired by the iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) framework. Q3R is based on a quadratic regularizer term which majorizes a smoothed log determinant serving as rank surrogate objective. Unlike other low-rank training techniques, Q3R is able to train weight matrices with prescribed, low target ranks of models that achieve comparable predictive performance as dense models, with small computational overhead, while remaining fully compatible with existing architectures. In experiments, we are able to truncate 60% of the parameters of a ViT-Tiny parameters with marginal loss in CIFAR-10 performance and up to 80% with only 4% accuracy drop. The efficacy of Q3R is confirmed on Transformers across both image and language tasks, including for low-rank fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Low-rank methods reduce the number of independent quantities needed to represent a model's weight matrices. They are successful for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, but maintaining useful low-rank structure during pretraining is more difficult. Q3R addresses this problem with a regularizer designed to encourage prescribed low target ranks during training.

The method draws on iteratively reweighted least squares. Its quadratic penalty upper-bounds a smoothed log-determinant objective that serves as a substitute for directly optimizing matrix rank. This gives training a way to encourage low-rank weights while remaining compatible with existing model architectures. The authors report small computational overhead and predictive performance comparable to dense models.

In a ViT-Tiny experiment on CIFAR-10, the method allows 60% of parameters to be removed with only marginal performance loss. Removing up to 80% produces a reported 4% accuracy drop. Experiments also cover Transformers in image and language tasks, including low-rank fine-tuning. These results support Q3R as a way to build compressible weight structure during learning while controlling the resulting performance tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Q3R encourages prescribed low-rank weights during training, enabling substantial parameter reduction with modest reported performance losses.

title: Q3R: Quadratic Reweighted Rank Regularizer for Effective Low-Rank Training

abstract: This position paper challenges the "scaling fundamentalism" dominating AI research, where unbounded growth in model size and computation has led to unsustainable environmental impacts and widening resource inequality. We argue that LLM development should be fundamentally reoriented toward capability-per-resource rather than capability alone. We present a theoretical framework demonstrating that resource-allocation decisions guided by gradient influence patterns can dramatically improve efficiency throughout the AI lifecycle. Our analysis shows that in transformer-based models, where a small fraction of parameters exert outsized influence (following heavy-tailed distributions), three critical insights emerge: (1) updating only high-influence parameters strictly outperforms full-parameter tuning on a performance-per-resource basis; (2) simple gradient norms provide computationally efficient proxies for identifying these high-influence components; and (3) coordinated parameter and data selection yields multiplicative efficiency gains, potentially reducing resource requirements by orders of magnitude. Building on these theoretical foundations, we propose a two-stage paradigm—marginal-return pretraining for foundation developers and influence-guided adaptation for downstream users—bridged by gradient blueprints, metadata describing which parameters matter most for various tasks. This capability-per-resource perspective transforms what were once considered pragmatic hardware workarounds into theoretically optimal strategies, democratizing access to cutting-edge AI capabilities while significantly reducing environmental impact. By embedding resource consciousness into how we develop, adapt, and evaluate models, we can reshape AI progress toward a more sustainable and equitable future.

Its motivation is that continually increasing model size and computation can worsen environmental costs and unequal access. The authors propose evaluating development choices through capability per resource and present a theoretical framework for allocating effort accordingly.

The analysis considers transformers in which parameter influence follows a heavy-tailed distribution: a relatively small subset has disproportionately large effects. Under this framework, updating high-influence parameters strictly improves performance per resource over updating every parameter. Gradient norms provide inexpensive indicators of influence, while selecting parameters and training data together yields multiplicative efficiency gains that could reduce resource needs by orders of magnitude.

The proposed workflow pairs pretraining guided by marginal returns with influence-guided adaptation. Gradient blueprints would communicate which parameters matter for different tasks. These are theoretical arguments and a proposed development paradigm; the potential resource savings should be understood within that framing, rather than as reported deployment measurements.
summary.tldr: This position paper proposes measuring AI progress by capability per resource and using parameter influence to guide more efficient training and adaptation.

title: AI Progress Should Be Measured by Capability-Per-Resource, Not Scale Alone: A Framework for Gradient-Guided Resource Allocation in LLMs

abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation assigns every pixel a label drawn from an open-ended, text-defined space. Vision–language models such as CLIP excel at zero-shot recognition, yet their image-level pre-training hinders dense prediction. Current approaches either fine-tune CLIP—at high computational cost—or adopt training-free attention refinements that favor local smoothness while overlooking global semantics. In this paper, we present OPMapper, a lightweight, plug-and-play module that injects both local compactness and global connectivity into attention maps of CLIP. It combines Context-aware Attention Injection, which embeds spatial and semantic correlations, and Semantic Attention Alignment, which iteratively aligns the enriched weights with textual prompts. By jointly modeling token dependencies and leveraging textual guidance, OPMapper enhances visual understanding. OPMapper is highly flexible and can be seamlessly integrated into both training-based and training-free paradigms with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness, yielding significant improvements across 8 open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks.

By jointly modeling token dependencies and leveraging textual guidance, OPMapper enhances visual understanding. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness, yielding significant improvements across 8 open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation assigns text-defined categories to individual pixels. Models such as CLIP are strong at recognizing whole images, but that training does not directly provide the detailed spatial information segmentation needs. Existing approaches either incur the cost of fine-tuning or refine attention locally while giving insufficient attention to global meaning.

OPMapper modifies CLIP's attention maps using both local compactness and global connectivity. Its Context-aware Attention Injection component adds spatial and semantic correlations. Semantic Attention Alignment then repeatedly aligns the enriched attention weights with textual prompts. Together, these operations combine relationships among visual tokens with guidance from the category descriptions.

The module can be added to both training-based and training-free segmentation methods with minimal computational overhead. Experiments report significant gains across eight open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks. The contribution is a lightweight way to improve the attention information used for dense prediction: local spatial coherence is combined with broader semantic connections and text guidance, supporting more effective pixel-level labeling in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: OPMapper enriches CLIP attention with spatial relationships, global semantics, and text guidance to improve open-vocabulary segmentation with little overhead.

title: OPMapper: Enhancing Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation with Multi-Guidance Information

abstract: Existing molecular machine learning force fields (MLFFs) generally focus on the learning of atoms, molecules, and simple quantum chemical properties (such as energy and force), but ignore the importance of electron density (ED) $\rho(r)$ in accurately understanding molecular force fields (MFFs). ED describes the probability of finding electrons at specific locations around atoms or molecules, which uniquely determines all ground state properties (such as energy, molecular structure, etc.) of interactive multi-particle systems according to the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem. However, the calculation of ED relies on the time-consuming first-principles density functional theory (DFT), which leads to the lack of large-scale ED data and limits its application in MLFFs. In this paper, we introduce EDBench, a large-scale, high-quality dataset of ED designed to advance learning-based research at the electronic scale. Built upon the PCQM4Mv2, EDBench provides accurate ED data, covering 3.3 million molecules. To comprehensively evaluate the ability of models to understand and utilize electronic information, we design a suite of ED-centric benchmark tasks spanning prediction, retrieval, and generation. Our evaluation of several state-of-the-art methods demonstrates that learning from EDBench is not only feasible but also achieves high accuracy. Moreover, we show that learning-based methods can efficiently calculate ED with comparable precision while significantly reducing the computational cost relative to traditional DFT calculations. All data and benchmarks from EDBench will be freely available, laying a robust foundation for ED-driven drug discovery and materials science.

title: EDBench: Large-Scale Electron Density Data for Molecular Modeling

abstract: Black-box Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (BUDA) aims to transfer source domain knowledge to an unlabeled target domain, without accessing the source data or trained source model. Recent diffusion models have significantly advanced the ability to generate images from texts. While they can produce realistic visuals across diverse prompts and demonstrate impressive compositional generalization, these diffusion-based domain adaptation methods focus solely on composition, overlooking their sensitivity to textual nuances. In this work, we propose a novel diffusion-based method, called Rectifying-reasoning Errors of Diffusion (RrED) for BUDA. RrED is a two-stage learning strategy under diffusion supervision to effectively enhance the target model via the decomposed text and visual encoders from the diffusion model. Specifically, RrED consists of two stages: Diffusion-Target model Rectification (DTR) and Self-rectifying Reasoning Model (SRM). In DTR, we decouple the image and text encoders within the diffusion model: the visual encoder integrates our proposed feature-sensitive module to generate inferentially-enhanced visuals, while the text encoder enables multi-modal joint fine-tuning. In SRM, we prioritize the BUDA task itself, leveraging the target model's differential reasoning capability to rectify errors during learning. Extensive experiments confirm that RrED significantly outperforms other methods on four benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing reasoning and generalization abilities.

paragraphs: RrED studies adaptation to an unlabeled target domain when neither the original source data nor the trained source model is accessible. It uses a diffusion model to provide supervision. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show substantial improvements over other methods. The findings support combining diffusion-based supervision with task-focused correction, rather than relying on generated visual compositions alone to improve target-domain reasoning and generalization.
summary.tldr: RrED combines separate visual and textual diffusion supervision with target-model error correction to improve black-box domain adaptation.

title: RrED: Black-box Unsupervised Domain Adaptation via Rectifying-reasoning Errors of Diffusion

abstract: Aligning visual features with language embeddings is a key challenge in vision-language models (VLMs). The performance of such models hinges on having a good connector that maps visual features generated by a vision encoder to a shared embedding space with the LLM while preserving semantic similarity. Existing connectors, such as multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), lack inductive bias to constrain visual features within the linguistic structure of the LLM’s embedding space, making them data-hungry and prone to cross-modal misalignment. In this work, we propose a novel vision-text alignment method, AlignVLM, that maps visual features to a weighted average of LLM text embeddings. Our approach leverages the linguistic priors encoded by the LLM to ensure that visual features are mapped to regions of the space that the LLM can effectively interpret. AlignVLM is particularly effective for document understanding tasks, where visual and textual modalities are highly correlated. Our extensive experiments show that AlignVLM achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior alignment methods, with larger gains on document understanding and under low-resource setups. We provide further analysis demonstrating its efficiency and robustness to noise.

paragraphs: AlignVLM focuses on the connector that translates image features into representations a language model can interpret. Conventional connectors learn this translation without explicitly respecting the structure of the language model's embedding space. The paper argues that this freedom can require substantial training data and produce visual representations that align poorly with linguistic meaning.

Its alternative constructs the translated visual representation as a weighted average of the language model's existing text embeddings. This introduces a structural constraint: visual features are expressed through representations already associated with language. The connector therefore draws on linguistic knowledge already encoded in the model instead of learning the entire relationship between visual and textual representations without that guidance.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance against previous alignment methods, with especially large gains for document understanding and settings with limited resources. Documents are a natural fit because their visual and textual information are closely connected. Additional analysis supports efficiency and robustness to noise. Together, the findings suggest that the connector's representation structure can materially affect how effectively a model combines vision and language.
summary.tldr: AlignVLM translates visual features through weighted combinations of language embeddings, improving alignment especially for documents and limited-resource settings.

title: AlignVLM: Bridging Vision and Language Latent Spaces for Multimodal Document Understanding

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities through test-time scaling approaches, particularly when fine-tuned with chain-of-thought (CoT) data distilled from more powerful large reasoning models (LRMs). However, these reasoning chains often contain verbose elements that mirror human problem-solving, categorized as progressive reasoning (the essential solution development path) and functional elements (verification processes, alternative solution approaches, and error corrections). While progressive reasoning is crucial, the functional elements significantly increase computational demands during test-time inference. We introduce PIR (Perplexity-based Importance Refinement), a principled framework that quantitatively evaluates the importance of each reasoning step based on its impact on answer prediction confidence. PIR systematically identifies and selectively prunes only low-importance functional steps while preserving all progressive reasoning components, creating optimized training data that maintains the integrity of the core solution path while reducing verbosity. Models fine-tuned on PIR-optimized data exhibit superior test-time scaling properties, generating more concise reasoning chains while achieving improved accuracy (+0.9\% to +6.6\%) with significantly reduced token usage (-3\% to -41\%) across challenging reasoning benchmarks (AIME, AMC, and GPQA Diamond). Our approach demonstrates strong generalizability across different model sizes, data sources, and token budgets, offering a practical solution for deploying reasoning-capable LLMs in scenarios where efficient test-time scaling, response time, and computational efficiency are valuable constraints. Code and dataset are available at the [LIMOPro GitHub repository.](https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/LIMOPro)
