paragraphs: Training language models on detailed reasoning traces can improve reasoning, but those traces can also teach costly verbosity. This paper distinguishes the progressive steps that develop a solution from functional elements such as checking answers, trying alternatives, and correcting errors. Its aim is to reduce unnecessary functional material while retaining the complete core solution path.

Perplexity-based Importance Refinement, or PIR, scores reasoning steps according to their effect on confidence in the predicted answer. It selectively removes low-importance functional steps and preserves all progressive reasoning components. The resulting refined traces become training data, so the efficiency change is learned during fine-tuning and expressed in the model's later reasoning outputs.

Models trained on the refined data produce shorter reasoning chains while improving accuracy on AIME, AMC, and GPQA Diamond. The abstract reports accuracy gains of 0.9% to 6.6% and token reductions of 3% to 41%. Results across model sizes, data sources, and token budgets support the approach's generalizability within the tested settings. The findings show that selectively refining reasoning data can improve both inference efficiency and answer quality.
summary.tldr: PIR removes low-importance auxiliary reasoning from training traces, producing models that use fewer tokens and achieve higher accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: LIMOPro: Reasoning Refinement for Efficient and Effective Test-time Scaling

abstract: It is a challenging problem to reproduce rich spatial details while maintaining temporal consistency in real-world video super-resolution (Real-VSR), especially when we leverage pre-trained generative models such as stable diffusion (SD) for realistic details synthesis. Existing SD-based Real-VSR methods often compromise spatial details for temporal coherence, resulting in suboptimal visual quality. We argue that the key lies in how to effectively extract the degradation-robust temporal consistency priors from the low-quality (LQ) input video and enhance the video details while maintaining the extracted consistency priors. To achieve this, we propose a Dual LoRA Learning (DLoRAL) paradigm to train an effective SD-based one-step diffusion model, achieving realistic frame details and temporal consistency simultaneously. Specifically, we introduce a Cross-Frame Retrieval (CFR) module to aggregate complementary information across frames, and train a Consistency-LoRA (C-LoRA) to learn robust temporal representations from degraded inputs. After consistency learning, we fix the CFR and C-LoRA modules and train a Detail-LoRA (D-LoRA) to enhance spatial details while aligning with the temporal space defined by C-LoRA to keep temporal coherence. The two phases alternate iteratively for optimization, collaboratively delivering consistent and detail-rich outputs. During inference, the two LoRA branches are merged into the SD model, allowing efficient and high-quality video restoration in a single diffusion step. Experiments show that DLoRAL achieves strong performance in both accuracy and speed. Code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Video super-resolution must recover convincing detail while keeping that detail consistent between frames. This paper argues that a pretrained diffusion model needs to preserve reliable temporal information from the degraded input while adding spatial detail. DLoRAL addresses these two requirements through separate but coordinated LoRA training branches.

A Cross-Frame Retrieval module first gathers complementary information across frames, and Consistency-LoRA learns temporal representations robust to degradation. During the detail-learning phase, those components are fixed while Detail-LoRA improves spatial appearance within the temporal representation established by Consistency-LoRA. Alternating the two phases lets the model refine both capabilities while keeping their objectives connected.

At inference, the two LoRA branches are merged into the stable diffusion model, which restores video in one diffusion step. The reported experiments show strong accuracy and speed while producing detailed, temporally coherent outputs. The approach matters because it explicitly organizes adaptation around the tension between frame quality and consistency, then combines the learned adaptations for efficient restoration.
summary.tldr: DLoRAL coordinates separate consistency and detail adaptations to restore detailed, temporally coherent video in one diffusion step.

title: One-Step Diffusion for Detail-Rich and Temporally Consistent Video Super-Resolution

abstract: Telling a cause from its effect using observed time series data is a major challenge in natural and social sciences. Assuming the effect is generated by the cause through a linear system, we propose a new approach based on the hypothesis that nature chooses the “cause” and the “mechanism generating the effect from the cause” independently of each other. Specifically we postulate that the power spectrum of the “cause” time series is uncorrelated with the square of the frequency response of the linear filter (system) generating the effect. While most causal discovery methods for time series mainly rely on the noise, our method relies on asymmetries of the power spectral density properties that exist even in deterministic systems. We describe mathematical assumptions in a deterministic model under which the causal direction is identifiable. In particular, we show a scenario where the method works but Granger causality fails. Experiments show encouraging results on synthetic as well as real-world data. Overall, this suggests that the postulate of Independence of Cause and Mechanism is a promising principle for causal inference on observed time series.

paragraphs: Determining which of two observed time series causes the other is difficult, especially when useful evidence cannot be extracted from noise. This paper assumes that a linear system transforms the cause into the effect. It then asks whether the relationship between the input signal and that transformation can reveal the causal direction.

The proposed principle treats the cause and its generating mechanism as independently chosen. More specifically, the cause's power spectrum is assumed uncorrelated with the squared frequency response of the filter producing the effect. The method looks for directional asymmetries in these spectral properties, allowing it to use information that exists even in deterministic systems.

The authors specify mathematical assumptions under which the causal direction is identifiable and present a scenario in which their method succeeds while Granger causality fails. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data are encouraging. These findings support independence of cause and mechanism as a promising principle within the studied setting, while the identification result remains tied to the linear-system model and its assumptions.
summary.tldr: Spectral independence between a cause and its linear mechanism can identify causal direction under stated assumptions, even in deterministic time series.

title: Telling cause from effect in deterministic linear dynamical systems

abstract: Low dimensional representations of words allow accurate NLP models to be trained on limited annotated data. While most representations ignore words’ local context, a natural way to induce context-dependent representations is to perform inference in a probabilistic latent-variable sequence model. Given the recent success of continuous vector space word representations, we provide such an inference procedure for continuous states, where words’ representations are given by the posterior mean of a linear dynamical system. Here, efficient inference can be performed using Kalman filtering. Our learning algorithm is extremely scalable, operating on simple co-occurrence counts for both parameter initialization using the method of moments and subsequent iterations of EM. In our experiments, we employ our inferred word embeddings as features in standard tagging tasks, obtaining significant accuracy improvements. Finally, the Kalman filter updates can be seen as a linear recurrent neural network. We demonstrate that using the parameters of our model to initialize a non-linear recurrent neural network language model reduces its training time by a day and yields lower perplexity.

paragraphs: A word’s useful representation can depend on the words around it. This paper develops a probabilistic sequence model that produces continuous word representations incorporating local context. Each representation is the posterior mean of a hidden state in a linear dynamical system: an estimate of that state after accounting for the observed text.

The linear structure makes inference efficient through Kalman filtering. Learning also uses a compact source of information: word co-occurrence counts support both initialization by the method of moments and subsequent expectation-maximization updates. This connects contextual word representations to a sequence-modeling approach whose training procedure is designed to scale.

The inferred representations improve accuracy when used as features in the reported tagging experiments. The authors also interpret Kalman-filter updates as a linear recurrent neural network and use learned parameters to initialize a nonlinear recurrent language model. In that experiment, initialization cuts training time by a day and lowers perplexity. The results therefore demonstrate uses both as contextual features and as a starting point for another model.
summary.tldr: A linear dynamical model learns contextual word representations efficiently and provides useful features and initialization for language models.

title: A Linear Dynamical System Model for Text

abstract: CUR matrix decomposition computes the low rank approximation of a given matrix by using the actual rows and columns of the matrix. It has been a very useful tool for handling large matrices. One limitation with the existing algorithms for CUR matrix decomposition is that they cannot deal with entries in a \it partially observed matrix, while incomplete matrices are found in many real world applications. In this work, we alleviate this limitation by developing a CUR decomposition algorithm for partially observed matrices. In particular, the proposed algorithm computes the low rank approximation of the target matrix based on (i) the randomly sampled rows and columns, and (ii) a subset of observed entries that are randomly sampled from the matrix. Our analysis shows the relative error bound, measured by spectral norm, for the proposed algorithm when the target matrix is of full rank. We also show that only O(n r\ln r) observed entries are needed by the proposed algorithm to perfectly recover a rank r matrix of size n\times n, which improves the sample complexity of the existing algorithms for matrix completion. Empirical studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets verify our theoretical claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: CUR decomposition approximates a large matrix using actual rows and columns from that matrix. Existing methods had difficulty when some entries were missing, even though incomplete matrices occur in many applications. This paper develops a CUR algorithm designed to operate with partial observations.

The algorithm combines randomly sampled rows and columns with a randomly sampled subset of observed entries. Its analysis addresses two different goals. For a full-rank target matrix, the authors establish a relative approximation-error bound measured in spectral norm. This evaluates the quality of the low-rank approximation even when the original matrix is not itself low rank.

For an n-by-n matrix of rank r, the paper also gives a perfect-recovery result requiring O(n r ln r) observed entries under its analyzed sampling setup. The authors report an improvement over existing matrix-completion sample complexity. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical claims and show the method's effectiveness. The contribution connects row-and-column-based approximation with recovery from incomplete information.
summary.tldr: A CUR algorithm handles partially observed matrices, with approximation guarantees and a low-rank recovery result using O(n r ln r) observations.

title: CUR Algorithm for Partially Observed Matrices

abstract: We provide a deterministic data summarization algorithm that approximates the mean $\bar{p}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p\in P} p$ of a set $P$ of $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, by a weighted mean $\tilde{p}$ of a subset of $O(1/\epsilon)$ vectors, i.e., independent of both $n$ and $d$. We prove that the squared Euclidean distance between $\bar{p}$ and $\tilde{p}$ is at most $\epsilon$ multiplied by the variance of $P$. We use this algorithm to maintain an approximated sum of vectors from an unbounded stream, using memory that is independent of $d$, and logarithmic in the $n$ vectors seen so far. Our main application is to extract and represent in a compact way friend groups and activity summaries of users from underlying data exchanges. For example, in the case of mobile networks, we can use GPS traces to identify meetings; in the case of social networks, we can use information exchange to identify friend groups. Our algorithm provably identifies the Heavy Hitter entries in a proximity (adjacency) matrix. The Heavy Hitters can be used to extract and represent in a compact way friend groups and activity summaries of users from underlying data exchanges. We evaluate the algorithm on several large data sets.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a large collection of vectors can be represented by a small, weighted subset while preserving its mean. The authors give a deterministic algorithm whose subset contains on the order of one divided by the chosen error parameter vectors. That count is independent of both the original collection size and the vector dimension.

The approximation comes with a concrete guarantee: the squared distance between the original and summarized means is bounded by the error parameter times the collection's variance. This ties acceptable error to the data's own spread. The authors also use the method to maintain an approximate vector sum over an unbounded stream, with stated memory requirements independent of dimension and logarithmic in the number of observations.

The main application is compact representation of social or activity relationships from exchanges between users. The algorithm provably identifies heavy entries in a proximity matrix, which can support summaries of friend groups and activity. The paper evaluates the approach on several large datasets, connecting its approximation guarantees to network summarization.
summary.tldr: A deterministic weighted-subset method approximates vector means with variance-scaled error guarantees and supports compact network summaries.

title: Coresets for Vector Summarization with Applications to Network Graphs

abstract: Confidence calibration – the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood – is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling – a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling – is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether a classifier’s confidence reflects how likely its prediction is to be correct. This property, called calibration, determines how meaningfully its probability estimates can be interpreted. The authors find that modern neural networks are poorly calibrated, contrasting them with networks studied a decade earlier.

Through extensive experiments, they identify depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization as important influences on calibration. They also evaluate methods that adjust confidence estimates after a model has been trained. The evaluation covers state-of-the-art architectures on both image and document classification datasets, connecting the investigation to different kinds of classification tasks.

Temperature scaling, a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling, proves surprisingly effective on most of the datasets studied. The practical finding is that a simple post-processing method can substantially help align confidence with correctness likelihood. The evidence supports its effectiveness across most tested datasets, while preserving the distinction between producing an accurate classification and assigning it a well-calibrated probability.
summary.tldr: Modern neural networks can be poorly calibrated, and simple temperature scaling effectively corrects confidence estimates on most datasets studied.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

abstract: We propose a generic stochastic expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm for the estimation of high-dimensional latent variable models. At the core of our algorithm is a novel semi-stochastic variance-reduced gradient designed for the $Q$-function in the EM algorithm. Under a mild condition on the initialization, our algorithm is guaranteed to attain a linear convergence rate to the unknown parameter of the latent variable model, and achieve an optimal statistical rate up to a logarithmic factor for parameter estimation. Compared with existing high-dimensional EM algorithms, our algorithm enjoys a better computational complexity and is therefore more efficient. We apply our generic algorithm to two illustrative latent variable models: Gaussian mixture model and mixture of linear regression, and demonstrate the advantages of our algorithm by both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. We believe that the proposed semi-stochastic gradient is of independent interest for general nonconvex optimization problems with bivariate structures.

paragraphs: Estimating high-dimensional latent-variable models requires learning parameters while accounting for hidden structure. This paper proposes a general stochastic expectation-maximization algorithm for that setting. Its aim is to reduce computational work while retaining strong guarantees about convergence and the statistical quality of the estimated parameters.

The main ingredient is a semi-stochastic gradient with reduced variance, designed specifically for the Q-function used by EM. Under a mild condition on initialization, the algorithm has a linear convergence guarantee toward the unknown model parameter. It also achieves a parameter-estimation rate that is optimal up to a logarithmic factor, linking optimization progress with statistical accuracy.

The authors establish better computational complexity than existing high-dimensional EM algorithms. They illustrate the method with Gaussian mixtures and mixtures of linear regressions, using both theory and numerical experiments to demonstrate its advantages. They also suggest that the gradient construction may be useful for other nonconvex problems with bivariate structure. That broader relevance is presented as a possibility beyond the two models studied.
summary.tldr: A variance-reduced stochastic EM method improves computational complexity and provides convergence and near-optimal estimation guarantees under an initialization condition.

title: High-Dimensional Variance-Reduced Stochastic Gradient Expectation-Maximization Algorithm

abstract: Datasets with significant proportions of noisy (incorrect) class labels present challenges for training accurate Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). We propose a new perspective for understanding DNN generalization for such datasets, by investigating the dimensionality of the deep representation subspace of training samples. We show that from a dimensionality perspective, DNNs exhibit quite distinctive learning styles when trained with clean labels versus when trained with a proportion of noisy labels. Based on this finding, we develop a new dimensionality-driven learning strategy, which monitors the dimensionality of subspaces during training and adapts the loss function accordingly. We empirically demonstrate that our approach is highly tolerant to significant proportions of noisy labels, and can effectively learn low-dimensional local subspaces that capture the data distribution.

paragraphs: Incorrect class labels complicate training because a neural network receives misleading supervision alongside useful examples. This paper studies the problem through the dimensionality of the representations learned for training samples. Its focus is the geometry of the network’s internal representation subspaces and how that geometry changes when some labels are wrong.

The authors find distinctive dimensionality-related learning behavior when comparing training with clean labels against training with a proportion of noisy labels. They turn that observation into a training strategy: monitor subspace dimensionality during learning and adapt the loss function accordingly. Representation geometry therefore becomes a signal that influences how the model continues to learn, rather than serving only as something examined after training.

Experiments show that the proposed approach tolerates substantial proportions of noisy labels and learns low-dimensional local subspaces that capture the data distribution. These are empirical findings about the studied training strategy. The contribution is a connection between measurable properties of learned representations and an adaptive loss, offering a way to respond to label noise through the network’s evolving internal structure.
summary.tldr: Monitoring learned representation dimensionality and adapting the loss yields strong empirical tolerance to noisy class labels.

title: Dimensionality-Driven Learning with Noisy Labels

abstract: Learning-based Text To Speech systems have the potential to generalize from one speaker to the next and thus require a relatively short sample of any new voice. However, this promise is currently largely unrealized. We present a method that is designed to capture a new speaker from a short untranscribed audio sample. This is done by employing an additional network that given an audio sample, places the speaker in the embedding space. This network is trained as part of the speech synthesis system using various consistency losses. Our results demonstrate a greatly improved performance on both the dataset speakers, and, more importantly, when fitting new voices, even from very short samples.

However, this promise is currently largely unrealized. We present a method that is designed to capture a new speaker from a short untranscribed audio sample. This is done by employing an additional network that given an audio sample, places the speaker in the embedding space. This network is trained as part of the speech synthesis system using various consistency losses. Our results demonstrate a greatly improved performance on both the dataset speakers, and, more importantly, when fitting new voices, even from very short samples.

paragraphs: A text-to-speech system that learns across speakers could potentially reproduce a new voice from only a short recording. The paper addresses the gap between that promise and the performance available in existing systems. Its aim is to capture a new speaker using audio that does not need an accompanying transcript.

The method adds a network that takes an audio sample and places its speaker in an embedding space, a learned representation used by the speech synthesis system. This gives the system a way to derive a speaker representation directly from the recording. The additional network is trained as part of the synthesizer, using several consistency losses to guide learning.

The authors report substantially improved performance for speakers in the dataset and, more importantly for the intended application, when fitting new voices. They also report improvements with very short samples. The findings support learning the mapping from audio to speaker representation jointly with synthesis as a way to make voice adaptation work with limited, untranscribed recordings.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained speaker-embedding network helps a text-to-speech system fit new voices from short recordings without transcripts.

title: Fitting New Speakers Based on a Short Untranscribed Sample

abstract: We consider the problem of learning a binary classifier from $n$ different data sources, among which at most an $\eta$ fraction are adversarial. The overhead is defined as the ratio between the sample complexity of learning in this setting and that of learning the same hypothesis class on a single data distribution. We present an algorithm that achieves an $O(\eta n + \ln n)$ overhead, which is proved to be worst-case optimal. We also discuss the potential challenges to the design of a computationally efficient learning algorithm with a small overhead.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of learning a binary classifier from $n$ different data sources, among which at most an $\eta$ fraction are adversarial. The overhead is defined as the ratio between the sample complexity of learning in this setting and that of learning the same hypothesis class on a single data distribution. We present an algorithm that achieves an $O(\eta n + \ln n)$ overhead, which is proved to be worst-case optimal. We also discuss the potential challenges to the design of a computationally efficient learning algorithm with a small overhead.

paragraphs: Learning from multiple data sources becomes harder when some sources are adversarial. This paper studies binary classification with n sources, assuming that at most an eta fraction are adversarial. The question is how much additional data collaborative learning requires compared with learning the same hypothesis class from one distribution.

The authors measure that extra burden through sample-complexity overhead: the ratio of the sample requirements in the two settings. They present an algorithm with overhead O(eta n + ln n) and prove that this dependence is optimal in the worst case. The bound separates a term tied to adversarial sources from a logarithmic term tied to the total source count.

This result characterizes the worst-case sample cost of collaboration under the stated corruption assumption. It does not settle computational efficiency: the paper separately discusses challenges in obtaining a computationally efficient algorithm with small overhead. The distinction matters because an optimal data requirement and an efficient implementation are different achievements.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a worst-case optimal sample overhead of O(eta n + ln n) for binary learning across partly adversarial sources.

title: Do Outliers Ruin Collaboration?

abstract: Due to the ability of deep neural nets to learn rich representations, recent advances in unsupervised domain adaptation have focused on learning domain-invariant features that achieve a small error on the source domain. The hope is that the learnt representation, together with the hypothesis learnt from the source domain, can generalize to the target domain. In this paper, we first construct a simple counterexample showing that, contrary to common belief, the above conditions are not sufficient to guarantee successful domain adaptation. In particular, the counterexample exhibits conditional shift : the class-conditional distributions of input features change between source and target domains. To give a sufficient condition for domain adaptation, we propose a natural and interpretable generalization upper bound that explicitly takes into account the aforementioned shift. Moreover, we shed new light on the problem by proving an information-theoretic lower bound on the joint error of any domain adaptation method that attempts to learn invariant representations. Our result characterizes a fundamental tradeoff between learning invariant representations and achieving small joint error on both domains when the marginal label distributions differ from source to target. Finally, we conduct experiments on real-world datasets that corroborate our theoretical findings. We believe these insights are helpful in guiding the future design of domain adaptation and representation learning algorithms.

paragraphs: A common strategy for unsupervised domain adaptation learns features that look similar across domains while maintaining low classification error on the source. This paper shows that those two properties are insufficient to guarantee success on the target. Its counterexample involves conditional shift, where feature distributions within classes differ between source and target.

The authors develop a generalization upper bound that explicitly accounts for this shift and provides a sufficient condition for adaptation. This changes what must be considered when evaluating a representation: similarity between the overall domain distributions and source accuracy alone can overlook differences in how features relate to classes.

The paper also proves an information-theoretic lower bound on joint source and target error for methods learning invariant representations. When the marginal label distributions differ, the result identifies a fundamental tradeoff between invariance and low error across both domains. Experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical findings. The message is conditional but consequential: distribution alignment needs to be understood together with class relationships and label proportions when designing adaptation methods.
summary.tldr: Domain-invariant features and low source error do not guarantee adaptation, with conditional shift and differing label proportions creating important obstacles.

title: On Learning Invariant Representations for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Recurrent neural networks are widely used on time series data, yet such models often ignore the underlying physical structures in such sequences. A new class of physics-based methods related to Koopman theory has been introduced, offering an alternative for processing nonlinear dynamical systems. In this work, we propose a novel Consistent Koopman Autoencoder model which, unlike the majority of existing work, leverages the forward and backward dynamics. Key to our approach is a new analysis which explores the interplay between consistent dynamics and their associated Koopman operators. Our network is directly related to the derived analysis, and its computational requirements are comparable to other baselines. We evaluate our method on a wide range of high-dimensional and short-term dependent problems, and it achieves accurate estimates for significant prediction horizons, while also being robust to noise.

paragraphs: Forecasting a sequence can benefit from accounting for the physical dynamics that generated it. The paper motivates its approach by observing that recurrent neural networks often overlook such structure. It develops a Consistent Koopman Autoencoder, drawing on Koopman-based methods for nonlinear dynamical systems to connect a learned forecasting model with an analysis of the underlying dynamics.

The distinguishing ingredient is the joint use of forward and backward dynamics. Rather than focusing only on how a system advances, the method also uses its backward behavior. The authors analyze the relationship between consistent dynamics and their associated Koopman operators, then directly connect the network design to that analysis. They report computational requirements comparable to those of the evaluated baselines.

Evaluation covers a broad range of high-dimensional problems with short-term dependencies. The method produces accurate estimates over substantial prediction horizons and exhibits robustness to noise in those evaluations. These findings suggest that incorporating consistency between the two directions of dynamics can be useful for forecasting, while keeping computation comparable to the alternatives considered.
summary.tldr: A Koopman autoencoder uses forward and backward dynamics to support accurate, noise-robust forecasting at computational cost comparable to evaluated baselines.

title: Forecasting Sequential Data Using Consistent Koopman Autoencoders

abstract: Factorizing tensors has recently become an important optimization module in a number of machine learning pipelines, especially in latent variable models. We show how to do this efficiently in the streaming setting. Given a set of $n$ vectors, each in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we present algorithms to select a sublinear number of these vectors as coreset, while guaranteeing that the CP decomposition of the $p$-moment tensor of the coreset approximates the corresponding decomposition of the $p$-moment tensor computed from the full data. We introduce two novel algorithmic techniques: online filtering and kernelization. Using these two, we present four algorithms that achieve different tradeoffs of coreset size, update time and working space, beating or matching various state of the art algorithms. In the case of matrices (2-ordered tensor), our online row sampling algorithm guarantees $(1 \pm \epsilon)$ relative error spectral approximation. We show applications of our algorithms in learning single topic modeling.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization is an important component of learning pipelines, particularly those involving latent variable models. This paper asks how to support it when vectors arrive as a stream. The proposed algorithms retain a coreset containing a sublinear number of the input vectors, reducing the amount of data needed for the factorization task.

The guarantee connects the summary directly to the intended computation: the CP decomposition of its p-th moment tensor approximates the corresponding decomposition constructed from all the data. The authors introduce online filtering and kernelization to build four algorithms. These provide different balances among coreset size, update time, and working memory, matching or improving various existing methods.

For matrices, which are second-order tensors, an online row sampling algorithm gives a relative-error spectral approximation within a factor of one plus or minus epsilon. The paper also demonstrates applications to single-topic modeling. The contribution therefore combines streaming data reduction with guarantees tied to the matrix or tensor structure used downstream.
summary.tldr: Streaming algorithms retain sublinear subsets of vectors while preserving approximations to moment-tensor decompositions, with several memory and update-time tradeoffs.

title: Streaming Coresets for Symmetric Tensor Factorization

abstract: Recent work has shown generative adversarial networks (GANs) can generate highly realistic images, that are often indistinguishable (by humans) from real images. Most images so generated are not contained in the training dataset, suggesting potential for augmenting training sets with GAN-generated data. While this scenario is of particular relevance when there are limited data available, there is still the issue of training the GAN itself based on that limited data. To facilitate this, we leverage existing GAN models pretrained on large-scale datasets (like ImageNet) to introduce additional knowledge (which may not exist within the limited data), following the concept of transfer learning. Demonstrated by natural-image generation, we reveal that low-level filters (those close to observations) of both the generator and discriminator of pretrained GANs can be transferred to facilitate generation in a perceptually-distinct target domain with limited training data. To further adapt the transferred filters to the target domain, we propose adaptive filter modulation (AdaFM). An extensive set of experiments is presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques on generation with limited data.

paragraphs: GAN-generated images offer potential for expanding small training datasets, but training the generator itself with little data remains a problem. This paper explores transferring knowledge from GANs already trained on large datasets. The source model can bring information that the limited target dataset does not contain on its own.

The authors investigate low-level filters close to the observations in both the generator and discriminator. Their natural-image experiments show that these filters can transfer to a target domain with a different perceptual appearance. Thus, useful reusable components can exist on both sides of the adversarial learning setup.

To adapt the transferred filters further, the paper introduces adaptive filter modulation, or AdaFM. This supplements filter reuse with a mechanism for adjusting the inherited components to the target domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques for image generation with limited data. The findings support transferring and adapting pretrained GAN components as a practical approach to this training constraint.
summary.tldr: Transferring low-level GAN filters and adapting them with AdaFM improves image generation in target domains with limited training data.

title: On Leveraging Pretrained GANs for Generation with Limited Data

abstract: Modeling sets is an important problem in machine learning since this type of data can be found in many domains. A promising approach defines a family of permutation invariant densities with continuous normalizing flows. This allows us to maximize the likelihood directly and sample new realizations with ease. In this work, we demonstrate how calculating the trace, a crucial step in this method, raises issues that occur both during training and inference, limiting its practicality. We propose an alternative way of defining permutation equivariant transformations that give closed form trace. This leads not only to improvements while training, but also to better final performance. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on point processes and general set modeling.

paragraphs: A set has no meaningful ordering, so a probability model for sets should assign the same density after its elements are rearranged. Continuous normalizing flows offer a way to build such permutation-invariant densities while supporting direct likelihood maximization and generation of new samples. This paper examines a computational obstacle that limits the practicality of that approach.

The obstacle is a trace calculation required by the flow method. The authors show that it creates difficulties during both training and inference. They propose a different construction of permutation-equivariant transformations, meaning that rearranging inputs rearranges the corresponding outputs consistently. Crucially, these transformations allow the required trace to be calculated in closed form.

The new construction improves training and final model performance, with benefits demonstrated on point processes and general set-modeling tasks. Its significance is that respecting the symmetry of sets and making likelihood calculations tractable are addressed together. The work retains the appeal of flow-based density modeling while changing the transformation design to simplify a central computation.
summary.tldr: Permutation-equivariant flow transformations with closed-form traces improve training and performance for probability models of sets.

title: Scalable Normalizing Flows for Permutation Invariant Densities

abstract: We study a stochastic program where the probability distribution of the uncertain problem parameters is unknown and only indirectly observed via finitely many correlated samples generated by an unknown Markov chain with $d$ states. We propose a data-driven distributionally robust optimization model to estimate the problem’s objective function and optimal solution. By leveraging results from large deviations theory, we derive statistical guarantees on the quality of these estimators. The underlying worst-case expectation problem is nonconvex and involves $\mathcal O(d^2)$ decision variables. Thus, it cannot be solved efficiently for large $d$. By exploiting the structure of this problem, we devise a customized Frank-Wolfe algorithm with convex direction-finding subproblems of size $\mathcal O(d)$. We prove that this algorithm finds a stationary point efficiently under mild conditions. The efficiency of the method is predicated on a dimensionality reduction enabled by a dual reformulation. Numerical experiments indicate that our approach has better computational and statistical properties than the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions under uncertainty when the relevant probability distribution is unknown. The available evidence consists of finitely many correlated observations generated by an unknown Markov chain with d states. The authors propose a data-driven distributionally robust model to estimate both the optimization objective and its optimal solution.

Using large deviations theory, they derive statistical guarantees for these estimates. Computation presents a separate obstacle: the model's worst-case expectation problem is nonconvex and has on the order of d squared decision variables. This makes directly solving it inefficient when the chain has many states.

The proposed solution exploits a dual reformulation to reduce dimensionality. A customized Frank–Wolfe algorithm then uses convex direction-finding subproblems of size proportional to d. Under mild conditions, the authors prove that it efficiently reaches a stationary point, which is a weaker conclusion than finding a global optimum of the nonconvex problem. Numerical experiments indicate better computational and statistical properties than leading alternatives, supporting both the modeling approach and the specialized solver.
summary.tldr: A robust optimization model handles correlated Markov-chain observations, with statistical guarantees and a specialized solver that efficiently finds stationary points.

title: Distributionally Robust Optimization with Markovian Data

abstract: We study how permutation symmetries in overparameterized multi-layer neural networks generate ‘symmetry-induced’ critical points. Assuming a network with $ L $ layers of minimal widths $ r_1^*, \ldots, r_{L-1}^* $ reaches a zero-loss minimum at $ r_1^*! \cdots r_{L-1}^*! $ isolated points that are permutations of one another, we show that adding one extra neuron to each layer is sufficient to connect all these previously discrete minima into a single manifold. For a two-layer overparameterized network of width $ r^*+ h =: m $ we explicitly describe the manifold of global minima: it consists of $ T(r^*, m) $ affine subspaces of dimension at least $ h $ that are connected to one another. For a network of width $m$, we identify the number $G(r,m)$ of affine subspaces containing only symmetry-induced critical points that are related to the critical points of a smaller network of width $r<r^*$. Via a combinatorial analysis, we derive closed-form formulas for $ T $ and $ G $ and show that the number of symmetry-induced critical subspaces dominates the number of affine subspaces forming the global minima manifold in the mildly overparameterized regime (small $ h $) and vice versa in the vastly overparameterized regime ($h \gg r^*$). Our results provide new insights into the minimization of the non-convex loss function of overparameterized neural networks.

paragraphs: Permuting neurons can produce different parameter settings with the same network behavior. This paper studies how those symmetries shape critical points and global minima when networks gain extra neurons. Its starting assumption is a network of minimal layer widths whose zero-loss minima are isolated points related by permutations.

Under that assumption, adding one neuron to each layer is sufficient to connect all those minima into a single manifold. For a two-layer network with h extra neurons, the authors describe connected affine subspaces forming the global-minimum manifold, each having dimension at least h. They also count affine subspaces of symmetry-induced critical points associated with narrower networks.

Closed-form combinatorial formulas reveal a change as width increases. With mild overparameterization, symmetry-induced critical subspaces outnumber the subspaces forming the global minima; with much greater overparameterization, the ordering reverses. These results explain how additional width reorganizes the loss landscape. They provide geometric insight into optimization without asserting that a particular training algorithm necessarily reaches a global minimum.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, extra neurons connect permutation-related minima and change the balance of symmetry-induced critical and minimum subspaces.

title: Geometry of the Loss Landscape in Overparameterized Neural Networks: Symmetries and Invariances

abstract: Histograms, i.e., piece-wise constant approximations, are a popular tool used to represent data distributions. Traditionally, the difference between the histogram and the underlying distribution (i.e., the approximation error) is measured using the L_p norm, which sums the differences between the two functions over all items in the domain. Although useful in many applications, the drawback of this error measure is that it treats approximation errors of all items in the same way, irrespective of whether the mass of an item is important for the downstream application that uses the approximation. As a result, even relatively simple distributions cannot be approximated by succinct histograms without incurring large error. In this paper, we address this issue by adapting the definition of approximation so that only the errors of the items that belong to the support of the distribution are considered. Under this definition, we develop efficient 1-pass and 2-pass streaming algorithms that compute near-optimal histograms in sub-linear space. We also present lower bounds on the space complexity of this problem. Surprisingly, under this notion of error, there is an exponential gap in the space complexity of 1-pass and 2-pass streaming algorithms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our algorithms on a collection of real and synthetic data sets.
originalAbstract: Histograms, i.e., piece-wise constant approximations, are a popular tool used to represent data distributions. Traditionally, the difference between the histogram and the underlying distribution (i.e., the approximation error) is measured using the L_p norm, which sums the differences between the two functions over all items in the domain. Although useful in many applications, the drawback of this error measure is that it treats approximation errors of all items in the same way, irrespective of whether the mass of an item is important for the downstream application that uses the approximation. As a result, even relatively simple distributions cannot be approximated by succinct histograms without incurring large error. In this paper, we address this issue by adapting the definition of approximation so that only the errors of the items that belong to the support of the distribution are considered. Under this definition, we develop efficient 1-pass and 2-pass streaming algorithms that compute near-optimal histograms in sub-linear space. We also present lower bounds on the space complexity of this problem. Surprisingly, under this notion of error, there is an exponential gap in the space complexity of 1-pass and 2-pass streaming algorithms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our algorithms on a collection of real and synthetic data sets.

paragraphs: Histograms compress distributions into regions with constant values. Traditional error measures sum discrepancies across every item in the domain, treating errors equally whether or not an item has probability mass. The paper argues that this can prevent even relatively simple distributions from having compact, accurate histogram approximations.

The proposed alternative counts errors only for items in the distribution's support: those carrying mass. Under this support-aware definition, the authors develop one-pass and two-pass streaming algorithms that construct near-optimal histograms using sublinear space. Changing which errors count is therefore central to the result, rather than merely changing the implementation of an existing approximation objective.

The authors also establish lower bounds on required storage. A striking finding is an exponential gap between the space complexity of one-pass and two-pass methods under this error definition. This shows that allowing another pass can substantially change the memory demands of the problem. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the algorithms' usefulness, alongside the theoretical analysis of how approximation quality, storage, and access to the data interact.
summary.tldr: Counting histogram errors only on a distribution's support enables compact streaming approximations and reveals an exponential one-pass versus two-pass space gap.

title: Streaming Algorithms for Support-Aware Histograms

abstract: We introduce the Poisson Binomial mechanism (PBM), a discrete differential privacy mechanism for distributed mean estimation (DME) with applications to federated learning and analytics. We provide a tight analysis of its privacy guarantees, showing that it achieves the same privacy-accuracy trade-offs as the continuous Gaussian mechanism. Our analysis is based on a novel bound on the Rényi divergence of two Poisson binomial distributions that may be of independent interest. Unlike previous discrete DP schemes based on additive noise, our mechanism encodes local information into a parameter of the binomial distribution, and hence the output distribution is discrete with bounded support. Moreover, the support does not increase as the privacy budget goes to zero as in the case of additive schemes which require the addition of more noise to achieve higher privacy; on the contrary, the support becomes smaller as eps goes to zero. The bounded support enables us to combine our mechanism with secure aggregation (SecAgg), a multi-party cryptographic protocol, without the need of performing modular clipping which results in an unbiased estimator of the sum of the local vectors. This in turn allows us to apply it in the private FL setting and provide an upper bound on the convergence rate of the SGD algorithm. Moreover, since the support of the output distribution becomes smaller as $\varepsilon \ra 0$, the communication cost of our scheme decreases with the privacy constraint $\varepsilon$, outperforming all previous distributed DP schemes based on additive noise in the high privacy or low communication regimes.

A tight privacy analysis shows the same privacy-accuracy trade-offs as the continuous Gaussian mechanism. The analysis uses a new bound on Rényi divergence between Poisson binomial distributions. The contribution links the distribution's design to privacy, unbiased aggregation, and communication efficiency.
summary.tldr: The Poisson Binomial mechanism combines discrete privacy, unbiased secure aggregation, and communication costs that decrease as privacy strengthens.

title: The Poisson Binomial Mechanism for Unbiased Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation

abstract: We study the faithfulness of an explanation system to the underlying prediction model. We show that this can be captured by two properties, consistency and sufficiency, and introduce quantitative measures of the extent to which these hold. Interestingly, these measures depend on the test-time data distribution. For a variety of existing explanation systems, such as anchors, we analytically study these quantities. We also provide estimators and sample complexity bounds for empirically determining the faithfulness of black-box explanation systems. Finally, we experimentally validate the new properties and estimators.

We show that this can be captured by two properties, consistency and sufficiency, and introduce quantitative measures of the extent to which these hold. Interestingly, these measures depend on the test-time data distribution. For a variety of existing explanation systems, such as anchors, we analytically study these quantities. We also provide estimators and sample complexity bounds for empirically determining the faithfulness of black-box explanation systems. Finally, we experimentally validate the new properties and estimators.

paragraphs: An explanation system is useful only insofar as its account of a prediction reflects the model being explained. This paper studies that relationship as faithfulness. It presents consistency and sufficiency as two properties that capture faithfulness and introduces quantitative measures for assessing how strongly an explanation system satisfies them.

A central finding is that these measures depend on the distribution of data encountered at test time. Faithfulness is therefore evaluated in relation to the inputs on which explanations are used. The authors analytically examine the measures for several existing explanation systems, including anchors, connecting their framework to methods already used to explain predictions.

The paper also develops estimators for assessing black-box explanation systems and bounds on the number of samples needed for that assessment. Experiments validate the proposed properties and estimators. Together, these contributions turn faithfulness into something that can be studied mathematically and estimated empirically, while making the role of the deployment data distribution explicit.
summary.tldr: The paper measures explanation faithfulness through consistency and sufficiency, with guarantees for empirical estimation.

title: Framework for Evaluating Faithfulness of Local Explanations

abstract: Empirically observed time series in physics, biology, or medicine, are commonly generated by some underlying dynamical system (DS) which is the target of scientific interest. There is an increasing interest to harvest machine learning methods to reconstruct this latent DS in a data-driven, unsupervised way. In many areas of science it is common to sample time series observations from many data modalities simultaneously, e.g. electrophysiological and behavioral time series in a typical neuroscience experiment. However, current machine learning tools for reconstructing DSs usually focus on just one data modality. Here we propose a general framework for multi-modal data integration for the purpose of nonlinear DS reconstruction and the analysis of cross-modal relations. This framework is based on dynamically interpretable recurrent neural networks as general approximators of nonlinear DSs, coupled to sets of modality-specific decoder models from the class of generalized linear models. Both an expectation-maximization and a variational inference algorithm for model training are advanced and compared. We show on nonlinear DS benchmarks that our algorithms can efficiently compensate for too noisy or missing information in one data channel by exploiting other channels, and demonstrate on experimental neuroscience data how the algorithm learns to link different data domains to the underlying dynamics.

Neuroscience experiments, for example, may record electrophysiological and behavioral observations together. This paper develops an unsupervised framework that combines such modalities to reconstruct nonlinear dynamics and analyze relationships between the observed data domains.

The framework uses dynamically interpretable recurrent neural networks to represent the underlying system. Modality-specific decoders from the generalized linear model family connect that shared dynamics model to each type of observation. The authors develop and compare expectation-maximization and variational-inference algorithms for training, providing two ways to fit the combined model.

On nonlinear dynamical-system benchmarks, the methods use information from other channels to compensate efficiently when one channel is too noisy or has missing information. An application to experimental neuroscience data demonstrates how the algorithm links different observation domains to the underlying dynamics. These findings support integrating simultaneous measurements within a shared dynamical model, especially when the available channels provide uneven amounts of usable information.
summary.tldr: A shared recurrent dynamics model with modality-specific decoders reconstructs nonlinear systems and uses complementary channels to compensate for noisy or missing observations.

title: Reconstructing Nonlinear Dynamical Systems from Multi-Modal Time Series

abstract: As a typical problem in time series analysis, traffic flow prediction is one of the most important application fields of machine learning. However, achieving highly accurate traffic flow prediction is a challenging task, due to the presence of complex dynamic spatial-temporal dependencies within a road network. This paper proposes a novel Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Aware Graph Neural Network (DSTAGNN) to model the complex spatial-temporal interaction in road network. First, considering the fact that historical data carries intrinsic dynamic information about the spatial structure of road networks, we propose a new dynamic spatial-temporal aware graph based on a data-driven strategy to replace the pre-defined static graph usually used in traditional graph convolution. Second, we design a novel graph neural network architecture, which can not only represent dynamic spatial relevance among nodes with an improved multi-head attention mechanism, but also acquire the wide range of dynamic temporal dependency from multi-receptive field features via multi-scale gated convolution. Extensive experiments on real-world data sets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Traffic flow depends on interactions across a road network and on how those interactions evolve over time. This makes forecasting difficult for models that rely on a predefined, static graph. DSTAGNN addresses the problem by using historical traffic observations to construct a graph that reflects dynamic spatial and temporal information.

The network combines two mechanisms for representing these dependencies. An improved multi-head attention mechanism represents changing spatial relevance among road-network nodes. Multi-scale gated convolution captures temporal relationships through features with different receptive fields, allowing the architecture to draw on patterns spanning different temporal ranges. The graph construction and network architecture together target the evolving relationships present in traffic data.

Experiments on real-world datasets report significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings support the paper’s premise that historical observations contain useful information about the network’s dynamic structure. The contribution is both a data-driven replacement for the static graph and an architecture designed to use spatial relevance alongside temporal patterns at multiple scales.
summary.tldr: DSTAGNN combines a data-driven dynamic graph, attention, and multi-scale temporal convolution to improve reported traffic forecasts.

title: DSTAGNN: Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Aware Graph Neural Network for Traffic Flow Forecasting

abstract: We revisit the classical problem of deriving convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) in finite mixture models. The Wasserstein distance has become a standard loss function for the analysis of parameter estimation in these models, due in part to its ability to circumvent label switching and to accurately characterize the behaviour of fitted mixture components with vanishing weights. However, the Wasserstein distance is only able to capture the worst-case convergence rate among the remaining fitted mixture components. We demonstrate that when the log-likelihood function is penalized to discourage vanishing mixing weights, stronger loss functions can be derived to resolve this shortcoming of the Wasserstein distance. These new loss functions accurately capture the heterogeneity in convergence rates of fitted mixture components, and we use them to sharpen existing pointwise and uniform convergence rates in various classes of mixture models. In particular, these results imply that a subset of the components of the penalized MLE typically converge significantly faster than could have been anticipated from past work. We further show that some of these conclusions extend to the traditional MLE. Our theoretical findings are supported by a simulation study to illustrate these improved convergence rates.

paragraphs: Finite mixture models represent a distribution through several components, whose parameters may be estimated at different speeds as data accumulates. Wasserstein distance is useful for analyzing these estimates because it accommodates interchangeable component labels and components whose weights vanish. However, it can hide differences between the remaining components by reflecting only their slowest convergence rate.

The authors penalize the log-likelihood to discourage mixing weights from vanishing. Under this setup, they derive stronger loss functions that distinguish how quickly different fitted components converge. These measures sharpen existing pointwise and uniform convergence results across several classes of mixture models, revealing behavior that a single worst-case rate obscures.

The results imply that a subset of components in the penalized maximum likelihood estimate typically converges substantially faster than earlier analyses suggested. Some conclusions also carry over to the ordinary, unpenalized estimator. A simulation study supports the theory. The main advance is a finer description of estimation error, allowing different components' statistical behavior to be visible within the same fitted model.
summary.tldr: New loss functions reveal that some estimated mixture components converge faster than Wasserstein-based analyses indicate.

title: Refined Convergence Rates for Maximum Likelihood Estimation under Finite Mixture Models

abstract: Detecting communities in real-world networks and clustering similarity graphs are major data mining tasks with a wide range of applications in graph mining, collaborative filtering, and bioinformatics. In many such applications, overwhelming empirical evidence suggests that communities and clusters are naturally overlapping, i.e., the boundary of a cluster may contain both edges across clusters and nodes that are shared with other clusters, calling for novel hybrid graph partitioning algorithms (HGP). While almost-linear-time approximation algorithms are known for edge-boundary-based graph partitioning, little progress has been made on fast algorithms for HGP, even in the special case of vertex-boundary-based graph partitioning. In this work, we introduce a frame-work based on two novel clustering objectives, which naturally extend the well-studied notion of conductance to clusters with hybrid vertex-and edge-boundary structure. Our main algorithmic contributions are almost-linear-time algorithms O(log n)-approximation algorithms for both these objectives. To this end, we show that the cut-matching framework of (Khandekar et al., 2014) can be significantly extended to incorporate hybrid partitions. Crucially, we implement our approximation algorithm to produce both hybrid partitions and optimality certificates for large graphs, easily scaling to tens of millions of edges, and test our implementation on real-world datasets against other competitive baselines.

This paper develops methods for hybrid partitions that account for both kinds of boundary, motivated by community detection and similarity-graph clustering.

The authors introduce two objectives extending conductance, a familiar measure of cluster separation, to hybrid vertex-and-edge boundaries. They then extend the cut-matching framework to obtain almost-linear-time algorithms with logarithmic approximation guarantees for both objectives. The guarantees connect computational efficiency with a quantified bound on solution quality.

This practical component matters because the paper addresses a gap between fast methods for edge boundaries and much less developed methods for overlapping or vertex-based boundaries.
summary.tldr: New hybrid clustering objectives support almost-linear-time approximation algorithms that handle shared vertices and scale to very large graphs.

title: Practical Almost-Linear-Time Approximation Algorithms for Hybrid and Overlapping Graph Clustering

abstract: In meta reinforcement learning (meta RL), an agent seeks a Bayes-optimal policy – the optimal policy when facing an unknown task that is sampled from some known task distribution. Previous approaches tackled this problem by inferring a $\textit{belief}$ over task parameters, using variational inference methods. Motivated by recent successes of contrastive learning approaches in RL, such as contrastive predictive coding (CPC), we investigate whether contrastive methods can be used for learning Bayes-optimal behavior. We begin by proving that representations learned by CPC are indeed sufficient for Bayes optimality. Based on this observation, we propose a simple meta RL algorithm that uses CPC in lieu of variational belief inference. Our method, $\textit{ContraBAR}$, achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art in domains with state-based observation and circumvents the computational toll of future observation reconstruction, enabling learning in domains with image-based observations. It can also be combined with image augmentations for domain randomization and used seamlessly in both online and offline meta RL settings.

paragraphs: In meta reinforcement learning, an agent faces an unknown task drawn from a known task distribution. Bayes-optimal behavior accounts for that uncertainty when choosing actions. Earlier approaches infer a belief over task parameters through variational inference. This paper asks whether contrastive predictive coding, or CPC, can supply a representation adequate for the same decision-making objective.

The authors prove that representations learned by CPC are sufficient for Bayes optimality. Building on that result, they introduce ContraBAR, which substitutes CPC for variational belief inference. The sufficiency result establishes that the representation can contain the information needed for optimal behavior; the algorithm then uses this representation as the basis for meta reinforcement learning.

ContraBAR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in domains with state observations. Avoiding the computational burden of reconstructing future observations also enables learning from images. The method supports image augmentation for domain randomization and works in both online and offline settings. These results connect a theoretical justification for contrastive representations with a practical route to handling more demanding observations.
summary.tldr: ContraBAR uses contrastive predictive coding for meta reinforcement learning, supported by a sufficiency result for Bayes optimality and experiments with state and image observations.

title: ContraBAR: Contrastive Bayes-Adaptive Deep RL

abstract: Without explicit feedback, humans can rapidly learn the meaning of words. Children can acquire a new word after just a few passive exposures, a process known as fast mapping. This word learning capability is believed to be the most fundamental building block of multimodal understanding and reasoning. Despite recent advancements in multimodal learning, a systematic and rigorous evaluation is still missing for human-like word learning in machines. To fill in this gap, we introduce the MachinE Word Learning (MEWL) benchmark to assess how machines learn word meaning in grounded visual scenes. MEWL covers human’s core cognitive toolkits in word learning: cross-situational reasoning, bootstrapping, and pragmatic learning. Specifically, MEWL is a few-shot benchmark suite consisting of nine tasks for probing various word learning capabilities. These tasks are carefully designed to be aligned with the children’s core abilities in word learning and echo the theories in the developmental literature. By evaluating multimodal and unimodal agents’ performance with a comparative analysis of human performance, we notice a sharp divergence in human and machine word learning. We further discuss these differences between humans and machines and call for human-like few-shot word learning in machines.

MEWL turns this ability into an evaluation problem for machines: given limited examples of words in visual scenes, how effectively can a model work out what those words refer to? The benchmark targets grounded word learning as a component of multimodal understanding.

The suite contains nine tasks designed around abilities emphasized in developmental accounts of children’s learning. These include reasoning across situations, using other available structure to support learning, and pragmatic learning. Organizing the evaluation around these capabilities allows the authors to probe several aspects of word acquisition within a common few-shot setting.

The paper evaluates agents that use multiple modalities as well as agents that use a single modality, and compares their performance with humans. The authors observe a sharp divergence between human and machine word learning. MEWL’s contribution is therefore both a structured benchmark and evidence that progress in multimodal systems leaves substantial differences in how people and machines acquire word meanings from limited exposure.
summary.tldr: MEWL uses nine few-shot tasks to evaluate word learning in visual scenes and reveals sharp differences between human and machine performance.

title: MEWL: Few-shot multimodal word learning with referential uncertainty

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has been a popular approach to enable collaborative learning on multiple parties without exchanging raw data. However, the model performance of FL may degrade a lot due to non-IID data. While many FL algorithms focus on non-IID labels, FL on non-IID features has largely been overlooked. Different from typical FL approaches, the paper proposes a new learning concept called ADCOL (Adversarial Collaborative Learning) for non-IID features. Instead of adopting the widely used model-averaging scheme, ADCOL conducts training in an adversarial way: the server aims to train a discriminator to distinguish the representations of the parties, while the parties aim to generate a common representation distribution. Our experiments show that ADCOL achieves better performance than state-of-the-art FL algorithms on non-IID features.

Different from typical FL approaches, the paper proposes a new learning concept called ADCOL (Adversarial Collaborative Learning) for non-IID features. Instead of adopting the widely used model-averaging scheme, ADCOL conducts training in an adversarial way: the server aims to train a discriminator to distinguish the representations of the parties, while the parties aim to generate a common representation distribution. paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple parties collaborate without exchanging their raw data, but differences between their datasets can undermine the resulting models. This paper focuses on differences in features: the information presented to a model can have different distributions across participants. The authors argue that this issue has received less attention than differences in the distribution of labels.

Their approach, ADCOL, replaces the usual emphasis on averaging models with an adversarial training process. A server trains a discriminator to identify which party produced a representation. Meanwhile, the participating parties learn representations whose distributions are shared across parties. These opposing objectives make the distinction between participants something the representation learning process explicitly tries to reduce.

The reported experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art federated learning algorithms on non-identically distributed features. The contribution is therefore both a different collaboration mechanism and empirical evidence for its usefulness in this setting. It directs learning toward common representations when variation between participants lies in their input features.
summary.tldr: ADCOL improves collaborative learning on differing feature distributions by training participants to produce common representations through an adversarial objective.

title: Adversarial Collaborative Learning on Non-IID Features

abstract: We extend PAC-Bayesian theory to generative models and develop generalization bounds for models based on the Wasserstein distance and the total variation distance. Our first result on the Wasserstein distance assumes the instance space is bounded, while our second result takes advantage of dimensionality reduction. Our results naturally apply to Wasserstein GANs and Energy-Based GANs, and our bounds provide new training objectives for these two. Although our work is mainly theoretical, we perform numerical experiments showing non-vacuous generalization bounds for Wasserstein GANs on synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: A generative model aims to represent a data distribution, so its generalization analysis needs to address distributional agreement beyond the training sample. This paper extends PAC-Bayesian theory to that setting. It develops guarantees based on Wasserstein distance and total variation distance, providing two ways to quantify differences between generated and target distributions.

The Wasserstein results use two distinct routes. The first assumes a bounded instance space, while the second takes advantage of dimensionality reduction. These details matter because they specify how the authors obtain the guarantees. The results apply naturally to Wasserstein GANs and Energy-Based GANs, and the resulting bounds also suggest new objectives for training these models.

Although the contribution is mainly theoretical, numerical experiments on synthetic datasets produce non-vacuous bounds for Wasserstein GANs. This means the reported guarantees provide meaningful information in those experiments rather than being too loose to be useful. The work therefore connects a generalization framework to both model optimization and concrete numerical certification, with the empirical evidence specifically supplied for the synthetic Wasserstein-GAN setting.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds for distributional distances yield new generative-model training objectives and non-vacuous Wasserstein-GAN guarantees on synthetic data.

title: PAC-Bayesian Generalization Bounds for Adversarial Generative Models

abstract: Understanding when the noise in stochastic gradient descent (SGD) affects generalization of deep neural networks remains a challenge, complicated by the fact that networks can operate in distinct training regimes. Here we study how the magnitude of this noise $T$ affects performance as the size of the training set $P$ and the scale of initialization $\alpha$ are varied. For gradient descent, $\alpha$ is a key parameter that controls if the network is lazy’ ($\alpha\gg1$) or instead learns features ($\alpha\ll1$). For classification of MNIST and CIFAR10 images, our central results are: *(i)* obtaining phase diagrams for performance in the $(\alpha,T)$ plane. They show that SGD noise can be detrimental or instead useful depending on the training regime. Moreover, although increasing $T$ or decreasing $\alpha$ both allow the net to escape the lazy regime, these changes can have opposite effects on performance. *(ii)* Most importantly, we find that the characteristic temperature $T_c$ where the noise of SGD starts affecting the trained model (and eventually performance) is a power law of $P$. We relate this finding with the observation that key dynamical quantities, such as the total variation of weights during training, depend on both $T$ and $P$ as power laws. These results indicate that a key effect of SGD noise occurs late in training, by affecting the stopping process whereby all data are fitted. Indeed, we argue that due to SGD noise, nets must develop a strongersignal’, i.e. larger informative weights, to fit the data, leading to a longer training time. A stronger signal and a longer training time are also required when the size of the training set $P$ increases. We confirm these views in the perceptron model, where signal and noise can be precisely measured. Interestingly, exponents characterizing the effect of SGD depend on the density of data near the decision boundary, as we explain.
