paragraphs: The paper asks when noise in stochastic gradient descent helps or harms generalization. It varies noise magnitude, training set size, and initialization scale. Initialization matters because it helps determine whether a network stays in a relatively fixed-feature, lazy regime or learns new features during training.

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR10 produce phase diagrams showing that noise can improve or degrade performance depending on the training regime. Increasing noise and reducing initialization scale can both move a network away from lazy behavior, yet have opposite performance effects. The authors also find that the noise level at which training begins to change follows a power law in dataset size.

The authors connect these patterns to late training, when the network finishes fitting the data. They argue that noise requires larger informative weights and longer training to achieve that fit, with larger datasets creating related demands. Perceptron results support this interpretation where signal and noise can be measured directly. The scaling exponents also depend on how densely examples lie near the decision boundary.
summary.tldr: SGD noise can help or hurt depending on the training regime, with its effects linked to dataset size and late-stage fitting.

title: Dissecting the Effects of SGD Noise in Distinct Regimes of Deep Learning

abstract: When launching a new product, historical sales data is often not available, leaving price as a crucial experimental instrument for sellers to gauge market response. When designing pricing experiments, there are three fundamental objectives: estimating the causal effect of price (i.e., price elasticity), maximizing the expected revenue through the experiment, and controlling the tail risk suffering from a very huge loss. In this paper, we reveal the relationship among such three objectives. Under a linear structural model, we investigate the trade-offs between causal inference and expected revenue maximization, as well as between expected revenue maximization and tail risk control. Furthermore, we propose an optimal pricing experimental design, which can flexibly adapt to different desired levels of trade-offs. Through the optimal design, we also explore the relationship between causal inference and tail risk control.

paragraphs: When a product is new, a seller may lack historical sales data for understanding demand. Varying prices can reveal how customers respond, but the experiment also earns revenue and exposes the seller to losses. This paper treats those consequences as three linked design objectives: estimating price elasticity, maximizing expected revenue, and controlling the risk of very large losses.

Under a linear structural model, the authors investigate trade-offs between causal estimation and expected revenue, and between expected revenue and tail-risk control. The distinction matters because an experiment’s average revenue does not describe its exposure to unusually bad outcomes. Likewise, a price choice that serves revenue objectives must also be assessed for how informative it is.

The paper proposes an optimal experimental design that can adapt to different desired trade-offs. It then uses that design to investigate the relationship between causal inference and tail risk. The contribution is a model-based framework for choosing pricing experiments according to how a seller values learning, revenue, and protection against severe losses.
summary.tldr: Under a linear structural model, an optimal pricing experiment balances causal learning, expected revenue, and exposure to severe losses.

title: Pricing Experimental Design: Causal Effect, Expected Revenue and Tail Risk

abstract: This study investigates the loss of generalization ability in neural networks, revisiting warm-starting experiments from Ash & Adams. Our empirical analysis reveals that common methods designed to enhance plasticity by maintaining trainability provide limited benefits to generalization. While reinitializing the network can be effective, it also risks losing valuable prior knowledge. To this end, we introduce the Hare & Tortoise, inspired by the brain’s complementary learning system. Hare & Tortoise consists of two components: the Hare network, which rapidly adapts to new information analogously to the hippocampus, and the Tortoise network, which gradually integrates knowledge akin to the neocortex. By periodically reinitializing the Hare network to the Tortoise’s weights, our method preserves plasticity while retaining general knowledge. Hare & Tortoise can effectively maintain the network’s ability to generalize, which improves advanced reinforcement learning algorithms on the Atari-100k benchmark. The code is available at https://github.com/dojeon-ai/hare-tortoise.

paragraphs: A neural network can remain trainable while losing its ability to generalize well. Revisiting warm-starting experiments, this paper finds that common methods intended to preserve plasticity through trainability offer limited generalization benefits. Reinitializing the network can help, but it can also discard useful knowledge accumulated earlier.

Hare & Tortoise addresses this tension with two networks that learn at different rates. The Hare adapts quickly to new information, while the Tortoise gradually integrates knowledge. Periodically, the Hare is reinitialized using the Tortoise's weights. This supplies the fast learner with a reset based on retained knowledge, connecting renewed adaptability with preservation of broader learning.

The design draws inspiration from complementary learning systems in the brain, using fast and slow components with different roles. The authors find that the method can maintain generalization ability and improve advanced reinforcement learning algorithms on Atari-100k. These results support evaluating plasticity through the ability to generalize, alongside the ability to continue fitting data, and show a practical benefit from resetting to slowly accumulated knowledge.
summary.tldr: Hare & Tortoise periodically resets a fast-learning network to a slow-learning network's weights to preserve adaptability and generalization.

title: Slow and Steady Wins the Race: Maintaining Plasticity with Hare and Tortoise Networks

abstract: We discuss the inhomogeneous Wigner spike model, a theoretical framework recently introduced to study structured noise in various learning scenarios, through the prism of random matrix theory, with a specific focus on its spectral properties. Our primary objective is to find an optimal spectral method, and to extend the celebrated (BBP) phase transition criterion —well-known in the homogeneous case— to our inhomogeneous, block-structured, Wigner model. We provide a thorough rigorous analysis of a transformed matrix and show that the transition for the appearance of 1) an outlier outside the bulk of the limiting spectral distribution and 2) a positive overlap between the associated eigenvector and the signal, occurs precisely at the optimal threshold, making the proposed spectral method optimal within the class of iterative methods for the inhomogeneous Wigner problem.

paragraphs: Recovering a signal from a noisy matrix becomes more complicated when noise has different structure across blocks. This paper studies that situation through the inhomogeneous Wigner spike model. Its goal is to find an optimal spectral method and characterize the point at which spectral information begins to reveal the hidden signal.

The authors rigorously analyze a transformed matrix. They track two events: an eigenvalue separating from the main body of the limiting spectrum, and its associated eigenvector acquiring positive overlap with the signal. The first is a visible change in the spectrum; the second establishes that the corresponding direction contains useful information about the signal.

They show that both transitions occur exactly at the optimal threshold for the studied problem. This extends the familiar BBP transition criterion from homogeneous noise to the block-structured setting. The proposed method is optimal within the class of iterative methods for this inhomogeneous Wigner problem. The result therefore connects a precisely characterized spectral transition with an optimality guarantee for that specific model and method class.
summary.tldr: A transformed-matrix spectral method reaches the optimal iterative-method recovery threshold in a Wigner model with block-structured noise.

title: Spectral Phase Transition and Optimal PCA in Block-Structured Spiked Models

abstract: Deep neural networks based on linear RNNs interleaved with position-wise MLPs are gaining traction as competitive approaches for sequence modeling. Examples of such architectures include state-space models (SSMs) like S4, LRU, and Mamba: recently proposed models that achieve promising performance on text, genetics, and other data that require long-range reasoning. Despite experimental evidence highlighting these architectures’ effectiveness and computational efficiency, their expressive power remains relatively unexplored, especially in connection to specific choices crucial in practice - e.g., carefully designed initialization distribution and potential use of complex numbers. In this paper, we show that combining MLPs with both real or complex linear diagonal recurrences leads to arbitrarily precise approximation of regular causal sequence-to-sequence maps. At the heart of our proof, we rely on a separation of concerns: the linear RNN provides a lossless encoding of the input sequence, and the MLP performs non-linear processing on this encoding. While we show that real diagonal linear recurrences are enough to achieve universality in this architecture, we prove that employing complex eigenvalues near unit disk - i.e., empirically the most successful strategy in S4 - greatly helps the RNN in storing information. We connect this finding with the vanishing gradient issue and provide experiments supporting our claims.

paragraphs: This paper examines the expressive power of sequence models that combine linear recurrent computations with position-wise multilayer perceptrons. Such architectures have shown strong practical performance, but their theoretical capabilities and the role of particular design choices remain less understood. The authors focus on diagonal linear recurrences, considering both real and complex-valued versions.

They prove that combining these recurrences with multilayer perceptrons permits arbitrarily accurate approximation of regular causal sequence-to-sequence maps. The proof separates two jobs: the recurrent component encodes the input sequence without losing information, and the nonlinear component processes that encoding. This explains how a linear recurrence can participate in an expressive nonlinear sequence model.

Real diagonal recurrences are sufficient for the stated universality result. However, the authors also prove that complex eigenvalues near the unit disk substantially help information storage. They connect this benefit with vanishing gradients and provide supporting experiments. The distinction matters: a design choice can improve information retention in practice even when it is not required for theoretical universality.
summary.tldr: Linear diagonal recurrences followed by nonlinear projections are universal for regular causal sequence maps, while suitable complex eigenvalues improve information storage.

title: Universality of Linear Recurrences Followed by Non-linear Projections: Finite-Width Guarantees and Benefits of Complex Eigenvalues

abstract: Modern Hopfield networks have enjoyed recent interest due to their connection to attention in transformers. Our paper provides a unified framework for sparse Hopfield networks by establishing a link with Fenchel-Young losses. The result is a new family of Hopfield-Fenchel-Young energies whose update rules are end-to-end differentiable sparse transformations. We reveal a connection between loss margins, sparsity, and exact memory retrieval. We further extend this framework to structured Hopfield networks via the SparseMAP transformation, which can retrieve pattern associations instead of a single pattern. Experiments on multiple instance learning and text rationalization demonstrate the usefulness of our approach.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield networks are memory-retrieval models connected to transformer attention. This paper develops a unified account of sparse versions, where retrieval can concentrate on selected memories. The authors build that account by connecting Hopfield networks with Fenchel–Young losses, linking the memory mechanism to a family of training losses.

The connection yields Hopfield–Fenchel–Young energy functions with update rules that are sparse transformations and remain differentiable end to end. The analysis also relates loss margins, sparsity, and exact retrieval of stored memories. This connects the mathematical properties of the loss to how selectively and precisely the network can retrieve information.

The authors extend the framework through SparseMAP to support structured retrieval. These networks can retrieve associations among patterns, expanding the retrieval target beyond an individual pattern. Experiments in multiple-instance learning and text rationalization demonstrate the approach's usefulness. Together, the theory and applications present sparse and structured memory retrieval as parts of a common differentiable framework.
summary.tldr: A loss-based framework unifies sparse Hopfield memory retrieval and extends it to retrieving structured associations among patterns.

title: Sparse and Structured Hopfield Networks

abstract: Given the critical role of graphs in real-world applications and their high-security requirements, improving the ability of graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) data is an urgent research problem. The recent work GNNSAFE proposes a framework based on the aggregation of negative energy scores that significantly improves the performance of GNNs to detect node-level OOD data. However, our study finds that score aggregation among nodes is susceptible to extreme values due to the unboundedness of the negative energy scores and logit shifts, which severely limits the accuracy of GNNs in detecting node-level OOD data. In this paper, we propose NODESAFE: reducing the generation of extreme scores of nodes by adding two optimization terms that make the negative energy scores bounded and mitigate the logit shift. Experimental results show that our approach dramatically improves the ability of GNNs to detect OOD data at the node level, e.g., in detecting OOD data induced by Structure Manipulation, the metric of FPR95 (lower is better) in scenarios without (with) OOD data exposure are reduced from the current SOTA by 28.4% ( 22.7% ). The code is available via https://github.com/ShenzhiYang2000/NODESAFE-Bounded-and-Uniform-Energy-based-Out-of-distribution-Detection-for-Graphs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks need to identify nodes whose data differ from the distribution they were trained to handle. An existing approach, GNNSAFE, improves this detection by aggregating negative energy scores across nodes. The paper identifies a weakness in that aggregation: extreme node scores can distort the combined signal and reduce detection accuracy.

The authors connect these extreme values to unbounded negative energy scores and shifts in model logits. Their method, NODESAFE, adds two optimization terms intended to control those sources of distortion. One makes the negative energy scores bounded, while the other mitigates logit shifts. Together, they reduce the generation of extreme scores before those scores are aggregated.

Experiments report substantial improvements in node-level out-of-distribution detection. For anomalies caused by Structure Manipulation, the reported reductions in FPR95 relative to the current state of the art are 28.4% without out-of-distribution exposure and 22.7% with exposure. Lower FPR95 is better. The result highlights the importance of controlling the scores being combined, alongside the use of graph-based aggregation itself.
summary.tldr: NODESAFE improves detection of unusual graph nodes by bounding energy scores and reducing logit shifts that can distort score aggregation.

title: Bounded and Uniform Energy-based Out-of-distribution Detection for Graphs

abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow in size and context length, efficient inference strategies are essential to maintain low-latency token generation. Unfortunately, conventional tensor and data parallelism face diminishing returns when scaling across multiple devices. We propose a novel form—attention-level speculative parallelism (ALSpec)—that predicts self-attention outputs to execute subsequent operations early on separate devices. Our approach overlaps attention and non-attention computations, reducing the attention latency overhead at 128K context length by up to 5x and improving end-to-end decode latency by up to 1.65x, all without sacrificing quality. We establish the fundamental pillars for speculative execution and provide an execution paradigm that simplifies implementation. We show that existing attention-approximation methods perform well on simple information retrieval tasks, but they fail in advanced reasoning and math. Combined with speculative execution, we can approximate up to 90% of self-attention without harming model correctness. Demonstrated on Tenstorrent’s NPU devices, we scale up LLM inference beyond current techniques, paving the way for faster inference in transformer models.

paragraphs: Generating tokens becomes increasingly expensive as language models and their contexts grow. Distributing inference across more devices does not automatically solve this problem, because conventional parallelization strategies offer diminishing returns. This paper targets the waiting time caused by attention: later computations ordinarily depend on attention outputs and therefore cannot start until those outputs are available.

ALSpec predicts self-attention outputs so that subsequent operations can begin early on separate devices. This speculative execution overlaps attention with other computation. The paper establishes foundations for this execution strategy and presents an implementation paradigm. It also distinguishes speculative use of approximations from attention approximation alone, which its evaluations find inadequate for advanced reasoning and mathematics despite working well on simple retrieval.

On Tenstorrent NPU devices, ALSpec reduces attention latency overhead at 128K context by up to a factor of five and improves end-to-end decoding latency by up to 1.65 times without sacrificing quality. Combined with speculative execution, it approximates up to 90% of self-attention without harming model correctness in the reported results.
summary.tldr: ALSpec speculatively predicts attention outputs to overlap computations across devices, improving reported decoding latency without sacrificing quality.

title: Attention-Level Speculation

abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown outstanding performance in node classification tasks, they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which are imperceptible changes to input samples. Adversarial training, as a widely used tool to enhance the adversarial robustness of GNNs, has presented remarkable effectiveness in node classification tasks. However, the generalization properties for explaining their behaviors remain not well understood from the theoretical viewpoint. To fill this gap, we develop a high probability generalization bound of general GNNs in adversarial learning through covering number analysis. We estimate the covering number of the GNN model class based on the entire perturbed feature matrix by constructing a cover for the perturbation set. Our results are generally applicable to a series of GNNs. We demonstrate their applicability by investigating the generalization performance of several popular GNN models under adversarial attacks, which reveal the architecture-related factors influencing the generalization gap. Our experimental results on benchmark datasets provide evidence that supports the established theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can classify nodes effectively while remaining vulnerable to small adversarial changes in their inputs. Adversarial training helps, but its success leaves a theoretical question: how well does robustness learned during training carry over to other examples? This paper develops a high-probability bound on that generalization gap.

The authors use covering number analysis, which describes model complexity through a collection of representatives covering possible behaviors. Their construction accounts for the entire perturbed feature matrix by first covering the set of allowed perturbations. This provides a way to include adversarial changes directly in the complexity analysis used to bound generalization.

The result applies to a range of graph neural networks. Applying it to several popular architectures reveals architecture-related factors that influence the gap between training and generalization performance under attack. Experiments on benchmark datasets provide evidence consistent with the theory. The contribution is therefore both a general analytical tool and an explanation of how architecture can affect robust generalization.
summary.tldr: A covering-number analysis bounds adversarial generalization in graph neural networks and identifies architecture-related influences on the generalization gap.

title: Adversarial Robust Generalization of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Graph generation is a critical task in numerous domains, including molecular design and social network analysis, due to its ability to model complex relationships and structured data. While most modern graph generative models utilize adjacency matrix representations, this work revisits an alternative approach that represents graphs as sequences of node set and edge set. We advocate for this approach due to its efficient encoding of graphs and propose a novel representation. Based on this representation, we introduce the Graph Generative Pre-trained Transformer (G2PT), an auto-regressive model that learns graph structures via next-token prediction. To further exploit G2PT’s capabilities as a general-purpose foundation model, we explore fine-tuning strategies for two downstream applications: goal-oriented generation and graph property prediction. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets. Results indicate that G2PT achieves superior generative performance on both generic graph and molecule datasets. Furthermore, G2PT exhibits strong adaptability and versatility in downstream tasks from molecular design to property prediction.

paragraphs: Graph generation models relationships and structured data for applications such as molecular design and social network analysis. Many modern methods represent graphs through adjacency matrices. This paper revisits a different representation: a sequence describing node and edge sets, designed to encode graph information efficiently.

Experiments across multiple datasets show superior generative performance on generic graphs and molecules, along with strong adaptability to downstream tasks. The contribution connects the choice of graph representation to a reusable generative modeling approach. By putting graph structure into a sequence format, G2PT makes next-token learning applicable to graph generation and demonstrates that the resulting model can be adapted to additional tasks involving structured relationships.
summary.tldr: G2PT learns to generate graphs through next-token prediction over node-and-edge sequences and adapts to generation and property prediction tasks.

title: Graph Generative Pre-trained Transformer

abstract: Class imbalance remains a major challenge in machine learning, especially in multi-class problems with long-tailed distributions. Existing methods, such as data resampling, cost-sensitive techniques, and logistic loss modifications, though popular and often effective, lack solid theoretical foundations. As an example, we demonstrate that cost-sensitive methods are not Bayes-consistent. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for analyzing generalization in imbalanced classification. We propose a new class-imbalanced margin loss function for both binary and multi-class settings, prove its strong $H$-consistency, and derive corresponding learning guarantees based on empirical loss and a new notion of class-sensitive Rademacher complexity. Leveraging these theoretical results, we devise novel and general learning algorithms, IMMAX (Imbalanced Margin Maximization), which incorporate confidence margins and are applicable to various hypothesis sets. While our focus is theoretical, we also present extensive empirical results demonstrating the effectiveness of our algorithms compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: When some classes have far more examples than others, learning a useful classifier becomes especially challenging. This paper develops a theoretical framework for that problem in both binary and multiclass settings. It questions the foundations of common remedies and demonstrates a failure of Bayes consistency for cost-sensitive methods: their objectives need not lead to the ideal classification rule considered by the analysis.

The proposed alternative is a margin loss designed for class imbalance. Margins describe how confidently a classifier separates competing decisions. The authors prove strong H-consistency for their loss, connecting optimization of that loss to classification performance within a hypothesis class. They also derive learning guarantees using empirical loss and a class-sensitive version of Rademacher complexity, which captures aspects of the model class relevant to generalization.

These results motivate IMMAX, a family of algorithms that incorporate confidence margins and support different hypothesis sets. Although theory is the main contribution, the paper also reports extensive experiments showing effectiveness against existing baselines. The framework connects the training objective, generalization analysis, and practical algorithm design.
summary.tldr: IMMAX combines an imbalance-aware margin loss with consistency and generalization guarantees to support learning from uneven class distributions.

title: Balancing the Scales: A Theoretical and Algorithmic Framework for Learning from Imbalanced Data

abstract: The Median of Means (MoM) is a mean estimator that has gained popularity in the context of heavy-tailed data. In this work, we analyze its performance in the task of simultaneously estimating the mean of each function in a class $\mathcal{F}$ when the data distribution possesses only the first $p$ moments for $p \in (1,2]$. We prove a new sample complexity bound using a novel symmetrization technique that may be of independent interest. Additionally, we present applications of our result to $k$-means clustering with unbounded inputs and linear regression with general losses, improving upon existing works.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes mean estimation when the data are heavy-tailed and only limited moments exist. Its goal is broader than estimating a single average: it seeks to estimate the mean associated with every function in a class simultaneously. A useful guarantee must therefore control estimation across the whole class, rather than treat each function as an isolated problem.

The authors study the Median of Means estimator under a moment assumption indexed by p, with p greater than one and at most two. They prove a new sample-complexity bound using a new symmetrization technique. The bound addresses how much data are needed for this simultaneous estimation task under the stated weak moment conditions.

The paper then applies the result to k-means clustering with unbounded inputs and to linear regression with general losses, improving on previous work. These applications show why uniform mean estimation matters beyond estimating averages directly: it can support guarantees for learning problems that compare many candidate functions or solutions. The symmetrization technique is also presented as potentially useful independently of these applications.
summary.tldr: A new Median of Means analysis improves simultaneous mean-estimation guarantees under weak moment assumptions, with clustering and regression applications.

title: Uniform Mean Estimation for Heavy-Tailed Distributions via Median-of-Means

abstract: Code editing is a foundational task in software development, where its effectiveness depends on whether it introduces desired code property changes without changing the original code’s intended functionality. Existing approaches often formulate code editing as an implicit end-to-end task, omitting the fact that code-editing procedures inherently consist of discrete and explicit steps, and thus suffer from suboptimal performance and lack of robustness and generalization. We introduce EditLord, a code editing framework that makes the code transformation steps explicit. Our key insight is to employ a language model (LM) as an inductive learner to extract code editing rules from the training code pairs as concise meta-rule sets. Such rule sets will be manifested for each training sample to augment them for finetuning or assist in prompting- and iterative-based code editing. EditLord outperforms the state-of-the-art by an average of 22.7% in editing performance and 58.1% in robustness while achieving 20.2% higher functional correctness, across critical software engineering and security applications, LM models, and editing modes.

paragraphs: A useful code edit must introduce the requested change while preserving the program’s intended functionality. This paper argues that treating editing as an implicit input-to-output task overlooks the explicit steps involved in transforming code. EditLord makes those steps visible by learning reusable transformation rules from examples of code before and after editing.

A language model acts as an inductive learner, extracting concise sets of meta-rules from training pairs. Those rules are then expressed for individual training examples. The resulting guidance can augment fine-tuning data or support editing through prompts and iterative procedures, allowing the same framework to operate across several ways of using a language model.

Across the evaluated software engineering and security applications, models, and editing modes, EditLord reports average gains of 22.7% in editing performance and 58.1% in robustness over the state of the art, alongside 20.2% higher functional correctness. These results support explicit transformation knowledge as a useful mechanism for improving both requested changes and preservation of program behavior.
summary.tldr: EditLord learns explicit code-transformation rules from examples to improve editing performance, robustness, and functional correctness.

title: EditLord: Learning Code Transformation Rules for Code Editing

abstract: Deep learning-based classifiers are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing methods for defending against such attacks require adding a defense mechanism or modifying the learning procedure (e.g., by adding adversarial examples). This paper shows that for certain data distributions one can learn a provably robust classifier using standard learning methods and without adding a defense mechanism. More specifically, this paper addresses the problem of finding a robust classifier for a binary classification problem in which the data comes from an isotropic mixture of Gaussians with orthonormal cluster centers. First, we characterize the largest $\ell_2$-attack any classifier can defend against while maintaining high accuracy, and show the existence of optimal robust classifiers achieving this maximum $\ell_2$-robustness. Next, we show that given data from the orthonormal Gaussian mixture model, gradient flow on a two-layer network with a polynomial ReLU activation and without adversarial examples provably finds an optimal robust classifier.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often pursued by modifying training or adding a defense mechanism. This paper asks when ordinary learning can instead produce a provably robust classifier. It studies a specific binary classification setting: data drawn from an isotropic Gaussian mixture whose cluster centers are orthonormal. That distributional structure is central to the result.

The authors first characterize the largest perturbation, measured in the l2 norm, that any classifier can withstand while retaining high accuracy. They then establish that classifiers achieving this maximal robustness exist. This defines both the limit imposed by the problem and a target against which the learning procedure can be evaluated.

Next, the paper proves that gradient flow on a two-layer network with a polynomial ReLU activation finds an optimal robust classifier for this data model, without adversarial examples. The result demonstrates that dedicated defenses are not always required for optimal robustness. Its scope is the specified distribution, architecture, and training dynamics, rather than arbitrary classification problems.
summary.tldr: For orthonormal Gaussian mixtures, gradient flow on a specified two-layer network provably learns optimal robustness without adversarial examples.

title: Gradient Flow Provably Learns Robust Classifiers for Orthonormal GMMs

abstract: In this paper, we focus on the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of self-supervised learning (SSL). By analyzing the mini-batch construction during the SSL training phase, we first give one plausible explanation for SSL having OOD generalization. Then, from the perspective of data generation and causal inference, we analyze and conclude that SSL learns spurious correlations during the training process, which leads to a reduction in OOD generalization. To address this issue, we propose a post-intervention distribution (PID) grounded in the Structural Causal Model. PID offers a scenario where the spurious variable and label variable is mutually independent. Besides, we demonstrate that if each mini-batch during SSL training satisfies PID, the resulting SSL model can achieve optimal worst-case OOD performance. This motivates us to develop a batch sampling strategy that enforces PID constraints through the learning of a latent variable model. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate the identifiability of the latent variable model and validate the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy. Experiments conducted on various downstream OOD tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can transfer beyond its training distribution, but it can also learn spurious relationships that break under distribution shifts. This paper examines mini-batch construction as one plausible explanation for its generalization behavior. A causal analysis then connects learned spurious correlations to reduced out-of-distribution performance.

The authors define a post-intervention distribution using a structural causal model. Under this distribution, the spurious variable and label variable are independent. They show that if every training mini-batch satisfies this distribution, the resulting self-supervised model can achieve optimal worst-case out-of-distribution performance. The batch-level condition is central to the theoretical statement.

To turn that result into a training strategy, the paper learns a latent-variable model and uses it to sample batches subject to the proposed constraints. Theoretical analysis establishes identifiability of the latent model and supports the sampling method, while experiments on downstream out-of-distribution tasks show its effectiveness. The approach makes data grouping during training an explicit means of reducing reliance on misleading correlations.
summary.tldr: A causally motivated batch-sampling strategy reduces spurious correlations in self-supervised learning and improves reported out-of-distribution performance.

title: On the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems are utilized in critical sectors such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance, but often rely on historical data that contains demographic biases, leading to decisions that perpetuate or intensify existing inequalities. Causal and counterfactual fairness provide a transparent, human-in-the-loop framework to mitigate algorithmic discrimination, aligning closely with legal doctrines of direct and indirect discrimination. However, current causal fairness frameworks hold a key limitation in that they assume prior knowledge of the correct causal model, restricting their applicability in complex fairness scenarios where causal models are unknown or difficult to identify. To bridge this gap, we propose FairPFN, a tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic causal fairness data to identify and mitigate the causal effects of protected attributes in its predictions. FairPFN’s key contribution is that it requires no knowledge of the causal model and demonstrates strong performance across a diverse set of hand-crafted and real-world causal scenarios relative to robust baseline methods. FairPFN paves the way for a promising direction for future research, making causal fairness more accessible to a wider variety of complex fairness problems.

paragraphs: Historical data can carry demographic biases into machine-learning decisions. Causal and counterfactual fairness frameworks address this by examining how protected attributes affect predictions, but existing approaches typically assume that the correct causal model is already known. That requirement makes them difficult to apply when the relevant causal relationships are uncertain or hard to identify.

FairPFN is a foundation model for tabular data that is pre-trained on synthetic examples of causal fairness problems. Through this training, it learns to identify and mitigate the causal effects of protected attributes in its predictions. Its central contribution is that using the model does not require prior knowledge of the causal model.

The authors report strong performance relative to robust baseline methods across both hand-crafted and real-world causal scenarios. These results suggest that synthetic causal pre-training can make fairness methods more accessible in settings where specifying a causal model is a major obstacle. The stated evidence supports a promising direction for causal fairness, rather than a universal guarantee that every resulting prediction is fair.
summary.tldr: FairPFN learns from synthetic causal fairness data to mitigate protected-attribute effects without requiring a known causal model.

title: FairPFN: A Tabular Foundation Model for Causal Fairness

abstract: Time series analysis is crucial across various fields like energy, environment, transportation, finance and health. Deep learning has significantly advanced this field, particularly, the Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) excels in multiple domains due to extensive pre-training. In this work, we focus on TSFM’s challenges in medical practice: limited computing resources and medical data privacy. TSFM variants include fine-tuned models and those pre-trained for rapid deployment on diverse data. There may not be enough computing resources to train physiological signals locally in hospitals, and generalized TSFM is still inferior to task-specific methods on private, imbalanced local data. To address this, we propose PhysioPFM, a framework for efficiently personalizing TSFM. Our approach involves low-rank pre-training on public datasets, generator training by trained LoRA weights, and efficient weight generation via local data. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating generated models with TSFM enhances performance, and transferability, and reduces the need for additional sensitive data training.

paragraphs: A broadly pretrained time-series model may still perform worse than task-specific methods on a hospital’s private, imbalanced physiological data. At the same time, local computing resources may be insufficient for extensive adaptation. PhysioPFM addresses this combination of personalization needs, resource constraints, and concerns about training on sensitive medical data.

The framework first performs low-rank pre-training using public datasets. It then trains a generator from the resulting LoRA weights and uses local data to generate adaptation weights efficiently. This sequence transfers information from public-data adaptation into a mechanism for producing personalized model weights, reducing the need to conduct additional sensitive-data training for each adaptation.

The experiments show that integrating the generated models with a time-series foundation model improves performance and transferability while reducing additional training on sensitive data. The contribution is an adaptation workflow tailored to the constraints described, with weight generation taking a central role. The stated privacy-related benefit is reduced sensitive-data training; the abstract does not present that benefit as a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: PhysioPFM generates personalized adaptation weights for physiological time-series models, improving performance while reducing additional sensitive-data training.

title: Efficient Personalized Adaptation for Physiological Signal Foundation Model

abstract: With the growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse domains, concerns regarding their safety have grown substantially. LLM unlearning has emerged as a pivotal approach to removing harmful or unlawful contents while maintaining utility. Despite increasing interest, the challenges of continual unlearning, which is common in real-world scenarios, remain underexplored. Successive unlearning tasks often lead to intensified utility degradation. To effectively unlearn targeted knowledge while preserving LLM utility, it is essential to minimize changes in model parameters by selectively updating those linked to the target knowledge, thereby ensuring other knowledge remains unaffected. Building on the task vector framework, we propose a new method named ALKN (Adaptive Localization of Knowledge Negation), which uses dynamic masking to sparsify training gradients and adaptively adjusts unlearning intensity based on inter-task relationships. Comprehensive experiments across three well-established LLM unlearning datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms baseline methods in both unlearning effectiveness and utility retention under continual unlearning settings.

paragraphs: Removing targeted knowledge from a language model becomes harder when removal requests arrive repeatedly. Each update can damage useful capabilities, so successive unlearning tasks may compound that damage. This paper studies continual unlearning, focusing on how to remove unwanted knowledge while retaining the model’s broader usefulness.

The proposed method, ALKN, builds on a task vector framework and concentrates updates through dynamic masking. The mask makes training gradients sparse, restricting which parameters receive changes instead of broadly modifying the model. ALKN also adjusts the strength of unlearning according to relationships between tasks. These mechanisms address both where an update acts and how strongly it acts as the sequence of removal tasks develops.

Across three established unlearning datasets, the authors report consistently better unlearning effectiveness and utility retention than baseline methods in continual settings. The findings support selective, adaptive updates as a way to manage repeated removal requests. They show improvements on both evaluation goals, rather than treating stronger forgetting alone as evidence of successful unlearning.
summary.tldr: ALKN selectively updates parameters and adapts unlearning strength to improve repeated knowledge removal while retaining useful capabilities.

title: Adaptive Localization of Knowledge Negation for Continual LLM Unlearning

abstract: In principle, explanations are intended as a way to increase trust in machine learning models and are often obligated by regulations. However, many circumstances where these are demanded are adversarial in nature, meaning the involved parties have misaligned interests and are incentivized to manipulate explanations for their purpose. As a result, explainability methods fail to be operational in such settings despite the demand. In this paper, we take a step towards operationalizing explanations in adversarial scenarios with Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs), a cryptographic primitive. Specifically we explore ZKP-amenable versions of the popular explainability algorithm LIME and evaluate their performance on Neural Networks and Random Forests. Our code is publicly available at : https://github.com/emlaufer/ExpProof.

paragraphs: Machine learning explanations are often requested to establish trust, including in situations where the parties involved have conflicting interests. The paper focuses on a practical obstacle: someone providing an explanation may have an incentive to manipulate it. In such settings, producing an explanation alone does not make the explanation operationally trustworthy.

ExpProof explores using zero-knowledge proofs as a cryptographic foundation for explanations of confidential models. The concrete technical work adapts LIME, a widely used explanation algorithm, into versions amenable to these proofs. This connects the explanation procedure with a mechanism intended to support verification while maintaining model confidentiality.

The authors evaluate these LIME variants on neural networks and random forests. The abstract presents the work as a step toward usable explanations in adversarial situations, rather than claiming to settle the broader trust problem. Its contribution is to bring explanation methods and cryptographic verification into the same design, addressing circumstances where the explanation provider's incentives are themselves part of the challenge.
summary.tldr: ExpProof explores proof-compatible versions of LIME to make explanations more usable when models are confidential and parties have conflicting interests.

title: ExpProof : Operationalizing Explanations for Confidential Models with ZKPs

abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are tractable representations of probability distributions allowing for exact and efficient computation of likelihoods and marginals. Recent advancements have improved the scalability of PCs either by leveraging their sparse properties or through the use of tensorized operations for better hardware utilization. However, no existing method fully exploits both aspects simultaneously. In this paper, we propose a novel sparse and structured parameterization for the sum blocks in PCs. By replacing dense matrices with sparse Monarch matrices, we significantly reduce the memory and computation costs, enabling unprecedented scaling of PCs. From a theory perspective, our construction arises naturally from circuit multiplication; from a practical perspective, compared to previous efforts on scaling up tractable probabilistic models, our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art generative modeling performance on challenging benchmarks like Text8, LM1B and ImageNet, but also demonstrates superior scaling behavior, achieving the same performance with substantially less compute as measured by the number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) during training.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits represent probability distributions while allowing exact, efficient calculations of likelihoods and marginals. Scaling them has involved either exploiting sparse structure or using tensor operations that fit modern hardware well. This paper seeks to combine those advantages, addressing the memory and computation costs of larger circuits.

The proposed parameterization replaces dense matrices in the circuits’ sum blocks with sparse, structured Monarch matrices. This changes how those blocks are represented and computed, reducing resource costs while supporting larger models. The authors also show that their construction arises naturally from circuit multiplication, giving a theoretical basis for the chosen structure.

On Text8, LM1B, and ImageNet, the method achieves state-of-the-art generative performance relative to previous efforts at scaling tractable probabilistic models. It also reaches the same performance with substantially fewer training floating-point operations. These findings connect the structural change to both modeling quality and computational scaling, showing that the evaluated circuits can use training computation more efficiently as well as achieve strong results.
summary.tldr: Sparse Monarch matrices reduce probabilistic-circuit costs and improve generative performance and training-compute scaling on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Scaling Probabilistic Circuits via Monarch Matrices

abstract: This paper explores how theory can guide and enhance practical algorithms, using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) in large language models as a case study. We rigorously prove that, under gradient descent, LoRA adapters align with specific singular subspaces of the one-step full fine-tuning gradient. This result suggests that, by properly initializing the adapters using the one-step full gradient, subspace alignment can be achieved immediately—applicable to both linear and nonlinear models. Building on our theory, we propose a theory-driven algorithm, LoRA-One, where the linear convergence (as well as generalization) is built and incorporating preconditioners theoretically helps mitigate the effects of ill-conditioning. Besides, our theory reveals connections between LoRA-One and other gradient-alignment-based methods, helping to clarify misconceptions in the design of such algorithms. LoRA-One achieves significant empirical improvements over LoRA and its variants across benchmarks in natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Code is available at: https://github.com/YuanheZ/LoRA-One.

paragraphs: LoRA adapts language models through low-rank updates, making the directions captured by those updates important. This paper studies how those directions relate to the gradient from one full fine-tuning step. Under gradient descent, the authors prove that LoRA adapters align with particular singular subspaces of that gradient.

The theory suggests initializing adapters from the one-step full gradient so the relevant alignment is present immediately, for both linear and nonlinear models. LoRA-One builds on this initialization principle. The paper also establishes linear convergence and generalization results for its analysis, and shows theoretically how preconditioners can reduce difficulties caused by ill-conditioning.

Experiments report significant gains over LoRA and its variants on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. The analysis additionally connects LoRA-One with other methods based on gradient alignment. The role of the single full-gradient step is to guide the adapter subspace and initialization; the stated result does not mean that all subsequent fine-tuning can universally be replaced by one update.
summary.tldr: LoRA-One uses a single full fine-tuning gradient to initialize aligned adapter subspaces, with theoretical support and empirical gains over LoRA variants.

title: LoRA-One: One-Step Full Gradient Could Suffice for Fine-Tuning Large Language Models, Provably and Efficiently

abstract: Diffusion distillation is a widely used technique to reduce the sampling cost of diffusion models, yet it often requires extensive training, and the student performance tends to be degraded. Recent studies show that incorporating a GAN objective may alleviate these issues, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this work, we first identify a key limitation of distillation: mismatched step sizes and parameter numbers between the teacher and the student model lead them to converge to different local minima, rendering direct imitation suboptimal. We further demonstrate that a standalone GAN objective, without relying a distillation loss, overcomes this limitation and is sufficient to convert diffusion models into efficient one-step generators. Based on this finding, we propose that diffusion training may be viewed as a form of generative pre-training, equipping models with capabilities that can be unlocked through lightweight GAN fine-tuning. Supporting this view, we create a one-step generation model by fine-tuning a pre-trained model with 85% of parameters frozen, achieving strong performance with only 0.2M images and near-SOTA results with 5M images. We further present a frequency-domain analysis that may explain the one-step generative capability gained in diffusion training. Overall, our work provides a new perspective for diffusion training, highlighting its role as a powerful generative pre-training process, which can be the basis for building efficient one-step generation models.

paragraphs: Diffusion distillation reduces sampling steps but can require extensive training and weaken the resulting student. This paper identifies a mismatch between teacher and student step sizes and parameter counts: they can converge to different local minima, making direct imitation suboptimal. The authors investigate whether adversarial training can avoid this obstacle.

They demonstrate that a standalone GAN objective, without a distillation loss, is sufficient to convert diffusion models into one-step generators in their setting. This supports viewing diffusion training as generative pre-training whose capabilities can be accessed through lightweight GAN fine-tuning. The proposal changes the role of the pretrained model from an imitation target to a foundation for further generative training.

The authors fine-tune a pretrained model while freezing 85% of its parameters, reporting strong performance with 0.2 million images and near-state-of-the-art results with 5 million. A frequency-domain analysis offers a possible explanation for the one-step capabilities acquired during diffusion training. That explanation is presented as suggestive, while the generation results provide empirical support for the pre-training perspective.
summary.tldr: GAN fine-tuning can convert pretrained diffusion models into one-step generators without a distillation loss, even with most parameters frozen.

title: Revisiting Diffusion Models: From Generative Pre-training to One-Step Generation

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is widely adopted to deploy Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices with limited memory budgets. Although MoE is, in theory, an inborn memory-friendly architecture requiring only a few activated experts to reside in the memory for inference, current MoE architectures cannot effectively fulfill this advantage and will yield intolerable inference latencies of LLMs on memory-constrained devices. Our investigation pinpoints the essential cause as the remarkable temporal inconsistencies of inter-token expert activations, which generate overly frequent expert swapping demands dominating the latencies. To this end, we propose a novel MoE architecture, Oracle-MoE, to fulfill the real on-device potential of MoE-based LLMs. Oracle-MoE route tokens in a highly compact space suggested by attention scores, termed the oracle space, to effectively maintain the semantic locality across consecutive tokens to reduce expert activation variations, eliminating massive swapping demands. Theoretical analysis proves that Oracle-MoE is bound to provide routing decisions with better semantic locality and, therefore, better expert activation consistencies. Experiments on the pretrained GPT-2 architectures of different sizes (200M, 350M, 790M, and 2B) and downstream tasks demonstrate that without compromising task performance, our Oracle-MoE has achieved state-of-the-art inference speeds across varying memory budgets, revealing its substantial potential for LLM deployments in industry.
originalAbstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is widely adopted to deploy Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices with limited memory budgets. Although MoE is, in theory, an inborn memory-friendly architecture requiring only a few activated experts to reside in the memory for inference, current MoE architectures cannot effectively fulfill this advantage and will yield intolerable inference latencies of LLMs on memory-constrained devices. Our investigation pinpoints the essential cause as the remarkable temporal inconsistencies of inter-token expert activations, which generate overly frequent expert swapping demands dominating the latencies. To this end, we propose a novel MoE architecture, Oracle-MoE, to fulfill the real on-device potential of MoE-based LLMs. Oracle-MoE route tokens in a highly compact space suggested by attention scores, termed the oracle space, to effectively maintain the semantic locality across consecutive tokens to reduce expert activation variations, eliminating massive swapping demands. Theoretical analysis proves that Oracle-MoE is bound to provide routing decisions with better semantic locality and, therefore, better expert activation consistencies. Experiments on the pretrained GPT-2 architectures of different sizes (200M, 350M, 790M, and 2B) and downstream tasks demonstrate that without compromising task performance, our Oracle-MoE has achieved state-of-the-art inference speeds across varying memory budgets, revealing its substantial potential for LLM deployments in industry.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few experts for each token, suggesting that inference could fit within limited memory. In practice, consecutive tokens may activate different experts so frequently that moving experts in and out of memory dominates latency. Oracle-MoE targets this temporal inconsistency in expert activation.

Its routing mechanism places tokens in a compact representation called the oracle space, derived from attention scores. Routing in this space preserves semantic locality across consecutive tokens, reducing changes in which experts are activated and therefore reducing swapping demands. The paper provides theoretical analysis supporting better semantic locality in routing decisions and improved consistency of expert activation.

Experiments use pretrained GPT-2 architectures at 200M, 350M, 790M, and 2B parameter scales, along with downstream tasks. Across varying memory budgets, Oracle-MoE achieves state-of-the-art inference speeds without compromising task performance in the reported evaluations. The result connects routing behavior to a practical deployment bottleneck: sparse activation helps memory-constrained inference most when the active experts also remain sufficiently consistent over time.
summary.tldr: Oracle-MoE improves routing consistency across consecutive tokens to reduce expert swapping and accelerate memory-constrained inference.

title: Oracle-MoE: Locality-preserving Routing in the Oracle Space for Memory-constrained Large Language Model Inference

abstract: On-policy Reinforcement Learning (RL) remains a dominant paradigm for continuous control, yet standard implementations rely on Gaussian actors and relatively shallow MLP policies, often leading to brittle optimization when gradients are noisy, and policy updates must be conservative. In this paper, we revisit actor policy representation as a first-class design choice for on-policy RL. We study discretized categorical actors, which represent each action dimension as a distribution over discrete bins and induce a policy objective analogous to classification cross-entropy loss. Building on architectural advances from supervised learning, we further pair discretized categorical actors with regularized networks, yielding RN-D. Across diverse continuous-control benchmarks, we show that simply replacing the standard Gaussian actor with our proposed actor substantially improves performance, achieving state-of-the-art results within on-policy RL. We release our code at https://github.com/alwaysbyx/RND-RL.

paragraphs: Continuous-control reinforcement learning commonly uses Gaussian actors and relatively shallow multilayer perceptrons. The paper identifies these standard choices as a source of brittle optimization when gradients are noisy and policy updates need to remain conservative. It investigates the actor’s representation as a central design decision.

The proposed actor represents each action dimension using a probability distribution over discrete bins. This produces a policy objective analogous to the cross-entropy loss used in classification. The authors then pair this discretized categorical representation with regularized networks, drawing on architectural advances from supervised learning to form RN-D.

Across diverse continuous-control benchmarks, replacing the standard Gaussian actor with the proposed actor substantially improves performance. The resulting method achieves reported state-of-the-art results within on-policy reinforcement learning. These findings indicate that changing how a policy represents its action choices can materially affect training outcomes, and that combining this representation with regularized network design is a productive direction for the evaluated control tasks.
summary.tldr: RN-D combines discrete-bin action distributions with regularized networks to improve on-policy continuous-control performance.

title: RN-D: Discretized Categorical Actors for On-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Model routing chooses which language model to use for each query. By sending easy queries to cheaper models and hard queries to stronger ones, it can significantly reduce inference cost while maintaining high accuracy. However, most existing routers treat this as a fixed choice among a small set of models, which makes them hard to adapt to new models or changing budget constraints. In this paper, we propose SCOPE (Scalable and Controllable Outcome Performance Estimator), a routing framework that goes beyond model selection by predicting their cost and performance. Trained with reinforcement learning, SCOPE makes reasoning-based predictions by retrieving how models behave on similar problems, rather than relying on fixed model names, enabling it to work with new, unseen models. Moreover, by explicitly predicting how accurate and how expensive a model will be, it turns routing into a dynamic decision problem, allowing users to easily control the trade-off between accuracy and cost. Experiments show that SCOPE is more than just a cost-saving tool. It flexibly adapts to user needs: it can boost accuracy by up to 25.7% when performance is the priority, or cut costs by up to 95.1% when efficiency matters most. We release the dataset and code at our project page: https://sullivan07043.github.io/SCOPE/.

Routers built around a fixed list of models can be difficult to adapt when new models arrive or budgets change. SCOPE instead predicts the cost and performance of candidate models before making the routing decision.

Trained with reinforcement learning, SCOPE reasons from retrieved examples of how models behave on similar problems. This grounds its estimates in observed behavior rather than fixed model names and enables routing to previously unseen models. Explicit estimates of expense and accuracy also let the routing decision respond to a user’s current priorities, rather than embedding one fixed trade-off in the selector.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 25.7% when performance is prioritized, or cost reductions of up to 95.1% when efficiency is prioritized. These figures describe different operating priorities, rather than a single simultaneous outcome. The findings support routing as a controllable decision process in which estimated model behavior can guide both economical and accuracy-focused choices.
summary.tldr: SCOPE predicts model cost and accuracy from behavior on similar problems, enabling flexible routing that extends to unseen models.

title: Models Under SCOPE: Scalable and Controllable Routing via Pre-hoc Reasoning

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) empirically boosts generalization by seeking parameters that minimize the worst-case loss in a small neighborhood, yet existing theory explains its behavior under either Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition or upper bounded perturbation radius. We revisit SAM through the bilevel minimax problem $\min_{\theta}\max_{\|\Delta\|\le\rho}l(\theta+\Delta)$ and derive a $(\theta,\Delta)$ gradient flow ODE whose equilibria coincide with the problem’s optimality conditions. A Lyapunov argument-free of convexity assumptions, quantifies how the optimality gap depends on the radius $\rho$ and local curvature. Discretizing the flow yields a Multi-step SAM algorithm that recovers classical SAM as $\rho\to 0$. Moreover, our analysis and the resulting algorithm remain valid even for large $\rho$, providing guidance for aggressive neighborhood exploration. Experiments on synthetic objectives and CIFAR-10 validate the predicted gains from multiple inner updates, bridging the gap between SAM’s minimax intuition and its practical implementation.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization seeks model parameters whose loss remains low even under an adverse perturbation within a small neighborhood. Although it improves generalization empirically, existing explanations rely on a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition or an upper bound on perturbation radius. This paper revisits the underlying problem as a bilevel minimax optimization.

The authors derive a continuous-time gradient flow for the parameters and their perturbations. Its equilibria match the optimization problem’s optimality conditions. A Lyapunov analysis quantifies how the optimality gap depends on neighborhood radius and local curvature without requiring convexity. The analysis remains valid for large radii, extending the treatment to more aggressive neighborhood exploration.

Discretizing the flow produces Multi-step SAM, which recovers classical SAM as the radius approaches zero. Experiments on synthetic objectives and CIFAR-10 support predicted benefits from taking multiple inner updates. The contribution links the minimax formulation to a concrete algorithm and explains how additional perturbation updates can improve the practical realization of SAM’s underlying objective.
summary.tldr: A minimax gradient-flow analysis yields Multi-step SAM and explains benefits of multiple inner updates, including at large perturbation radii.

title: Understanding SAM through Minimax Perspective

abstract: We study in-context learning for nonparametric regression with $\alpha$-Hölder smooth regression functions, for some $\alpha>0$. We prove that, with $n$ in-context examples and $d$-dimensional regression covariates, a pretrained transformer with $\Theta(\log n)$ parameters and $\Omega(n^{2\alpha/(2\alpha+d)}\log^3 n)$ pretraining sequences can achieve the minimax optimal rate of convergence $O(n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d)})$ in mean squared error. Our result requires substantially fewer transformer parameters and pretraining sequences than previous results in the literature. This is achieved by showing that transformers are able to approximate local polynomial estimators efficiently by implementing a kernel-weighted polynomial basis and then running gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper asks how efficiently a pretrained transformer can learn a regression relationship from examples supplied in its context. The analysis concerns nonparametric regression functions with α-Hölder smoothness, where α is positive. Smoothness restricts how irregular the relationship can be, and the input dimension d also enters the statistical guarantee.

With n examples in context, the authors show that a transformer with Θ(log n) parameters can achieve mean squared error O(n^(-2α/(2α+d))). This is the minimax optimal convergence rate for the studied setting. Their result uses Ω(n^(2α/(2α+d)) log³ n) pretraining sequences and requires substantially fewer parameters and pretraining sequences than earlier theoretical results.

The construction works by efficiently approximating local polynomial estimators. The transformer implements a kernel-weighted polynomial basis and then performs gradient descent. This gives a concrete computational route from attention-based machinery to an optimal statistical estimator. The claim establishes that a suitably pretrained transformer can attain the rate under the stated smoothness setting; it does not assert that arbitrary transformers automatically do so.
summary.tldr: A theoretical transformer construction achieves minimax-optimal in-context regression with logarithmically many parameters under Hölder smoothness.

title: Efficient and Minimax Optimal In-context Nonparametric Regression with Transformers

abstract: Hallucination is a central limitation of large language models (LLMs), and substantial effort has been devoted to understanding and mitigating it. Towards this, Kalai and Vempala (STOC 2024) introduced a probabilistic framework formalizing calibration and hallucination, and showed that, with high probability, calibrated LLMs hallucinate roughly at the rate of the "missing mass", a measure of how incomplete the training data is relative to its source. This raises two fundamental questions: (i) what property of a calibrated LLM makes hallucinations unavoidable? and (ii) can hallucinations be avoided by giving up calibration? We answer these questions by introducing a simpler property we call innovation that measures the tendency of a model to produce outputs outside the training data. We show that innovation is implied by the condition for hallucination identified by Kalai and Vempala, and, further, that it is an almost characterization of hallucination: hallucination implies innovation, and conversely, innovation implies hallucination with high probability. We also provide lower bounds on the hallucination rate based on the "innovation rate", and by relating innovation rate back to missing mass, we obtain new hallucination rate lower bounds based on missing mass that extend the results of Kalai and Vempala.

paragraphs: A prior probabilistic account connects hallucination in calibrated language models to missing mass: the portion of the source distribution absent from training data. This paper asks what property underlies that connection and whether abandoning calibration would avoid the problem. It introduces innovation, a measure of how often a model produces outputs outside its training data.

Within the probabilistic framework, the authors show that the previously identified condition for hallucination implies innovation. They then establish an almost characterization: hallucination implies innovation, while innovation implies hallucination with high probability. The qualification matters because the converse is probabilistic; the result does not label every individual output absent from training data as a hallucination.

The paper derives lower bounds on hallucination rates from innovation rates. By connecting innovation back to missing mass, it also obtains new missing-mass-based lower bounds extending the earlier results. The contribution is to identify a simpler property through which to study unavoidable hallucination, shifting attention from calibration alone toward the model’s tendency to produce material beyond its observed training examples.
summary.tldr: In a probabilistic framework, producing outputs beyond training data almost characterizes hallucination and yields new lower bounds on its rate.

title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

abstract: Density-based anomaly detection methods often provide accurate and interpretable predictions but their performance can be severely degraded by the inherent noise of data, such as changes arising from environmental conditions during data collection or background noise. To deal with such noise, we present noise-robust density estimation (NRDE) for tabular data anomaly detection. We aim to estimate the density of pure data with the influence of noises isolated, which is a non-trivial task since the data-generating process is completely unknown. Specifically, NRDE learns a Jacobian-regularized normalizing flow to estimate the sources of data and categorizes sources into two groups, where one group generates pure data and the other generates noise. After generating pure data, we can use the density of such pure data to detect anomalies caused by the sources of pure data solely. Therefore, NRDE is robust to inherent noise. We provide theoretical results to support the effectiveness of NRDE and compare NRDE with $17$ baselines on $47$ benchmark datasets under different settings, including vanilla anomaly detection, anomaly detection with anomaly contamination, anomaly detection on noisy data, and transductive outlier detection.

paragraphs: Density-based anomaly detection identifies unusual data through its estimated probability density. Noise from measurement conditions or the surrounding environment can distort that estimate and degrade predictions. NRDE aims to isolate this nuisance variation so that anomaly decisions reflect the sources generating the underlying data.

The method learns a normalizing flow with Jacobian regularization to estimate the data’s sources, even though the generating process is unknown. It divides those sources into two groups: one responsible for pure data and another responsible for noise. It then generates pure data and uses its density to detect anomalies attributable to the pure-data sources.

This separation is the basis of the method’s claimed noise robustness, and the paper supplies theoretical results supporting its effectiveness. The evaluation compares NRDE with 17 baselines across 47 datasets, covering ordinary detection, anomaly contamination, noisy data, and transductive outlier detection. These settings examine the approach under several distinct detection conditions; the abstract establishes the evaluation’s breadth without specifying numerical comparative outcomes.
summary.tldr: NRDE separates estimated data and noise sources to base tabular anomaly detection on the density of underlying pure data.

title: Noise-Robust Density Estimation for Tabular Data Anomaly Detection

abstract: Agents that can reason and plan in the real world must be able to predict the consequences of their actions. World models possess this capability but require action annotations that can be complex to obtain at scale. Latent action models address this issue by learning an action space from videos alone. Our work studies the training of latent action world models on in-the-wild videos, expanding the scope of existing works that focus on simple robotics simulations, video games, or manipulation data. While diverse videos enable modeling richer actions, they introduce challenges of environmental noise and lack of a common embodiment across videos. To address these, we carefully study the design and evaluation of latent actions. We find that constrained continuous latent actions are better suited for complex in-the-wild videos, compared to vector quantization. For example, actions specific to in-the-wild videos such as humans entering the room, can be modeled and then transferred across videos. However, in the absence of a common embodiment, learned latent actions are localized in space, relative to the camera. Nonetheless, we are able to train a controller that maps known actions to latent ones, allowing us to use latent actions as a universal interface to solve planning tasks on par with action-conditioned baselines.

paragraphs: World models predict how actions change an environment, but collecting explicit action annotations can be difficult at scale. Latent action models learn an action representation from videos instead. This paper studies that approach on diverse in-the-wild videos, where environmental noise and the absence of a shared body or agent make action learning harder.

The authors examine how latent actions should be designed and evaluated. They find that constrained continuous representations suit these complex videos better than vector quantization. The findings show both the reach of video-only action learning and the camera-relative structure that emerges from heterogeneous visual experience.
summary.tldr: World models trained on diverse videos learn transferable latent actions that support competitive planning, though those actions remain camera-relative without shared embodiment.

title: Learning Latent Action World Models in the Wild

abstract: Error-correcting codes enable reliable communication, yet practical soft decoding remains challenging across code families and block lengths. We propose SB-ECC, a score-based decoder that casts decoding as continuous-time denoising. A neural denoiser defines a probability-flow ordinary differential equation (ODE) that iteratively updates the noisy channel observation toward a valid codeword, guided by parity constraints. The model is trained across noise levels without time/SNR conditioning, enabling inference without SNR estimation and supporting a direct latency–accuracy trade-off controlled by the ODE solver budget. We use the raw signed channel observation as input for learning a continuous denoising field. Across $42$ code/SNR settings, SB-ECC achieves the best BER in $39/42$ entries, with an average SNR gain of $0.17$ dB and a maximum gain of $0.46$ dB over the strongest competing baseline, we showed that swapping the solver from Euler to DPM preserves $-\ln(\mathrm{BER})$ while reducing end-to-end decoding time by $8.86%$ on average (up to $12.82%$).
